Behold the one who ascends the hall! Vertically pervasive and horizontally encompassing, like the belly of a horse or the womb of a donkey. When the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted, the ancient path is covered in moss.
There is no need to close the door to ward off guests; how many people are there who truly love leisure?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] took up his staff and said: "This staff has been stubborn for half its life; it will not tolerate being deceived.
When casually cast aside, the green mountains dare not be green, and the white clouds dare not be white. Having reached this day, it binds itself without a rope;

not even a single breath of energy can be used, yet it cannot avoid following along with the coarse woolen cloth. In autumn, one walks the path of withered leaves; in spring, one steps through the village of falling blossoms. And so—"
Passing through in this manner. Nevertheless, though it be so, the land is vast and people are few.
[Ascending the hall: The mountain trees cast deep shadows; the cold flowers, some pale, some deep in hue. The cranes resent the clouds in their nests; the monkeys wail as they hang by the moon.
A master hand like Wang Wei could not paint this. [Patting his knee, he says: Shen Guang sought peace of mind in vain.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] held up his staff. "Throughout immeasurable kalpas, there have been the seven topsy-turvy turns and eight inversions.
(He struck it down and said: "Shatter empty space! (He threw down the staff. "The whole body enters the weeds.
Ascending the hall, he thanked West Hall Master Aiyun for visiting him. He cited the verse by Zen Master Fuyan Zhi: "Mount Fuyan..."
The clouds above drift and unfurl, yielding to morning and evening. Suddenly they fall upon the level ground; when a guest arrives, it is difficult to find the gate. [The Master] picks up the theme:
"Although at Fuyan the seal is extremely tight, alas, where there are no traces, there are still traces.
Folong, however, is not like this. On Folong Mountain, the clouds are one piece, then three or four pieces. When suddenly a guest pushes open the door, they scatter and then unfold again.
A scroll: where there are traces, yet no traces remain; the whole body is eyes. Seeking it is hard to see, yet seeking it one finds it.
Leaves fall from the thousand forests; light floats upon the azure peaks.
Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace: At Fulong’s opening of the furnace, cold ashes and dead embers—when one stirs them up into a spark, it is a transgression that fills the heavens.
It makes even the Broken Oven’s Fall at Mount Song laugh to his heart's content.
Yungfeng Shanguan raised this up, saying: "Thirteen provinces and seventy monks—donkey jaws and horse chins, detested by all.
Had you from various quarters possessed the hands of a fisherman, today there would have been no opportunity to reach Jingyin. This was his late master from Mount Jing.
Master Fojian held up [the case] and said: "The Great Master Ying'an spoke quite a bit; it is a pity his tongue was too long.
Jingshan is not like this: 'Five hundred and more monks from eighty prefectures, with tattered, ragged robes and wrinkled faces.'"
"There are those in all directions who possess the Way yet are unwilling to learn; they would rather join this mountain monk in dragging logs. He then remarked:
"Our late Master of Jingshan spoke quite a lot, yet it is a pity his tongue was too short. Although Fulong’s tongue has no bone, he merely continues the 'dog's tail' after the 'fox fur.
Try offering a turning word; thirty-odd monks have eyes like eyebrows, deep within the white clouds."
They gather their heads in play; they burn dry firewood to roast mountain yams. They drag wood and haul baskets, yet remain entirely unaware.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The days grow longer on the winter solstice. (Holding up his whisk, he said: "How long is this? Space itself as a measuring rod cannot measure it.
It fits perfectly within the eye of a gnat. It fits perfectly. It dazzles the divine light; those who encounter it while lost find their way."
Polishing.

Ascending the hall to express gratitude for the Head Seat’s holding of the whisk and the administrative officers’ offering of a vegetarian feast. The Eye of the Human and Heavenly Eyes, the Head Seat within the Hall:

with a single phrase that cuts off the stream, all manifold distinctions lose their illumination. How does this compare to the chestnut thorn and the iron-sour stuffing? Arranged beyond the norm—this is the Eye.
First, wrap it up. It requires all of you to block off the faculty of hearing and shut your throats tight. If you can hear this, you will be able to bite through it.
Once you have bitten through it, what then? Thirty strokes of the black staff—do not say I did not warn you.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I too have come here to dwell upon the mountain without end. Busily, my karmic consciousness has never been at rest.
When the white clouds are swept away, one arrives at the withered leaves; fearing they might obstruct the passage of woodcutters coming and going. The cold pines rustle, the secluded birds warble.
Once the household goods are fully distributed, who would say the sounds are barbarian?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Throughout my life I have spoken great falsehoods; now I am receiving the retribution of the living hell.
This boneless tongue of mine has been rotting at its very root for several days. Is there anyone among you who can skillfully provide the medicine to save it?
(He then sticks out his tongue and says: Ah, Grandpa!"

Ascending the hall: Ancient cypresses sighing in the wind, cold crows deploying in formation—this does not fall within the realm of seeing or hearing; how many have mistaken it? If one does not mistake it:
the Daoist raises his fists, and the *kalyāṇamitra* bows in greeting.
Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday: Mount Zhurong, ten-thousand-year-old pines, Green shade enshrouding cranes, auspicious mists coiling like dragons.
These are offered as a tribute to the Sage and Enlightened Son of Heaven; Branch by branch, leaf by leaf, they are nourished by the spring breeze.
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: For six years he was frozen in snow yet did not die; upon seeing the morning star, he spoke of his awakening.
He traded his deerskin robe and walked out of the mountains—look at that man, his face is as stubborn as iron! Tell me, can he still be cured?
(Shaking his head, he says: Difficult, difficult!

On account of a certain matter, he ascended the hall and said: "Cooking rice where there is no grain; facing toward where there is no smoke or fire. Severing meaning and forgetting gratitude; violating causes and turning one's back on results.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time were like this; the patriarchs of successive generations were like this; the old, frozen masses of the world were like this;
and the entire assembly at Fulong was like this. Now tell me: is there any distinction of superior or inferior among them? (Liang)
Jiuyun said: "For now, let us share the same bed and hearth during these difficult times; we must know that at year's end, each shall have their own door.
In this mountain hamlet, farmers plow and woodcutters toil; the gate is closed by green creepers. When one is wealthy and proud, such moments are rare; when one is poor, there is much joy.

The wife shakes the loom with a rhythmic *zha-zha*, and the children play with their mouths making *guo-guo* sounds. The sound of the mountain stream blends with the pine wind in a harmonious cadence. (He strikes the meditation seat and says: "How does this compare?"
Song of the East Mountain Tile Drum.
Spreading a new mat upon the hall. Entering a wild field without picking; grasping whatever weed comes to hand. Weaving across the earth and threading through the heavens.
Every single thing is wondrous; when everything is forged into one, the full power is revealed. Blue-eyed and yellow-headed alike are brought low. Have you not seen?
The practitioner Changqing Leng sat until his meditation cushions were worn through—one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
(He slaps his knee and says: How much of this family tradition’s disarray do you know?
Master Xueya of Shanlu, Xie Nanlu, ascends the hall: Mountain tresses, winds rushing, cause the pine-crests to fall; Cold hearths hold smoke, for midday has not yet come for the meal.
The yam tubs simmer with fragrance but cannot reach full ripeness; This old monk endures the cold as he gathers withered wood.
To see this is to engage in habitual activity; it is an extraordinary arrangement. Lanzan’s poverty was not yet exhausted; his life was buried in dung-fire.
Ascending the hall on the day of the Start of Spring (he lifts up his staff): "On this spring day, they strike the spring ox; with one blow, it is shattered into a hundred fragments.
The stone maiden of Huangmei secretly startles her womb, giving birth to a single piece of nameless matter. He asks the Four Sages: the Four Sages do not know. He asks the Six Mundane Beings:
the Six Beings do not understand. (He throws down the staff: Scattered before the wind, it becomes the spring of ten thousand households—more humble than yellow gold.
Gold is as precious as dust.
On the first day of the year, he ascended the hall: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all dust motes. An old woman with a purple silk skirt tied at her waist;
a young son holding a red silk fan in his hand. At Nan’ao and Dongcun, at Zhang’s shop and Li’s store, everyone bows and offers New Year greetings."
The spring breeze fills his face; in a state of joyful spirit, he unconsciously raises his voice, startling the falling plum blossoms—here one, there two, three, four.

On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, he ascends the hall: "The Great Way has no fixed direction; the Supreme Honored One has no fixed station. Sages are wise and luminous; they hang their robes and rule."
Governance! May the era of Yao’s wind and Shun’s sun endure for ten thousand years. Throughout the world, there is no one who does not look up to Heaven with gratitude.
This is the Dharma Hall address offered to thank the new and former Assistant Abbots, the Chief Administrator, and those who have provided the annual winter retreat meals.
Selling ginger at a high price, yet snow-white pearls fill the bed. Though my pure poverty pierces to the very bone, my wealth dares to rival that of the King. It is truly so.
Dicing my own body for food and soaking my blood for drink, I offer these with all my heart, yet it is still not equal [to your merit].
If even this is not sufficient, I shall till the green fields amidst the mist and let the withered flute send off the slanting sun.
Ascending the hall for the Lantern Festival: (He raises his whisk. This one lamp—where does it arise? It leaves no trace and is beyond conjecture.
The Three Worthies and Ten Sages see it as if they were blind; the "mustard-seed dogs" and "mud-pigs" emit light that shakes the earth.
(He blows on the whisk and says: Everyone, blow it out and walk in the dark. Dīpaṃkara Buddha is right under your feet.
Offering incense on the anniversary of Baizhang Huashang’s passing: He wandered aimlessly, greedily watching wild ducks; He violated the monastic groves and ought to recite the *Qinggui*.
Having pinched his nose until it bled, he finally knew shame; I burn this stick of maple incense to make an offering to him.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Adding gold to the yellow only serves to defame its lack of fragrance. Bodhidharma did not understand; he traveled through Wei and sojourned in Liang.

Yet there were even those who failed to recognize good from evil. Standing waist-deep in snow, he lived on alms in a remote village. (He pats his knee and says: "Hearing the cry of the gibbon at Mount Wu, one’s heart breaks in vain."

Ascending the hall: Flowers restrain the cold with their crimson leaves; grass rivals the misty peaks with its emerald hue. Though many pigments are exhausted, they cannot capture it when one attempts to paint it.
Drenched by smoke and rain, it wets the balustrades. O Zen practitioners: I have nothing hidden from you.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "One is direct; two is circuitous. Eyebrows and eyelashes; from the edge of the earth to the ends of the sky. Yunmen’s 'moldy bread' and Zhaozhou’s 'tea.
Huichong’s wild geese among reeds and Zhaochang’s flowers. If you understand, it is a single crane in the autumn Milky Way;
if you do not understand, it is a thousand households with their pestles at night."

An occasion for ascending the hall due to snow: Withered trees are sprinkled with jade flowers; the empty courtyard is sealed with jade steps. Shaoshi [Shenguang] needlessly sought peace of mind; Shen Guang vainly broke his arm.
Not falling into the realm of uniformity through merit—(beating his knee and saying)—With whom can one lean upon the balustrade?
The Buddha Ascends the Hall on the Occasion of His Nirvana: For forty-nine years, he deceived the Hu and mocked the Han. He entered nirvana swiftly, saving only one... (text fragmentary).
[He] gazes intently at his purple-golden body. (Patting his knee, he says: "It soils one's natural eyes. Entering the hall:
I have a device that reaches the utmost subtlety: when hungry, eat; when cold, put on clothes. I have a phrase that encompasses all time:
a dog barks at a withered stump; a cat catches a mouse. Tell me, is this the Buddha-dharma?
"Is it conventional truth? (After a long silence, he said: Go ask the stone pagoda in front of the gate.
Bimiō held up his staff; Jūchi raised a finger. A false dharma is difficult to support. How can one attain what is correct?
This mountain monk has pondered this in vain, and could do nothing but swallow my voice and drink my breath. Why? "To devote oneself to heterodox doctrines—this is harmful indeed."

Ascending the hall. The assembly has finished their inquiries; the attendant has finished burning incense. (Holding up the staff, he says: "Next, it is the turn of the Master of the Staff to proclaim the essential Dharma.
(He draws a single line and says: "Too much talent—this is a man born with a brush. (He strikes the floor once and says: "Too many words—this is a man born with a mouth.
(He leans the staff against the wall and says: "Let the white mold grow upon it as it hangs on the wall."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] held up the staff and said: "Face-to-face, seizing the opportunity: surging eastward, submerging westward.
A precipice on level ground; muddying the waters amidst clarity. It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. (He threw the staff down and said: "Cast away into the realm of non-arising."

Ascending the hall on Qingming: Flowers and brocade, butterflies fluttering red; Willow mist, orioles weaving the dawn. Never stirring a single thread of mechanism, They seize all the subtle artistry of spring.
The mystery within mysteries, the wondrous within wonders— The Buddhas of the three ages cannot see through them;
The patriarchs of successive generations cannot exhaust them. If one were to exhaust them: On Cold Food and Qingming, every household performs the ancestral rites.
Recorded by the attendant Liao-shun from the *Fahua Yulu*.
On the ninth day of the sixth month in the Gengshen year of the Jingding era, the Master entered the monastery.
Three gates. A road traverses clear waves; mountains stretch across emerald cliffs. The doors of the pavilion stand open. (Snaps fingers: Enter here. The Buddha Hall.
Thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. A horse’s jaw and a donkey’s chin—passing through the net that covers the heavens. New Dharma.
Flowers! Why have you pierced my brain and thrust me into this lacquer basin? (Inserting incense, he says: The fault lies with you; the calamity reaches me, the local deity.
You are upright and wise, elegant and refined; you steadfastly protect the city of the Dharma and have recorded meritorious achievements for a thousand years.
General Li—your reputation is well-established. (The Local Deity is Li the Observer.)
The Patriarch’s Hall. Before Vulture Peak, hot blood spurts forth; at the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment, there is a bottomless pit.
For one who has lost their footing, it matters not whether it was first or last. How can this deluded old man compare to my own mad wind? (Chijue, the founder, occupies the room.
[Holding up the staff, he says: Wisdom merges with principle; spirit meets with the environment. He shatters the couch of Vimalakīrti and cuts through the realm of Vairocana.
The topknot. Blue eyes and a yellow head; look closely (Zhuzhu says: "Zhuozhuang" [a staff]). All shattered! The Dharma seat.

The crown of the head. The pivot of the mechanism. The seat of the emptiness of dharmas. To know without engaging thought; to arrive without moving a step. (He shouts: To enter the weeds for no reason.

The official summons: borrowing the ancestral "Imperial Net" silk, he lowers his line for the immortal tortoise of the noble youth. He twists the nose of the patch-robed monk and provokes a laugh from all quarters.
Whether the *kūn* fish transforms into a soaring *péng* bird remains entirely unknown; pushing back the sail, he faces the moon, sharing it in equal halves.
I now request the Rector to raise the sails and strike the oars.

This official letter contains the very entrails of Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan, and the very marrow of Su Shi and Huang Tingjian. Once the Zen robes are donned, a fragrant breeze pervades the earth, and the seventy-two peaks increase in their refined spirit.
A Disentanglement from the Rivers and Lakes. Sharing a meal with those of the rivers and lakes—why must one incite strife? To spit blood at others first defiles one's own mouth;
thus, a grievance so deep that heaven cannot cover it is formed, every word of which is nothing but an insult.
Preface to the Mountain Gate: A three-hundred-jin iron cangue has lain for years without anyone to bear it; cast aside at the foot of the wall, it can only wait for the arrival of its accuser.
The confession is clear and cannot be overturned; though one’s old shoulders lack strength, they must still carry it.
I pray that you may observe these auspicious signs and fragrances. May you serve as a pillar and foundation for the imperial house, widely disseminating the virtues of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou;

may you act as a golden fortress for the Buddha-dharma, perpetually upholding the spirit of Pei Xiu and Li Yuan. May your longevity be as enduring as pine and cypress, and your blessings as profound as the rivers and seas.
The General Outline: Not doing a single thing; the phoenix entangled in a golden net. All mechanisms of activity stilled and pared away; the dragon terrified in the azure pool.
If one goes thus, the teaching style of Shaoshi’s Gate is like withered weeds. Opening up the path, he condescends to the exigencies of the times.

Borrowing the drum of Mount Dong, he plays to the delight of the assembly. He sets all people ablaze with fervor—then, with a laugh, he departs. (He takes up the staff, holds it crosswise, and makes a gesture.)
(The gesture of striking the long drum: "Beng-ba-la-za. Do you hear it? A newly translated melody, a style of local dialect beyond compare.
Its meaning flows afar like a stream; its sound arrests the cold of the vast clouds. Those on Mount Dòuzi do not understand it. (Leaning on his staff:
"The moon shifts, casting its reflection upon the balustrade."

Citing the public case of Prime Minister Pei, who held up a Buddha statue and requested Huangbo to name it. (He picks it up and says: Prime Minister Pei possessed a dignified and extraordinary countenance;
his body was adorned with a hundred blessings, manifesting the reality-body in its perfection, yet he was unaware of being defiled.
Old Huangbo stubbornly took five colors to embroider the great void. Before those with clear eyes, this does not even merit a laugh. Why? Because that house already possesses its own gold.
Golden bones, needing no sandalwood to enter the fine carvings.
For the Grand Preceptor, Duke Zhenghui of Zhou, and the Lady of Zhou, ascending the hall: coming from a state of noble dignity, the retribution-land is without error.
With jade pendants in the courtyards and brocade upon the pavilions—how can these compare to listening to the Lotus Sūtra at Vulture Peak? A steady, secure carriage.

Riding the white ox-cart on the fifteenth day, he took his leave of the two classes of attendants and ascended the hall. An old man dwelling in the mountains, he possesses no skillful means whatsoever; he bows low for guests and joins his palms upon meeting monks.

Although he thus conforms to the requirements of the times, it does not hinder his ability to gather and release according to the occasion. Why is this? Because the Kun-fish has undergone its transformation.
The wings of the Peng-bird are fully spread; with a single strike against the *fú* tree, it soars into the azure heavens.
For the practitioner, he establishes the standard of inquiry; Old Lu, for no reason, casts down the firewood. From the head of the mortar, the ancient rhombus-flower is ground out.
A foul reputation has remained in disarray for a thousand years. Who among those who raise children knows how to manage the household?

Entering the city, he returns to the hall; for three months of the dog days, he wanders among men. The heat is so stifling that sweat falls like rain; there is no time for rest, nor any place to lodge.
(He raises his staff. This staff—its back is cast of solid iron. Amidst the vast swirl of dust, it can discern the master. Returning, it rests its shadow deep within the emerald peaks;

it brushes the moon and robes itself in the clouds. (He strikes once with the staff and says: *Note: The term "zhuzhangzi" (拄杖子) refers to the Zen master’s staff, often personified as a spiritual companion or a manifestation of the Buddha-nature.*
Severing the paths of a thousand differences. Entering the hall:
"The five days since the summer retreat has ended—what of the water buffalo? To the east of the stream and the west of the stream; to the south of the mountain and the north of the mountain.
The white artemisia is fragrant and fine; the green grasses cast thick shadows. Gathering and releasing without restraint, going and staying according to one's own ease. Yet, alas—"
The nose-rope is in the mountain monk’s hand. If you wish to know how to reach home with steady steps, where one hides the body without leaving a trace—listen:
the sound of a few pipes from a Qiang flute as the misty village darkens; a monkey clings to a cold branch as the moon shines bright.
Nevertheless, the seventy-two peaks of Mount Dongting still lie between us.

The eighth month is autumn. Where is it hot? When one steps out the gate, the wild grasses are withered and scattered; when one sits facing the wall, the cold crickets chirp with piercing lamentation.

If a patch-robed monk can accommodate Mount Sumeru within his eyes and contain the four great oceans within his ears, then sound and form are pure and true, yet he has only attained a single fragment.
But tell me, what is the phrase for "covering sound and riding over form"? (After a long silence, he says: "People."
Leaning against the painted pavilion, the river moon is cold; the jade flute plays its three strains as the azure clouds turn autumnal.
On the Double Ninth, he ascends the hall for this occasion: chrysanthemums spread their yellow across the fence, and dogwood spews forth its fragrance.

Yet even if one were to follow the error of Tao Yuanming and indulge in the pleasures of the Double Ninth, how could that compare to the patch-robed monk in the forest, who knows neither honor nor disgrace and has nothing to ponder, contently devouring his fill from the fragrant storehouse?
A meal. Reclining high upon an ancient Zen seat, both Buddha and Mara have had their traces swept away; there is no path for offering flowers, and the birds flutter in vain.
On the fifth day of the tenth month, incense is offered on the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing. This "special transmission outside the teachings" has no handle at all.

He met the Second Patriarch and mistakenly pointed to the "original mind"; he shattered the six schools and knocked out the teeth right in front of his gate. His offenses fill the heavens, leaving him no place to hide.
Dizang: "The little monk from the *Lotus Sūtra* was unable to cut the grass at its roots; why then does he burn incense and pay obeisance?
Have you not heard it said: 'In the application of ritual, harmony is prized'?"
Xie Sanfeng, Chief Seat of the West Hall, ascends the hall: The lakes and mountains are verdant and vast; the lake waters stretch boundlessly. Crimson maples scatter like brocade;
golden oranges spread a carpet of yellow. For the clear-eyed monk, the sacred and the profane shift with every circumstance; there is nowhere to find his traces or his concealment.
Although it may suffice to deceive just one person, such as the Lotus Sutra, if you encounter those who truly belong within the house, there is no need to bring it out.
But who, pray tell, is the one within the house? (Looking around, he says: Listen!
A letter from the late Master Bieshan of Tiantong has arrived. Entering the hall: On the peak of Mount Taibai, I employ a modest artifice; profound silence...

The thunder and lightning strike, yet people fear them not; even rubble and debris are transformed into the palaces of Śakra and Brahmā. The ancient Buddha-dharma style is once again vigorously revitalized.
Not falling into the trap of merit or achievement, one plays at ease. When the golden-maned lion suddenly turns its body, the grasses, trees, insects, and moths all shed tears.
To shed tears is certainly not a matter of doubt, but where do you see Elder Brother Tiandong? (After a long silence, he says: The bright sun shines resplendently.
"O Celestial One! A blind man groping on the ground. [He] ascends the hall.
"At the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment, this small grove of trees is surrounded by sandalwood. The lion roars;

the moon through the ivy fills the four windows, and clouds fill ten thousand valleys. All that is seen is a single piece of the Patriarch’s mind. (He lets out a shout: "Those with no sinews in their eyes for a lifetime..."
Poverty. Entering the hall for discourse: The mountain folk are desolate, yet they are as busy as if in a fire. They reap the thatch while the sun is bright; they gather the oranges amidst the frost.
The mountain monk reflects in his cold solitude: they have utterly squandered their private wealth. Day after day the sun rises in the east; day after day the sun sets in the west.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "There is a thing, black as lacquer, constantly entering and exiting through the gate of the face. It rides upon sound and covers over form; it is a perilous precipice within the subtle and secret.
When used perversely, it is a subtle and secret mystery within the perilous precipice. To the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the further they distance themselves, the closer it becomes."
The white ox and the cat—having gained them, they lose them again. The *Lotus Sūtra* does not spare its own eyebrows.
(Holding up the staff) For your sake, I have brought this out into the open. It is lively and agile; it is shimmering and rugged.
You thought it was the "tortoise-nosed snake" of the South Mountain, but it is actually the *zhilu* staff of Tiantai. (Casting down the staff, he says) Not worth a single coin.
Ascending the hall while ill: "Prolonged illness has left my legs weak; like an infant learning to take steps, I have lost all the mechanisms before my eyes.
Though I can discern the Master amidst the dust—nose straight, eyes askance, skin pierced through to the bone—neither donkey nor horse am I.
(He pats his knee once and says: "For now, there is no place for a brushstroke. (After a long silence, he says: "What a pity for the monks Wuzhao and Wu Daozi!"

Rising from Illness: A Hall Discourse to Thank Former and Current Officials. (Holding up the staff) This illness that Caoshan could not consolidate was difficult even for the physician Lu to apply his skillful artistry.
Since I emerged from my mother’s womb, I have experienced all four hundred and four ailments;
even worldly physicians have stood with hands folded in helplessness. Suddenly, amidst the cessation of thought and the stilling of conditions, I tore asunder the myriad errors.

He shattered all states of existence and beheld the True Person of No-Station. Facing him, he offered a deep greeting, saying, "I am glad to hear that lately, in all matters great and small, your comings and goings have been appropriate.
Upon hearing these words, it was as if he had obtained a secret manual from behind the elbow or a wondrous elixir that penetrates the spirit.
Thus, regarding the body and mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, whether hunger or satiety, toil or pestilence, wind, cold, heat, or dampness—all such things [were transcended].
"Illness. (Zhuo strikes the meditation staff once and says: "It does not take more than one dose; the entire body becomes cool and refreshed.
Do you all wish to reach the land of peace and happiness together? (He leans on the staff. "Since they have no sores themselves, do not wound them.
Entering the hall for the inauguration of the Tianji Festival: (He holds up the staff. "This staff transforms into a messenger with a direct tally, pervading everywhere..."
He traveled through the heavens and visited the Southern Peak, Wutai, Emei, Tante, Luofu, India, and China. As he proceeded, he announced in succession:
"The Yellow River clears once every three thousand years; a Sage appears once every five hundred generations. Now is precisely that time.
Having delivered this proclamation, he hurried back to the foot of Mount Juecheng. He gathered the assembly of humans and devas, beat the drum, ascended the hall, and [delivered] the third [sermon].
"Long live the Emperor! Since Fahua had exerted himself so diligently, [Zhaozhou] comforted him, saying, "You have truly fatigued your spirit and vision.

Upon hearing these words, he returned to his original form, leaned against the monk’s staff (the *zhuzhang*), and withdrew into the corner of the meditation seat to let his body and mind rest, immersing himself in the sacred transformation.
Why is this? When Yao and Shun sat with their robes hanging down, the world was well-governed; what need was there for the wooden clapper to warn the Chinese and the barbarians?

The Buddha ascends the hall after attaining the Way. He cast aside the sovereign rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King; whether noble or ignoble, what use is there in contending over such idle vexations amidst the deep snow of hunger and cold?
Seeing the morning star, he was left with no handle to grasp—yet he further says that all sentient beings throughout the great earth have attained perfect enlightenment.
*Hūṃ, hūṃ!* Even now, has the staff not yet been broken?

The Dharma Hall Master Xie Yingzang (a native of Mianzhou) arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "Mount Dakang and Mount Yangfu collide head-to-head and strike forehead-to-forehead, speaking their local dialects together.
Among them, no one understands the 'cutting' [phonetic] characters. The entire Great Canon has been translated twice over from the Hu-language into Fan;
tell me, what kind of characters are these? You must not say *bōluóniáng*. Now listen to the heated words of the people from Puhuxun Village."
Busy! Cutting rushes and hauling firewood to ascend the hall. (Holding up the whisk) The path of ultimate mystery at the tips of the hundred grasses; leaning over the hitching post of entanglements;
pressing through the phrase of the perilous cliff. With rotten wood, one cannot distinguish light from heavy. The sickle for cutting rushes does not reveal its sharp edge. Furthermore—
Consciousness plays tricks with the head of the Patriarch; Old Lu still does not know how to read characters. (He strikes the whisk. With a single pivot, he turns the mechanism;
releasing and gathering it at will. Fortunately, Tiantai was able to pick this up. (With the whisk, he blows once and says:
Spreading fire and flying stars—there is no place for you to lodge, no place for you to sit.
Ascending the hall: The western wind clusters the flower-ripples; Lake Tai freezes to its very bottom. Coldly reflecting in a jade mirror, it is pure—a single seamless expanse.
Face and features are distinct; the eyes are steady and alert. Do not fall into empty stillness, for that would split you into ten thousand errors.
(Patting his knee, he says: "A lacquer bucket! A lacquer bucket!"
On account of the snow, he ascended the hall. At the gate of Mount Ao, beneath the courtyard of Shaolin, arm-blood splashed toward heaven;

the demon of sleep retreated from its quarters, and the mind became like a blank wall. A mangy horse tied to a jeweled post—this flowed forth from his breast. "A single bubble arises in the vast ocean" (he raised his staff).
"The staff cannot restrain its impatience" (he struck once with the staff). To patch the nose and heal the scars, to strike fragment by fragment.
[He] struck [him]. Then he slowly said to him: "The Master has a great deal of snow ahead. Ascending the hall on New Year’s Day:
The plum blossoms open in brilliant splendor; Their petals fall thickly, blurring the falling snow. Adorning the countenance of early spring, They celebrate the festival of the New Year.

The ancestral style of Shaoshi is fully revealed; It is laughable that Shen Guang did not perceive it. — Bai [Zhang] (Note: The final character "瞥" is likely a scribal error for "瞥" or "瞥見," meaning "to catch sight of" or "to perceive.")
Breaking off one arm—there is a grievance difficult to extend. Without cause, this staff speaks again.
(He strikes the ground once with the staff. "Alala! Alala!
Entering the hall on the occasion of the Tianji Festival: (He takes up the staff) "The Son of Heaven mounts the Flying Dragon; peace prevails throughout the realm."
Under the sun of Shun and the breeze of Yao, this rustic of the forest seeks to repay his debt of gratitude. (He throws down the staff. Relying solely upon this staff, he transmits the Dharma;
even as he lies amidst the clouds, he cannot escape the reach of the Supreme Transformation.

The Head Seat and the Administrative Monk (Jiansi) of Xie [Temple] ascend the hall. The "thorny chestnut" of Yangqi and the "cooling tree" of Linji—this handleless spade is precisely ready for planting and nurturing.
Though the teeth on the wooden board have grown with hair, it does not hinder swallowing or spitting out. One draws three, two adds four;
the limping Yunmen strides alone through heaven and earth. Blinding the eyes of men and gods, he distinguishes the black from the white.
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: In the human world, ten-thousand bushels of golden lotuses compete for display during this auspicious Lantern Festival.
But the Dharma Flower (Lotus Sūtra) is utterly impoverished; rather than competing for excellence, it competes for inferiority. Within the room is a single lamp, its brilliant heart-flower blooming.
This light of the non-night illuminates past and present. To see it clearly is to add more grit to one’s eyes.
The seventeenth day of the first month: offering incense for the anniversary of Baizhang’s passing. Stepping across Mazu’s gate, one immediately commits an offense as vast as the heavens.
A shout deafens the ears; a grip breaks the nose. Letting loose the great and heroic tiger, its claws and fangs are briefly revealed.
Shedding Baizhang’s wild fox skin, one is not ignorant of cause and effect. To speak of a thread of mindfulness is, in the original text, groundless. Not only does it deceive others...
Self-deception. Ascending the hall:
Frost has broken the withered plum; two or three branches droop low. Fragrance passes over the wild bridge; shadows stretch across the thatched cottage.
The practitioner’s sense of smell is forgotten; though having eyes, they are as if blind. Not being obstructed by these things, one may pity those who hide their bodies within a ghost cave.
"Call him up! A snowball strikes a snowball! Entering the city, he returns to the hall.
(Holding up his staff) Grasping the staff, he emerges from the mists; the path through the red dust is far removed.

Golden tassels hang like willow threads; cold jade dots the plum blossoms. At every glance, the myriad forms are distinguished; at the moment of action, ten thousand errors are rent asunder. Is it not so?
I see it. Upādhyāya Fu of Taiyuan blows the painted horn from the top of the tower; he has utterly exhausted his entire life’s work. (He strikes the staff once.
Alive, he is buried deep in a pit—Shexun Duwen, along with the guest Xitang.
Thunder rolls and wind whirls, shaking heaven and overturning earth; with one extended arm of wrath.
Assisting those who are leaning toward ruin, he listens to the raw ginger growing in the ancient cave, which causes its price to double. He repairs the dilapidated bricks of Yangqi’s ruined house;
thus, at Fahua, one wins the luxury of sleeping until the sun is high. When the clear dream awakens within the ivy-covered window, he leads his guests to walk through the pine gate.
On this spring day, long and filled with the clamor of birds—(he strikes the meditation seat once)—I travel through the wild weeds, while you enter deep into the village.

Ascending the hall for the *nirvāṇa* ceremony, he thanked his guests for visiting him. He displayed his inner coffin, revealing his two crossed feet. Behold them clearly: they are the color of purple-polished gold.

His face is covered in dust; his entire body is bound in fetters. The *Lotus Sūtra* does not know how to conceal such things; he has been coldly subjected to the ridicule of his guests and friends. He has now exposed everything with full sincerity:
the secluded valley returns to spring, mountain birds cry out in plaintive sorrow and flowers weep tears. Layer upon layer, the petals part to reveal the heart of *nirvāṇa*.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] took up the staff. (He struck once to the left. "The heavens rotate to the left. (He struck once to the right. "The earth revolves to the right. (He struck in the center, saying:
"The primordial pivot of the thousand sages is brilliant on all eight sides. Yet for us patch-robed monks, our mouths are usually dripping with water.
When we encounter a single mechanism or a single scene and cannot shake it off, glue forms in our mouths and stagnation gathers in our bellies."

Feverish and distressed, Fahua leans over the bed of moxibustion scars. (He strikes the table once. To the added pain of needle and cupping, he waits for you to recover and rise, then slowly says to him:
"Your home is on Mount Min and Mount E; the journey back is somewhat long."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If we discuss this matter, it is like being aboard a dilapidated and leaking boat crossing Lake Tai.
Suddenly, a black wind arises and lashes out; great waves roll like snow, and white surf floods the heavens.

Oars and rudders vanish, and masts and sails are cast down. At such a moment, one’s life hangs by a thread. Whatever has been learned, remembered, or expounded from the past—ten thousand mechanisms and myriad..."
A transformation! A single point cannot be grasped; you have no choice but to move forward and each seek your own way of survival.
Neither the great matter nor the small matters can be accomplished for you. You, this entire band of men—seeing such a state of affairs as this, you still do not realize it.
Coming here now, with brows knit and eyes glaring—what kind of bowl are you looking for? (He drags his staff and descends from the seat;
the assembly disperses all at once. He then calls to the attendant: Attendant, take up the staff. [The Master] ascends the hall: "A hundred birds sing in the spring breeze;
in every village, flowers and willows bloom of their own accord. Revealing the mechanism before one's very eyes, all people throughout the great earth—"

Knowing there is existence, one follows sound and pursues form, living trapped within a heavy siege. Riding upon form and mounted on sound, one instead creates a nest of habitual patterns. (Striking the gavel, he says:
When the sturdy barrier is shattered, the seas and mountains sink level. The mountain birds sing of their own accord and the flowers smile of their own accord;
in the end, not a single point concerns the mind.
Xie Daojiu ascends the hall to pay respects to his old acquaintances: My home dwells in a hollow among the clouds; thatch covers my head.
My humble door has no lock—whom can it possibly knock? All sounds have subsided; birds sing in the deep valley. A thousand forests are hushed; the moon hangs from the cold branches.
At the wind-swept eaves, a solitary man seeks lodging. He sleeps until dawn, his limbs entwined. If you wish to ask for the ultimate truth within this, look at the bedside.
A wooden pillow, its center hollowed out by the *gé-tǎn* (coarse hempen cloth).

It covers the head of the monk ascending the hall; it is a wondrous carving of the tip of the nose. With skillful application of the chisel and adze, it has been brought to cover the heads of the thousand sages.
Dense and continuous, without any leakage; not refusing to mix earth with lime, it completes the cowshed and the horse stall.
Stable. He simply seeks to be one who is ungrateful, eating and sleeping, turning night into day.

He even mocks the Venerable Xié and the Practitioner Líng for being "not clever enough"—Xié never letting his side touch the mat, sitting until his meditation cushions were worn through, following like a donkey behind a horse;
yet to this day, they spread their family's disgrace across the lakes and seas.
Offering incense on the anniversary of the passing of Master Fojian: A nest of venomous bees, a following of evil forms. If the staff does not reach the heart, one dies;

if the shout does not reach the ear, one goes deaf. One must turn the pivot of the profound at the point where the mechanism revolves, and lose one's private attachments amidst the sound of a small jade bell.
Resentment is endless, hatred is endless; though one has a mouth, it cannot clear the matter. Once a year, once a year—just listen to the falling petals.
Crying birds lament the spring breeze.
Entering the hall: He pulls back the twelve hours and does not confront the various sensory objects. Satiated by the meal of *ra* and *ha*, he strolls leisurely with his lean staff.
Three form a cluster; four make a troop. Toward the cloud-clefts and winding ravines, they gather ferns and mushrooms to brew tea, and shred bamboo shoots and celery for sashimi.
Maitreya does not know; Śākyamuni does not understand. They are merely caught by the spring breeze piercing their subtle mechanisms.
In the high forests, at the break of dawn, the orioles sing in fragments. Hearing sounds with one’s eyes—stay outside the gate for now.

The three attendants of the Dharma Hall arrived; the Master ascended the hall. He gazed at the rhinoceros, called for Xiaoyu, and remarked: "A singular air of distinction, yet ten parts of worldly vulgarity.
The diligent man from Ba suffers a malady that has reached the vital organs; Old Yanguan’s laughter harbors the poison of a venomous bird.
Flowers cluster, brocades cluster—Old Yunfeng once raised his eyes in recognition. I come from amidst mountains and waters, and I say of myself..."
"Looking at it while alive is never enough; looking is never enough. In the blink of an eye, the clouds return to the secluded valley.
Ascending the hall [he said]: "High? Not high—just a span across the skin. Low? Not low—the Mount Taihua. Deep? Not deep—a puddle in a hoofprint. Shallow? Not shallow—the vast ocean.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, high and low, deep and shallow, cannot deceive you by even a single point. You people, high and low..."
Profound! The *Lotus Sūtra* cannot be tainted by even a single speck of delusion. (Holding up the staff, he draws a line. He has severed it completely; do not attempt further deliberation.
The rice in the bowl is as white as floating clouds; the tea in the clear cup wafts the fragrance of falling snow.

Ascending the hall: The road is separated by the layered lakes; not a single speck of dust reaches here. Patches of white clouds, warbling and chirping in the secluded birds—leaning quietly against the stone railing to listen, or resting securely upon the mossy robes.
This joy belongs only to those beneath the forest trees; it is rare in the human world.
For us monks, Mount Sumeru can be contained within the eye, and the four great oceans within the ear. Amidst the mass of sounds and forms, one remains at ease.
Practicing while sitting in seclusion. (He strikes the meditation seat. The whole body enters the wild weeds;
bathing the Buddha, he ascends the hall. Washing hard stones with water; waves strike the withered willow tree. Pure wisdom adorns the mass of merit.
Although it is entirely free from dust, it is not yet the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body. What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body?
There is only lake-water and no path to walk upon. Descending from the seat, he proceeds to the Great Buddha Hall; with the tip of his ladle, he takes up the essence.

He thanks the Head Seat for holding the whisk; the Prior manages the *ruyi* bag; the Rector coordinates the incense and candles for the *Laṅkāvatāra* assembly. Ascending the hall, he overturns the tea ladle;
eyebrows hang like swords—life and death are not distinguished, and the heterodox and the orthodox are difficult to discern. Ancient and modern are one.

Their tracks do not follow the same path; their wondrous realization of the profound mechanism turns like a waterwheel. Nevertheless, tell me: at what age did the Head Seat leave home to become a monk, and at what age did he practice the Way?
Wait until the Transformation Buddha emits light and the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel falls into his hands, and then I shall clearly explain it to you all.
Ascending the hall: Swallows chatter upon the carved beams; green shade covers the walls. The sound of silk-wheels whirrs; the wind carries the fragrance of cocoons.
The Old Śākyamuni has cast all three hundred and sixty joints of his bones before you all with full sincerity.
One cannot add even a single thread; one cannot subtract even a single thread. One must by no means disturb it.
To disturb it would be to shatter Cai State. Why is this so? (After a long silence, he said:
"Since the time of the Patriarchs, the study hall has been built upon the roof; the family possesses nothing but four walls. It is fundamentally empty and solid from the start—without cause."

Handed down through successive generations, they have taken the non-action for something existent; tearing down the eastern fence to patch the western wall, they open up windows and doors, thereby partitioning the vast void.
They even go so far as to carve the rafters and paint the pillars, where such ornate decoration leads to the loss of virtue. How can one return to simplicity and restore the state of purity?
When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, it is merely the speech of a cormorant imitating a crane.
On the occasion of the Dragon Boat Festival, I ascended the hall and said: "Last night at the third watch, I entered an inconceivable realm in a dream and encountered the True Person of No Rank.

He bestowed upon me the numinous talisman from behind the elbow; thus, mental dharmas vanished and the meaning of the characters shone forth clearly. The strokes were not ancient seal script, and their form transcended [convention]."
The Brahma-script cannot be known by sagely wisdom, nor can it be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
Now, encountering the Festival of Heaven, I bring it forth for all people to wear upon themselves. (With the whisk, he dots three points in the air and draws a single stroke, saying:
There is no need to hang up the Baidai talisman; what use is there to eat calamus? A thousand demons and a hundred monsters are all eliminated. —Master Zhang.
The sorcerer Li, seeing the wind, fled in terror, shedding his bones. (Holding up a whisk, he said: "Leaving behind only a medicinal gourd for the practitioners to offer their inquiry.
On the cloud-covered peaks, pine trees are planted; with a broken hoe, Buddhas and Patriarchs are buried alive. In the moonlit courtyard, the mortar and pestle pound."

A stand or mirror does not become stained by dust; yet you, you sordid fellow, leave tracks of evil everywhere upon the ground. A supervisor is naturally dull-witted, yet you tread in the footsteps of those who overturned the carriage before you.
A fine horse, catching the scent of the whip, turns at a single nudge; a hound like Han-ru, chasing after clods of earth, does not turn back even after three attempts.
The weeds of ignorance must be cleared away with sharp tools; when breaking wood and pushing through obstacles, are there no men of great strength to carry the burden?
"Ha! Furthermore, before speaking of the midnight transmission at Huangmei, one must first know that the *Lotus Sūtra* has recently re-established the rules and regulations.

Whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, during the twelve periods of the day, one must guard against the six thieves. Those who are stubborn, foolish, or wicked are driven out through the three gates with thirty blows.
To report such matters [in this way] is to invite the laughter of bystanders. But tell me, what is there to laugh at? Not much."
In his youth, he once resolved the battle arrays of dragons and snakes; now in his old age, he sings as a child again.
He further presented this verse: "I do not intend to compose verses in the style of Hanshan, Nor have I transmitted the dharma-garments of Old Lu.
Taking the living path directly beneath one's feet, One comes to penetrate the mechanism for weeding the courtyard."
Ascending the hall: Reclining on a stone, sleeping in peace; mountain clouds gather from all four sides—there is no saving them. Wash, wash! What more need be said of Deshan and Linji?
Their blows fell like raindrops, their shouts like rolling thunder. (Patting his knee) Grass obscures the traveler’s path;
the moon hangs over the village of the weary wanderer.
The West Hall of the Thūṣita Thatch Hut has been reached; ascending the hall, a new poem is composed for the thatch hut.

Seeking a true friend within the inner courtyard, the body comes from a sublime realm, and the verses are obtained from the living Dharma. Neither body nor verse—beyond the slightest hair’s breadth or speck of dust.
How could Maitreya or Du Fu have known this? Even the *Lotus Sūtra* dares not presume to speak lightly, fearing only that the speech of mountain birds may carry a subtle resonance.
On one occasion, he ascended the hall and said: "Linji studied under Huangbo; Yunmen received the lineage from Xuefeng. These 'thieves' have no fixed form and merely play with appearances.
They speak of Huanglong shattering the seal of Cheng and San, and of spreading the chest of antiquities belonging to Ciming."
"Bandits have no drum of the marks of lineage. Is there anyone with such a strategy at the gate of the Lotus Sūtra? (He says to himself: "There is.
[The Master] gives him thirty blows and drives him out the door. Why? Because he is nothing more than a petty king’s small-wave straw sandal.

On account of a matter, he ascended the hall. "The feathers of the *zhèn* bird; water containing *gǔ* poison. If the poison does not harm a person, why should it hinder one from taking it as medicine?
(With his whisk, he drew a circle and said: "There is only this much, yet it harbors venom that sprays upon people, penetrating deep into the very marrow of the bones.
The Buddhas of the three periods fear it as a rabbit fears a hawk; the patriarchs of successive generations keep their distance from it as a dragon fears a golden mountain."
Wings! There are only living monks who crave this like a flavor from a cauldron; they would grind their bones and crush their bodies yet still not have enough.
They covet what belongs to others and cling to what belongs to others. (Striking the meditation seat once with the whisk, he says: Even the Buddha—how could he save you?
To open the light for the noble Saṃgha: at the very beginning, one does not meet a true master.

Though you may boast of having been liberated first by Kātyāyana, even if you were to suddenly transcend all outflows, in the end you would still be stained. Not stained. (Pointing the brush to the eyes, he says:
The living eyes are opened; the light swallows the universe.

Returning to the Sangha Hall for the formal assembly: at the gateway of the six modes of functioning, one must exert strength to contend and seize. The battle-axes slay the enemy as clouds of arrows cross the ranks; the hordes of demons flee into the pores of a lotus fiber.
At last, they draw the River of Heaven to wash away the weapons of war. The Hall of Luminous Smoke is completed, and the merit of their "sweat-and-blood" toil is achieved.
Resting high upon the round *bō* grass mat, the dream of dust is shattered; through the window, the secluded birds speak of peace and prosperity. It is truly thus—ten thousand [times].
Holy Alliance. All you practitioners of dhyāna: if your heels are still floating and unsteady, the painted hall will instantly transform into the Iron Ring Mountains.
Ascending the hall to pray for fine weather: after long rains that do not cease, the waters level high and low, soaking rotten the nostrils of Śākyamuni and drowning the eyes of Kāśyapa.
(Holding up the staff, he says: "O Master Staff! In the chaotic dawn of heaven’s creation, it is fitting to establish feudal lords, yet there is no peace."
At such a moment, where would one spread out the leather and straw mats? (He strikes the table once. The true eye opens wide, bright as the sun;
the heavy darkness is swept away, and the heavens are clear.

Ascending the hall: It has been exactly one year since I took up residence here. Day and night I have been driven to exhaustion. The garden is overgrown, so I must hoe it myself; the buildings are dilapidated, so I am constantly afraid they will collapse.
I have exhausted my mind and spirit, resulting in a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses. Now I reflect back on the time beneath the three-beamed roof, where I simply ate and slept.
The sentiments of both ordinary and sage are empty; where the mind acts, all is extinguished. Bare and unadorned, one’s way of life is unique. This way of life is unique:
a goat-headed cart pushes along the bright moon.
The letter from Duanqiao arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "By the banks of Lake Nangang, atop Mount Tiantai, he trampled the stone bridge, cutting off all human traffic.
How many who fail to penetrate this barrier must look upon the precipice in vain lament? Clenched, it does not become a fist;
extended, it does not become a palm. A living word turned into a dead confession—do not vainly speak of a lotus fiber pulling a jade elephant."
Ascending the hall, he said: "For all the manors, drought and flood are no cause for worry; I only fear it will be difficult to tame the water-buffalo.

Having pulled off the nose-rope, it sleeps soundly and contentedly; with a few notes from a Qiang flute, the autumn fills the wild fields. Utterly devoid of form or shadow—who releases it, who gathers it in? Its whole body is white, its whole body is black;
it plays at ease amidst the wind and smoke atop the hundred grasses."
Ascending the hall: Amidst the scorching heat of the three months of summer, sweat flows like rain. This old, decrepit white cloud speaks of delusion and speaks of enlightenment;
upon a single blade of grass, he erects a jade tower. (He lets out a shout: "Deep sleep abounds with delirium. Ascending the hall:
The whole body is fully manifest, never concealed. The sound of cicadas gathers in the ancient temple; the shadows of birds cross the cool pond.
The eyes have no sinews; to steal a glance is to go blind. The ears have apertures; what harm is there in ceasing to hear?

How laughable is Meng Bālang of Qínchuān, who does not know the place from which all Buddhas emerge. He errs in his calculations. When the phoenix comes from the south, the halls and pavilions grow cool;
this merely incites bystanders to struggle in their feverish agitation. (Patting his knee, he says: How could the magpie rock ever have released its light?
Ascending the hall, he said: "It cannot be known through intellect; Vajrapāṇi wields an eight-sided mallet. It cannot be cognized through consciousness; a great radish emerges from Zhenzhou.
It cannot be constructed through words and speech; mountain birds gather and cry at the clear dawn.
It cannot be communicated through silent stillness; an octagonal tortoise and a crow swallow a tiger. These four layers of barriers have, throughout antiquity and the present, been many..."
"Few people can penetrate this. I have given you the *Lotus Sūtra*; it has been opened wide with eight characters. Is there anyone here who can pass through the barrier with a casual wave of the arm?

Those who have heard of it across the lakes and seas all cover their ears; it would be best to hide one's clumsiness in the shade of an ancient cliff.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Ten thousand layers of green mountains, a single stream of flowing water; the warbling of secluded birds, where misty vines lock in the emerald hues.
Ruiyan’s livelihood is no more than this, yet it merely hangs upon the lips and teeth of others. It is poverty to the very bone, yet wealth that perfumes the heavens.
A gust of western wind brings the fragrance of the vermilion cassia. (After a long pause, he said: Disciples, I have nothing hidden from you."
Ascending the hall, he opened the furnace and expressed his gratitude to the Hall Master. On the hall, they ate oil-cakes; the ghosts and spirits have ceased their prying.

The geese’ shadows sink into the cold water; what use is it to display such exhausted artifice? Though one may say this is for sowing the field to obtain food, how does it compare to returning to the hall to face the fire?
In profound stillness and warming heat, there is no need for shared conversation of guest and host. The patched robe covers [the body].
The myriad phenomena are empty before one’s head. How could there ever have been a living dragon in dead water?
Entering the hall, he said: "The vast ocean is not necessarily deep; Mount Sumeru is not necessarily perilous.

For the practitioner of the patched robe, the mechanism of the precipice cannot be bargained with, and the profound, secret mind cannot be scrutinized. (He took up the staff. The staff could not restrain its impatience. (With the staff...)
(Acting out the gesture of probing the water’s flow) Let me try to probe and feel it. It is not even half an inch deep. (Acting out the gesture of climbing up) It is as level as a mirror’s surface.

There is the roar of a vast thunder, yet not a single drop of rain. (Leaning on his staff) It is best to remain hidden like a tortoise in deep clouds; even with Buddha-eyes, one cannot find the tracks.

Even if one were to find them, Ruiyan would simply offer a cup of tea and say to him slowly: *(Note: The final line is a traditional Chan kōan response, implying that the ultimate reality is beyond conceptualization or verbal description.)*
The sun sets and the road is at its end; my hometown is still far away.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] held up the staff (measuring stick). "A stringless lute," he said, striking it once. "There is a lingering melody; its tune is loftier than flowing water, and its sound vibrates through the monastic forest.
Blue-eyed and yellow-headed ones vie to play upon it. Without cause, they tear apart the heart of the Patriarch. Ruiyan has never been subtle."

With his hand, he mimics the expression and plays a melody. (He rests his staff horizontally and makes a gesture of stroking it. *Ding-dang, ding-dang.* Subjugating the hearing, Ziqi was lost in the rhythm. (He leans against the staff.
Hanging high with the clouds above the ancient pine’s shade, he ascends the hall.
For forty years, he has forged them into a single piece. A mangy horse tied to a withered post; the old monk has brought it under his command. Twelve.

Even the sovereigns Yao and Shun still possessed such a transformative power. (Holding up the staff) Master of the Staff, you have wandered the lakes and seas, traversing every hardship and difficulty;
yet here, you cannot revive even a single spark of life. You lot—men with no blood beneath your skin—have come here to jostle shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, seeking [enlightenment].
[The Master] ascends the hall. [He sets down his staff and sits.

At the inauguration of the Water and Land Assembly at Dusi, [the Master] ascended the seat: "Great wisdom is profoundly clear; the ten directions are utterly transparent. The mysterious pivot turns wondrously, and the tracks of a thousand sages are lost.

"The way lies ahead. (He strikes the meditation seat. "Only when you see through this can you truly know that Dongshan and the Fifth Patriarch were nothing but old, frozen scabs.

Eye meeting eye, it is like a mirror facing a mirror, utterly free of blemish or flaw. Reaching this point, there is no mind to cultivate and no vow to fulfill."
There are no calamities to avert; there is no kindness to repay. One sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse, unaware of where the boundaries of one’s domain lie.

Although it is said that under the gate of a patch-robed monk, there are a hundred thousand miles and eight thousand leagues—why is this so? The old monk smiles and points toward the place where the monkeys cry:
"There is yet another sacred trace atop the high peak. (Verse) The Great Saber has long been buried in Fengcheng; it was only upon passing Zhang Hua that its brilliance was revealed.
Light immediately flashed forth; the enmities accumulated over lifetimes were all swept away. The hibernating dragon was placed within a silver casket and preserved with reverence.

Entering the hall, he thanked the Head Seat for examining his whisk and the Administrative Head (Dusi) for the midday meal. He crushed the nostrils of Dongshan and tore through the ear-rings of Foyan;
in one stroke, he displayed his lethal hand. The strength in his wrist weighs as much as a thousand *qun*; having devoured the flavor of the Dharma, he is now fully satiated by what he has heard.
The Perfect Sound: The majesty and decorum of the Han dynasty are seen once more; the fragrance of purple mushrooms disperses through the spring of the emerald cliffs.

On the anniversary of the Prince’s passing: The Great Way is vast and empty, utterly transcending words and explanations. The single nature is harmoniously fused, making no distinction between the ordinary and the sage.
The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. The common people use it daily yet remain unaware of it.

Therefore, the Way of the gentleman is rare indeed. Thus, the sages who toil for others—some carrying snow to fill the well, some renouncing the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King, and some appearing in the body of a high official—they carry on the noble legacy of the thousand Buddhas and spread the sacred transformation of the hundred kings.

Though there are a thousand differences, they follow the same track; though there are ten thousand streams, they all flow toward the central source. At such a time as this, tell me: what of my former post at Fenghua County?

The King conferred upon him the posthumous title of "Pure and Sensitive" (Ch'ŏngmin). He received a prophetic record from Mount Insan and loftily protected the Citadel of the Dharma. He served his sovereign and nourished the people, establishing the work of peace and prosperity.
His merit was perfected and his fruition fulfilled; he shifted his station and turned his faculties. Where does he now attain Buddhahood?

He is not born in the Tuṣita Heaven, but certainly dwells within the Lotus World. (Verse) Loyalty and purity shine like the constellations for a thousand ages; his brilliance surpasses all in this world.
Fame, achievement, wealth, and honor arise; where has he gone, surrounded by banners and jade pendants amidst the clouds? He strolls through the pavilions of the *vīṇā* (lute).
Entering the hall, he thanks the Head Seat Yuanweng for visiting him. He tosses and turns heaven and earth; the numinous serpent is in his palm.
Its blade is revealed, its frost contained—who can approach it? Before the chief villain has been slain, the hibernating dragon guards its case, firmly concealing its resistance. Return!

"This is his true ground. A sword from Jianzhou is no different from the Great Scimitar (Ta'a). Brought forth here at the Moon-Cutting Pavilion, it is shared by all the Chan practitioners of the Five Lakes.
Let us wipe our eyes and gaze upon it, acclaiming it with repeated praise."

The Buddha ascended the path to enlightenment; at midnight he leaped over the city wall. For six years he dwelt amidst the snows, until his intestines were withered by hunger and his bones broken by the cold.

What more need be said of his seeing the morning star? His two eyes were filled with heavy frost. The descendants of later generations suffer like sheep, vying with one another for eloquence year after year.
(He strikes his knee once. As for the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, it is fitting that it be entrusted to this blind donkey.
Extinction.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Heavenly skill cuts the jade flowers, leaking forth the true message. (Holding up his staff) He prods Master Moshang;
with the force of a thousand-jun weight, he playfully extends his old arm to support the precarious peak. He vivifies the perfect mechanism, manifesting illusions.
The Fragrant Accumulation above need not strain its concentration; it accomplishes the full merit at once. (A single strike of the staff) Shattering the profound gate, he speaks of non-duality.
(Another strike) Summoning back lingering dreams to hear the distant bell.

On the first day of the first month, ascending the hall for the New Year’s service. The first day of the first month is the New Year; every household celebrates, and everywhere there is a bustling clamor. (Holding up the staff)

Only this staff-master remains unchanged through the shifting seasons. Seated steadily at the roots of the pines, sleeping peacefully upon the rocks, he suddenly lets loose a song of simple innocence.
(He strikes the ground once. "Luo luo li luo luo li luo. Now tell me, is this the same as Dongshan’s "Song of the Earthen Drum," or is it different?
The wooden man listens without satiety. (Leaning on his staff: Standing gaunt amidst the mist of green vines.

Ascending the hall on the fifteenth day of the first month, [the Master] thanked the *zhisui*, the attendant, the bath-master, and the head of the administrative office. "A single lamp of the mind: its cold light is brilliant, shining eternally through past and present.

How many have truly opened their eyes? Those old, frozen scabs from all quarters burn the fields to plant their millet; three calls and three responses, they attain a wondrous realization of the nature of water.

This is an extraordinary Lantern Festival; how could it not be worthy of appreciation?
Incense Offering on the Anniversary of Master Baizhang’s Death. Sitting alone upon Great Hero Peak, he often played with danger when facing critical moments.

Having met the tiger’s maw, he could not distinguish between the killing and the saving; having shed the fox’s skin, it was difficult to discern the true from the false. How much more so when he established the pure monastic rules—level ground turned into deep pits and trenches!
He has formed an unforgivable, mortal enmity. (Inserting incense) I burn this stick of maple incense to bring an end to all grievances.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Guest Master Hui and the Attendant Gong. (Coming from Xuefeng, like falling snow. A person has come from Xuefeng, bringing a message from Lurong.

The Earth Lord of Songshan turns over in his cold spot; the Dragon King of Yintan awakens in a dream.
Hastily summoning his spirit, he recited one mantra for departing from fear: *Namo samanta-buddhānām.
Oṃ bu-liṅ. Oṃ ci-liṅ. Hūṃ hūṃ. Act swiftly according to the command!* "The Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen.
The Sanskrit words are difficult to correct into Chinese."
On the fifth day of the second lunar month, he ascended the hall to express his gratitude for the visit of Inspector Fan. His home is on Mount Penglai; his rainbow robes shimmer like clouds.

His *buxu* chants follow a rhythmic measure; his contemplation of the boundaries of reality is without error. The azure dragon guarding the sword cries out from its precious casket; the emaciated crane listens to the zither as it leans against the courtyard flowers.
With the nine-fold elixir perfected, the talisman sweeps away all malevolent influences. He shall not fail the covenant of the Lotus Society at Donglin, riding upon—
A light carriage has arrived to visit the home of the Indian Sage. Though we have not yet been able to part at Tiger Creek, we shall enjoy the Zhaozhou tea with courtesy.

[The Master] ascends the hall to thank the Abbot Xiu, the Head of the Kitchen Bo, the Administrative Monk Tu, the Librarian Zhuang, the Head of the Monks Yuan, the Librarian Kai, the Custodian of the Tripitaka Zhang, and the Chan Master Chuan for tilling his ancestral fields.
For many years it has been neglected and abandoned; farmers do not attend to their plowing, and fishermen pursue profit alone.

But tell me, does this encompass the entirety of the Great Canon? Wait until the wooden band of the water-tub bursts, and then I shall tell you.
Ascending the hall: Ninety days of spring are now about to pass; how much of this radiant light can a human life truly behold? The source of Qin was already deceived by peach blossoms;
the banks of Sui still witness the wild flight of willow catkins. (Holding up the staff) O Master Staff, you who know the principle of non-transmigration—your seal has not been kept secret.
(Striking once) A mouthful of ice and frost. Of a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, no one understands. (Casting it down)

he intended to let his shadow rest and his form cease, yet who would have thought he would so clearly play with danger? (He strikes with the whisk and says: He points out the night.
Crossing the heart (drawing a single line), he splits open the Bodhisattva’s face. With such ugliness so grotesquely displayed, even the Buddha’s hand cannot cover it.
All that is won is the spring mountains weeping for the cuckoo; fresh blood stains the flower branches, every cry full of resentment.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "The red sun burns the sky; the parched seedlings wither to death. The farmers drawing water labor until their sweat falls like rain.
Reflect deeply on those beneath the three-beamed roof and before the seven-foot mat, who, having eaten their fill, sleep soundly—disliking the very act of being a Buddha. It is indeed thus."
To spend ten thousand taels of gold like dross and soil—should this not be so, Huangbo would become a donkey’s crupper, and all that follows would be nothing but suffering.

Snow. It is difficult to preserve a wax figure from the ice. An entire summer has been spent in vain, eating and sleeping. Now the autumn wind plays with the sickle for reaping the grain.
Possessing both authority and utility, impartial and without faction, how many patriarchs have had their heads severed? Establishing the teaching transforms a year of famine into one of abundance.
Ascending the hall (to thank Layman Dong for his visit): The autumn sun is scorching; thunder rolls across the earth.

It washes away my stifling heat, and I rejoice so much that I cannot sleep. The Mountain King of Exquisite Virtue has sent me a verse: "A great drought meets sweet rain; In a foreign land, one encounters an old friend.
Waterfalls cascade like jade over cliffs; Tasting rice, snow turns over the spoon. *Yi-ming-yi!* Who knows this moment of hardship?
Once again, one sees the time of Great Peace. (Holding up the staff) The Master of the Staff hears it in the dark; his hands dance and his feet leap for joy.
The heat has receded and the cool air arises; the path ahead is alive. (Casting it down) With a single leap, he transforms into a dragon and emerges from the Celestial Pond.
He wins the smile that broadens the brows of Master Pang.

Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. (To thank the stewards of the various manors for returning with the harvest, and to welcome guests: "A single grain of rice in a monk’s bowl is a drop of blood from the farmer's field.
Gathering it back after the toil of war—think of how many words were spent on its account! Bright pearls and polished jade; rice steamed separately in fragrant cauldrons.

Here, we accompany our guests by burning firewood in an earthen stove, discussing matters beyond the duality of host and guest. Nevertheless, one must take care not to add gold to what is already perfect."

On the first day of the intercalary tenth month, he ascended the hall. After declining visitors, he said: "After the rain, the sound of the stream plays cold melodies for Nongyu; Before the wind, the tree leaves scatter like shattered gold.
Seeing and hearing function interchangeably, beyond sound and form; Flowers split open the heart-mind of the Ancient Buddha Weiyin. Thus, the family was established.
Joyfully hosting distinguished guests in a banquet of pipes and zithers—do not say that the peaks of Ruiyan are too secluded; every time one picks it up, it is ever new.

Breaking through the Jianmen Pass with a pearl, he departed from this world before his time was spent. He wrote a verse to seal himself within, white-handedly shattering the black dragon pearl.

their voices arrest the drifting clouds as they part like a row of geese, vanishing beyond the thousand peaks.
Ascending the hall (to thank Layman Wang of Shuangyu and Librarian Hongzang): "To swallow up the waters of the West River in a single gulp is still only halfway there.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: An outsider asked the Buddha, "I ask neither for a word of affirmation nor for a word of negation" (a golden wrapping around a clod of rotten mud).

Furthermore, how can one discern this clearly? If you can discern it, the fine horse has already been eight *ke* late in looking for the whip.
If you cannot discern it, the masters of this eastern land are not as good as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) of the western heavens. Verse:
Ten thousand *li* of clear river, as pure as a white silk scroll; water and sky one color, coldly imbued with luster. The fisherman recognizes the path to the misty village;
threading his catch on willow-strings, he returns under the moon.
Ascending the hall, he gave thanks [to the Head Seat of the Rear Hall, the Librarian who held the whisk, and the Administrator for the winter feast]:
"In the Tuṣita Heaven palace, the dream was first told; in the Sūtra-piṭaka, emptiness is again discussed. Every person is satiated with the flavor of Cunda’s meal;
this is not the same as ordinary festive occasions. The moon through the slender vines, the rustling pines and wind—this life of four walls, poverty to the bone, rivals the Lord."
The King’s wealth and joy were inexhaustible.

He ascended the hall and raised up the case of Tripitaka Master Dairi, who had attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. When he had an audience with Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, the Emperor ordered the National Teacher to test him.

As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the National Teacher, he prostrated himself and stood to one side before him. The National Teacher said, "I have heard that the Tripitaka Master has attained the power of knowing others' minds."
Xitong asked, "Is this so? Zang said, "I dare not say. The National Teacher said, "Tell me, where is the Master right now?
Zang said, "The National Teacher of the entire land is watching the boat races in Xichuan. The second time he asked, "Tell me, where am I, the old monk, right now?
Zang said, "I am on the Tianjin Bridge watching the monkey tricks. The third time—
Dadu asked again, but the Tripitaka Master remained silent. The National Teacher rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your power of knowing others' minds?
He added, "The Great-Eared Tripitaka did not say he lacked the power of knowing others' minds; it is simply a pity that his head is a dragon’s while his tail is a snake’s.
Had he been one whose entire body was eyes, when asked for the third time, 'Where is the old monk?', he would have simply pointed toward [the questioner] himself."
The Master of the Way. A national teacher making his living inside a ghost cave.
If you can grasp this statement, then even if the National Teacher does not hoist his banner high, he cannot avoid raising his hands and touching his forehead in relief. Verse:
Ten thousand pieces of gold wrapped around a lump of rotten mud; he does not spare himself as he performs this spectacle for all to see.
His failure has been scrutinized by others, yet in the end, he is still deceived by it.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of the Sixth Patriarch Master of Caoxi:

when he arrived at Faxon Temple in Guangzhou and heard two monks debating the wind and the banner, he remarked, "This wood-seller from Xinzhou, who stole the robe and bowl on the dais at Huangmei, in the middle of the third watch of the night..."
Hurriedly startled, he ran away. Upon seeing the wind-blown banner, he immediately said, "It is the mind that moves. This too is like the saying, "The heart of a thief is naturally timid.
Nevertheless, while the wind and banner have not moved, where can one seek the mind? When the white clouds have vanished, the green mountains appear;
yet the traveler stands even beyond those green mountains. (Versicle): Mist and rain obscure the eyes as they wander; A small painted boat moors by the bridge.

Entering the hall: Wild vines entangle the silk skirts; mountain clouds shroud the straw hats. They dance and rejoice to celebrate the New Year; the Stone Woman laughs aloud.
To call this the "Buddhadharma of the New Year" is to mislead many people; yet, if one does not call it the "Buddhadharma of the New Year," what then?
The Buddha-dharma has saved and delivered countless people.

It is not like those ten-thousand-bushel golden lotuses that delude and distract the foolish for their appreciation. Today is the Yuanxiao Festival; I bring this forth and invite you all to look.
(He draws a circle with his whisk. Do you see? If you hesitate or engage in discursive thought, it is like empty flowers obscuring your eyes.

he wrongly adjudicated the terminology of all quarters. Ruiyan wanted to ask: *Note: This passage concerns a kōan involving Zhaozhou, the National Teacher Nanyuan, and the masters Qin and Ma.
