This was to let this old fellow know: while the cicada raises its arms in rage, the yellow magpie is already vying to seize it.
[Verse]: In the midst of the field he strikes down the illness and cuts off all ties; A fist comes, a kick goes—no room for yielding. Who would have known?

The young masters ride side by side to admire the flowers; greedy for their jade cups, they become drunk as mud. Amidst the clusters of flutes and songs, they are escorted home.
Upon entering the hall, [the Master] thanks Chief Administrator Yidu of Xuedou, Chief Librarian Dingning, and the guests, and then cites Master Ciming.
One day, an old friend came to the hall and said: "In this wind-swept, cool landscape, companions visit a place of solitude.

Tea is brewed with water from beneath the mountain; incense burns from firewood gathered in the cave. Master Ciming may indeed be said to have thrown open his eastern gate to entertain his distinguished guests.
At Zhipeng’s thatched cottage, pearl curtains are hung; I shall now勉强效顰 (struggle to imitate) and see you all off.
A traveler from beyond the clouds, wondrous and rare; seeking our covenant, he arrived at the purple mushrooms. Beholding the flowers, he thought of the brocade mirror;

facing the moon, we spoke of Mount Emei. The flavor of the Way is sweeter than sweet wine; our feelings for our homeland are as familiar as thick gruel. Leaning against a pine tree, we shared a smile; the joy of poverty is vast and boundless.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] thanked the Administrative Officer and the Hall Master. "In old age, dwelling in the mountains, one possesses some core substance.

The dilapidated house of Yangqi has been supported by an experienced hand; the oil-flask of Touzi relies on a master to be lifted up. The Buddhas of the three periods kick out the tips of their straw sandals;
the demon armies of the five aggregates flee into the pores of a lotus fiber. One forgets sorrow through joy, and rejoices without end."
Sleep! Even if you must endure hunger to mend a barrel, O Zen adepts, "The neighbor to the east slaughters an ox; it is not as good as the simple sacrifice of the neighbor to the west.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "Do not be hindered by the ordinary mind; do not fear the words of the precipice. Eat your fill and sleep soundly at will; have no aversion for the Buddha."
If he is willing to do so, the karmic winds will blow him before the Twelve Peaks. He will turn his back on the Dharma Hall and depart wearing straw sandals.
For now, call him back and give him a cup of tea; then, speak gently to him: "Be careful on your way."
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: When Wuzhuo went to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, he encountered an old man on the road.
Wuzhuo asked, "Could this be Mañjuśrī? The old man replied, "How could there be two Mañjuśrīs? As Wuzhuo rose from his prostration, the old man vanished. The Master commented:
"It is truly laughable that Wuzhuo, with the thief right before him, was unable to seize him; he merely closed his door in vain."
He cried out in distress. What common ground is there for conversation? At that time, had you waited for him to say, "How can there be two Mañjuśrīs? you should have spat right in his face.
Although the old man possessed schemes that pierce the heavens, he was certain to sink three feet into the earth. Verse:

Gazing afar at Penglai, he departed to study the arts of the immortals. On the way, he suddenly encountered Master Li. Receiving a single grain of returned elixir, he swallowed it and spat it out again;
turning his head, he walked alone through the empty mountains.
[The Master] cited the case of Magu asking Linji: “Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye?
Linji said, “Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, what is the true eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Magu dragged Linji down from his meditation seat and sat upon it himself.
Linji said, “I do not know you. As Magu hesitated, Linji gave a shout, dragged him off the seat, and sat back down. Magu then desisted.

"Go! [The Master] picks up the staff and says: "Linji and Magu are like two armies of a million men arrayed for battle; their black banners flash, their snow-white blades flash across the field. There is a formidable, invincible air about them. Yet when the two generals challenge one another, they attack each other with nothing but shards and rubble. Look closely: what does this amount to? It is merely the play of small children. Verse: Two great generals stand face-to-face, Their banners fluttering, their blades flashing bright. A hundred thousand troops are arrayed in formation, Yet they strike each other with shards and rubble. If you look closely at the scene, It is no more than children’s play. In the midst of the fray, who can discern the truth? Only those who have seen through the clouds of delusion. Go! Go! A hundred thousand troops are arrayed in formation, Yet they strike each other with shards and rubble. If you look closely at the scene, It is no more than children’s play. In the midst of the fray,
The Great Compassionate True Eye is revealed in full majesty; from a hundred paces away it stirs like a flash of lightning. Seized by a mad wind, the physician has been blinded;
in the darkness he drags [the patient] down from the meditation seat.
Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s birthday: Clouds atop the ridge rub against the drooping pines; waterfalls before the crags rinse the rocks with a resonant *cong-cheng* sound.
The face and eyes of Gautama are fully revealed; who says he was born only this morning? The lame Yunmen’s staff—do not let it strike the blind.
A ladle of fragrant soup and three prostrations: let him bear his ill repute for a thousand ages.

Ascending the hall at the commencement of the summer retreat: for an entire spring it has rained continuously; the people’s hearts are filled with anxiety and dread, and their wives and children cry out from hunger.

There is nowhere to buy rice. Take care, O living monks, you who are a mass of merit! With your patched robes drawn over your heads, free from thought and worry, observe the ninety-day restriction of the feet.

The dull-witted bird perches upon the reeds for the three-month summer retreat; the hibernating insects seal their burrows. Turning over one’s own iron-faced hide, one begrudges the Buddha and refuses to practice.
To act in such a manner is to squander ten thousand ounces of gold as if it were a mere inch of soil. If this is not yet the case, Huangbo will serve as a donkey’s crupper;
from then on, there will be nothing but suffering.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Head Seat and the Librarian: "Last night, by the Moon-Cutting Pavilion, the *Gāo-shān liú-shuǐ* (High Mountain and Flowing Water) was played.
Though it is said that the strings are made of lion sinew, the performance must rely on skillful fingers. Not falling into the registers of *gōng* or *shāng*, the listeners pricked up their ears;
the Great Statue of Jiazhou gained a hundredfold its spirit, and the Old Dragon of Jingxi added tenfold its vitality. One would have thought this was the true sound..."

There has been no news at all. Who would have expected that amidst the "Zheng" music that disrupts the "Ya," there would be such pure lute-playing as this? (Then, joining his palms, he said: "I am ashamed, I am ashamed.
The report of the passing of Master Wuwen has reached us as we ascend the hall. Like thunder crashing against the Jianfu Stele, Heaven conceals the Seal of Wuwen. The characters—"
The meaning is difficult to clarify; who can correctly receive the mind-to-mind transmission? The East Lake pours forth waves of resentment that overflow the heavens.
Startled and trembling, the lingering dream of Ruiyan awakens. (He slaps the meditation seat. He strikes the railing violently; he cries out to Heaven, but there is no response.
Unable to weep, unable to laugh—wild flowers drip with tears, moistening the shadows of a thousand peaks.

Ascending the hall, he raised the passage from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*: "An imperial decree was issued to all the fierce and evil ghosts and spirits, entrusting them with the protection and maintenance of the True Dharma.
(Not realizing that disaster arises within the inner walls, they sit idly waiting to defend a fortress ten thousand *li* away. If there were even one person who did not arrive...
He causes hot iron wheels to fly from the gates of the four directions to pursue them (forcing people to act in such a manner). Among them, one demon king says:
"I shall only give rise to the bodhicitta once all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood" (fearing this may not be the true King;
let us adjust the straw hat and wear it elsewhere).
The Master holds up his whisk and says: "The Yellow-Faced Old Man [the Buddha] spread an all-encompassing iron net, hoping to capture the phoenix and ensnare the dragon.
Yet even this Demon King is not easily caught. Since he was able to tear through the net and escape, it is a pity that his wing-strength was incomplete and he was subsequently bound and slain.
Had he said at that time: 'I would rather sink into eternal samsara than seek liberation from the various saints,' not only..."
The sandalwood from Elephant Head alone has caused withered trees to flourish once more. It shall also cause the Elder Śāka to retreat three paces.

On the first day of the ninth month, he ascends the hall; for three months, military expeditions cease. Literature is cultivated and arms are laid aside, bringing a reign of Great Peace that reaches all quarters. Living beings rejoice and dance.
Without cause, the horses of the borderlands neigh in the wind, wishing again to raise dust and scatter soil; they secretly employ their strategic wits and solemnly prepare their armies.
The Journey: North of the Great Wall and South of Annam were won in a single battle; life-and-death enmities and demons were all swept away.

Great rewards were bestowed upon the original meritorious ministers, and the sounds of triumphal songs shook the path to Mount Zhifu. Nevertheless, one wonders: who was the bystander, Sun Wu, observing this?
Ascending the hall to thank the Abbot of Yuyang: On the day of the robe-bestowing ceremony in the ninth month, Mount Zhi has nothing to bestow.
Clad in a tattered patchwork robe amidst cold clouds, I am too weary to open my mouth to guests. How can the Great Canon—its sudden and gradual, its partial and complete teachings—be analyzed?
The meaning of the wild geese writing characters in the sky is brilliantly clear; yet, when seen with such clarity, even gold dust becomes a heavy obscuration over the eyes.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the two seats, Taibai and Nanshan Yuweng, and Yuanzhi. He cited an ancient poem which says: "When the mountain reaches its finest spots, my journey grows weary;
(one version says: 'When a book brings swift joy, it is easily read to the end') / When there is a guest who is a true friend, I call for them but they do not come."
The ways of the world are often at odds like this; how many times can a good heart be opened? Jipong was not so;
his disposition became a habit through his love for the mountains. He would not show a smile unless he encountered a fine place. Now, the brocade screens and the sword-gates meet once again.
Doubt lingers amidst the verdant mists of Mount Min and Mount Emei.
Entering the hall, he thanked Master Jichuang of Yuyang for visiting him. One, two, three, four, five; six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
(In the Min dialect) Sanskrit and Chinese cannot fully translate one another. Upon the Jade Terrace, a new commentary has been added; the meaning of the characters shines forth clearly.
However, no one understands this. Fortunately, there is one who knows the same wind; nodding his head, he says it is strange.
It is hazy and indistinct, much like the "Song of the East Mountain’s Earthen Drum. The melody is identical, yet the sound has neither high nor low pitch.
Do you all wish to know the dialect beyond the norm? (He makes the gesture of playing a long drum and says: “Peng-ba-la-ca! Is it here? Is it not here? (In the Min dialect.)

Ascending the hall to thank those who held the whisk and prepared the vegetarian feast, he said: "The clouds gather to open the banquet; the Wheel of Dharma turns as the Wheel of Food. To look at it, both eyes go blind;
to taste it, one must swallow three times with spittle. Yunmen’s 'moldy bread' is merely a vain boast; Yangqi’s 'chestnut burr' must be quickly rolled up.
But tell me, after it has been rolled up, what is it like? The pillar and the lantern—spring wind fills their faces."
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Daoist Master and the Head Seat, Xing, for their visit. "The Five Thousand Words of the Daodejing" profoundly clarify the mysterious and subtle verses;
"Yunmen’s Single-Word Barrier" cuts off the path laid out across the way. Before the Twelve Peaks, danger is distributed and peril is arrayed.
He awakens the master of the house who was dozing on the "Awakened Stone," shaking hands to deliberate and raising eyebrows in laughter, startling them with a cold release.

A single branch of plum blossoms betrays the arrival of early spring, sending the imperial messengers rushing along. (Striking the meditation seat) Hush! Countless are those who seek the fragrance and pursue the stench.
The Memorial Day of the Prince of the Commandery. General Outline: The upward-moving mechanism; the eye at the crown of the head.
Where one discerns the finest hair, it is dark and murky; where one penetrates the steep precipice, it is level and plain. The Buddhas of the three periods have no door for their direct gaze;
white oxen and stray cats—how many are buried alive? (Striking the seat with the whisk, he says: If you see through here, you will see that all the sages of antiquity have shed their skins.

He treasures and honors fine robes, yet wears tattered and soiled garments; he gathers in and rescues the multitudes of sentient beings, entering the mud and the water. Therefore, I, the Prince of Huaguan, transmit his teachings without composing new doctrines.

Having fully realized the Samādhi of Illusion, he conceals the marks of a Bodhisattva and manifests the body of a civil official. He brings peace to the sovereign and bestows grace upon the people; he establishes feudal lords and maintains the ritual standards.
Wielding the hand that heals the state, he loftily guards the city of the Dharma. In him, the sentiments of both mundane and sacred realms are emptied, transcending birth and death.
The dream is shattered; the realm of worldly toil is stilled, and the flower of wisdom blooms. All beings within the nine realms and four modes of birth receive the power of this grace.
Now tell me: what practice or vow did he cultivate to attain such excellence? (Holding up the whisk, he says: The wondrous place is beyond words when one wishes to speak of it;
the moon shifts its reflection upon the flowered balustrade.
The session concluded. He personally followed Maitreya down to Changting. With the "Single-Character King" script, he received a distinguished title;
having fulfilled his service to the state, he returned to the inner court. His descendants were graced with the honor of brocade robes.

Ascending the hall on the first day of the first month of the year, he thanked the guest prefect: "The eye that distinguishes the ancient and the modern does not exist; it is the tongue that distinguishes the ancient and the modern.
One may speak with tenfold truth, but how does this compare to seeing through to the bottom? To see through to the bottom—there the heart-lamp burns bright, dispelling the chill of night.
Year after year, one celebrates the Lantern Festival."

Ascending the hall to thank the visiting Daoist: Deep within the springtime of this thatched cottage, the seasonal splendor is most pleasing to the eye. Mountain flowers are heavy with emerald dew; the grasses and mists are like a lush carpet.
Moreover, a guest seeking the hidden depths has arrived, with a brocade pouch to seek out poetic lines and a *lí* staff to carry his zither.
Grasping hands at the foot of the pines, we share a single laugh; such lofty spirit never sought to guard the Eastern Grove.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A letter from Xuedou Fang’an has arrived. The 'Horse Colt' of Guanghan, a monk among the Arhats of the ten directions, does not eat the millet of the golden rooster;
he specializes in carrying the grievances of a bloody battle. He has sucked the ancient dragon pool dry to its very bottom; he has toppled the cool, refreshing tree until it stands rootless.
Moving the field of action through five locations, he dabbles in the treacherous; his transformative mechanism never once involved the conditions of spring. Cease your seeking and hide away."
Mystery. The earth sinks and the heavens collapse; the *tángdì* flowers wither and the wild geese vanish from view. Beating one’s breast, one cannot avoid crying out to the azure heavens.

On the first day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall: "The spring of the third month passes in the snap of a finger; the ninety-day summer begins once more. Tea buds as slender as sparrow-tongues are hurriedly plucked;
wheat plays with its shrimp-like whiskers as it is gathered in turn. He preaches the Dharma with blazing intensity, his voice shaking the forests."
"Kū! (He picks up the staff. National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang is coming. Seeing that you all do not recognize him, (he throws it down and says:
He is riding backward on the Buddha Hall, going straight into the eye of a gnat."

Ascending the hall, he thanked those who had held the whisk and provided the vegetarian feast. "The delicacies of the celestial kitchen and the choice cuts of the imperial table—bear's paws and fish—these two rare delights have been obtained together.
This assembly of mine has long endured withered stillness; now, the two wheels of food and Dharma are simultaneously set in motion.

Having fully tasted the true flavor, there is a place of joy free from attachment, which may be called unsurpassed *dharmaprīti*. Though this was the offering of Cunda, tell me: how does it compare to the celestial [feast]?"

The "Forbidden Fatty Cuts" from the kitchen—how far apart are they [in quality]? (Striking the desk: The jade-like ribs of the Five Tombs, indulging in their fatness and softness—how can they compare to the lush growth of bamboo shoots and bracken on the spring mountains?
Ascending the hall on the first day of the fifth month: it has already been half a month since the summer retreat began. What of the water buffalo?

It loves to wander off into the wild weeds and refuses to travel upon the level path. Tugged by the rope amidst the clamor, spurred by the whip in stillness, it sleeps on the bare ground under the white moon and clear wind;
the sound of the herdsman’s flute echoes through the misty village.

Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival: A modest offering for the Midsummer Day; though my household is poor, there is more than enough to enjoy. Wrapped in reed leaves are glutinous rice dumplings; for tea, we have stone calamus.

There is no need to send a boy to seek medicinal herbs, nor any necessity for ghosts to draw talismanic charms. All manner of demons have been swept away, and throughout the long summer, we may dwell in peace.
Nevertheless, within the gate of the patch-robed monk, the difference is as vast as heaven and earth.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Put it down! Do not engage in deluded thoughts. An unperforated iron hammer—half a pound is eight ounces.
Thrown out through the gateway; the earth is vast and people are few. The baseless Zhaozhou never understood at all; Fenglin merely speaks of 'tha' in vain."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the sixth month: In the sixth month, the heat is bitter; how can a wax figure endure?
The fire-clouds boil it until it dissolves; once dissolved, it remains whole. It is laughable that Old Yunmen was so crazed by the wind.

Covered in stinking sweat, a slight coolness arises in the halls and pavilions. He strikes away the spirits of ghosts. If you wish to understand where all Buddhas emerge—(after a long silence, he slaps his knee)—a donkey!
"Year after year, donkey after donkey.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you can fit Mount Sumeru into your eyes and the four great oceans into your ears, consider this carefully:
your body is no larger than a coconut. Why do you allow so much dust and debris to settle within it? Ruigan said: "I place sound into my eyes."
It cannot be done. One must not apply color to the ears. Being nearly eighty years old, one barely has enough to save oneself from death;

what leisure is there to dally with the sons and daughters of others before sound and after form? This morning I am filled with joy; the ancestral fields and gardens have received rain upon their parched seedlings, and both high and low lands will be richly matured.

A full meal may now be expected. With bellies drumming and songs of praise, what happiness, what happiness! You— [Note: The final character "你這一" (you this one) appears to be an incomplete fragment of the original text.]
"You fellows! You have little sense of gratitude. Coming here again, you jostle shoulders and crowd feet to seek such a bowl. (He drags down his staff and descends from the seat;
the assembly scatters at once. He speaks again: "Attendant, take up the staff. Entering the hall, I request the presence of the Supervisor.
The rain has ended and the dragons are idle; the harvest is bountiful and the people rejoice. From his sleeve he draws forth the sickle for reaping grain—the entire great earth..."
All is withdrawn. Returning before the Twelve Peaks, he cooks fragrant rice in a separate cauldron; his alms bowl is full of bright pearls.

He feeds the living monks until they are satiated, then rests his arm on his knee and sleeps soundly. "The Buddha-dharma and one's own body and mind are as rotten as mud. (Patting his knee) "Silence! There is no medicine for this illness."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "To shorten the cranes and lengthen the ducks; to level the valleys and fill the peaks—Master Zhao, why exert all this effort?

The heavens and earth of antiquity are the heavens and earth of today; the sun and moon of antiquity are the sun and moon of today. Mountains are mountains, waters are waters; monks are monks, laypeople are laypeople.
You must not disturb them for a moment. Why? 'If they have no sores, do not wound them.'"
Ascending the hall, he thanked the new and old two classes of officials: Before the Twelve Peaks stands a puppet stage, entirely pulled and guided by the master of the strings.
The arrangement of acts knows neither new nor old; they dance and sing at an autumn wind banquet of flutes and pipes.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Abbot Xun of Jiangxi. "A man from Xuefeng has arrived; a messenger from Fuzhou has come.
I have received news from Jiangxi reporting that the wooden ball of Xuefeng has rolled into the Eel Well at Yuyang Monastery. Furious waves toss the sky, and fish and dragons beg for their lives.
Then, an autumn wind blows it onto the 'Awakened' Rock, startling the Master of the House awake from his deep slumber. (He paused for a long while. "Rolling it up! (He lifted the robe.)
A single smile from the brows stills a thousand peaks.

Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the Mid-Autumn Festival, everyone vies to admire the moon at the edge of the heavens, yet they do not realize that the mind-moon is solitary and perfect.
It does not involve waxing or waning; light and shadow vanish. Master Mazu and his father were mistaken in their deliberations. [He] brushes it away.
He moves his sleeve and departs, yet has not yet reached the end. Do you all still see the moon in the mind? (With the whisk, he makes the ○ mark.
Look quickly with your eyes! Layer upon layer of golden dust.
Striking the board, he ascends the hall: the rock-orchids waft their fragrance, the well-plum trees shed their leaves. The living mechanism of the Patriarchs is revealed layer after layer.
To see it clearly is for the eyes to resemble eyebrows; to speak it completely is for the tongue to be as if knotted. Do you all wish to know the intimate phrase?
For three months on the meditation cushion, it was cold as ice. Today, sit steadily and listen quietly as I explain it for you.
Ascending the hall on the Double Ninth: On the ninth day of the ninth month, the Festival of Double Yang, one does not go to the eastern hedge to admire the chrysanthemums;

instead, one simply sips a cup of *zhuyu* tea. Its bitter astringency is difficult to taste, leaving the tongue as if paralyzed by force. Furthermore, swallowing the "thorn-bush acorns" tears the liver and entrails asunder.
Tell me, did Tao Yuanming ever know this flavor? (He shakes his head and says: Do not speak, do not speak!

Ascending the hall: On the day in the ninth month when robes are bestowed, there is nothing in the mountain forests to bestow. With tattered rags embracing the lingering clouds, one sits dazed upon the *pútán* (grass mat) and penetrates through.
Changqing Ling rolled up the curtain and awakened to the Way; it was like a diseased eye seeing floating flowers. Xianglin Yuan wrote "Great Robe" upon a paper garment;
with sleeves torn, they vied to emerge from within. Ducks are short, cranes are long; donkeys precede, horses follow. (Patting his knee, he said: I do not know what to laugh at.
Breaking the mouths of others.
Ascending the hall to thank the Daoist for returning from his mountain excursion. "Only the Sage is able to take all things as himself. (Holding up the staff) O Staff!
You despise the Buddha and refuse to act as one; you do not abide in the ranks of either the mundane or the sacred, yet you have created an enemy for yourself.
What further thing is there to be understood? Wandering at dawn on Mount Tante, lodging at dusk on Mount Luofu; at Yandang and Tiantai, roaming freely according to conditions.
Trudging through the green grass paths, lying exhausted at the base of the white clouds—how leisurely and carefree! What a life of joy and ease!
Now tell me, who is the fellow traveler? (Leaning on his staff, he looks around and says: Listen! Entering the hall:
A new thread has been added to the embroidered chamber; with a golden needle, they compete in ingenuity to craft a mandarin duck.
(Holding up his whisk, he says: Who knows how long this is? Do not recklessly measure it with tortoise hair.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] addressed the assembly for the sake of Inspector Qin’s entrusted water-land ritual: "Where is the wish-fulfilling jewel? Gather it all with your whole heart into the secure treasury.
Light as a hair-tip, yet heavy as a mountain; base as gold, yet precious as soil. It cannot be opened by the hammer of a wheel; though scattered by the Vairambha winds, it gathers back together.
What need is there to speak of the Sui pearl that illuminated a chariot-load? Even the Zhao jade, worth a city, is difficult to compare with this."
Have you not seen Master Yū riding his donkey across the broken bridge? He fell and was killed, yet he knew where he had fallen.
A chilling cold light shines through the ages. And have you not seen this monk Jaku? His whole body has a mouth, yet it is difficult to swallow or spit out.
He pours forth the pearls from the bamboo basket and respectfully offers them to the two elders of Tōji. Whom can these family treasures be entrusted to? Inspector Kin, *nyo*! Remember this well.

A small *can* for a winter night: a place beyond yin and yang, where the roots of evil grow long; branches and twigs do not sprout, and flowers bloom without shadow.
It forms clusters of fruit; its color is not blue, yellow, red, or white, yet it possesses form. Its flavor is not sweet, sour, bitter, or astringent, yet it is replete with nourishment.

Now, meeting this auspicious season of "Writing on the Clouds," I have broken open the bag of stinginess and presented it whole upon the platter;

To cast aside one's arms and walk forward is precisely what constitutes having a share of true freedom; thus, one does not fall into the lowly class of those within the Buddha-dharma.

As for what is called the lowly class of those within the Buddha-dharma: it refers to those who steal names and usurp robes, who live off our school by proxy, who wage fierce battles for fame and profit, and who indulge their passions in mere peddling—such as these are excluded from this category.
To point out those who possess even a slight foundation or who harbor some degree of will and knowledge, they would be considered superior; yet instead, they rush toward [the aforementioned path].
This is the inferior [approach]. Some, perhaps having caught a glimpse of the path of subtle principles, drift midway and refuse to press forward;
they then claim that the myriad dharmas are swept away into emptiness and suddenly deny cause and effect.

Or, having caught a stray word or half-phrase from the treatises of the ancients or from the lips of various masters, they compose flowery prose like "four-six" parallelism and store it within their bellies, pasting it...

Throughout their foreheads, they everywhere treat the superior stream with contempt and commit acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). Sometimes they flaunt their own strengths while disparaging the shortcomings of others;

sometimes they value long-standing practice while slighting those who are beginners; sometimes they honor partial views while rejecting the hearing of the Perfect Teaching (*vairocana-śruti*); or they lose the profound capacity for awakening while boasting of their clever eloquence.
Rather than being laughed at by the wise, what is the cause of this ailment? It is simply because they do not establish a great resolve or give rise to a great vow.
There is no reality whatsoever; they strive only for the superficial and hollow. It is like planting spring branches in loose soil:
though they may flourish for a time, they soon wither. This is the malady of those with sharp faculties, which one must recognize.

As for those of dull faculties, they contend over non-entities, stubbornly clinging to a rigid emptiness that lacks any penetration. They grasp at this as if it were a wooden puppet, unaware that it is not a wooden puppet.
They grasp at it as being walls and take no account of its not being walls. They see gods and see ghosts; they laugh one moment and weep the next.
When a demon has possessed the mind, ten thousand medicines cannot resolve it. If one possesses sharp faculties, they turn their backs on the Dharma Hall and depart wearing straw sandals;

they see the beckoning fan across the river and hasten toward it. Those of dull faculties sit until seven cushions are worn through; only when they roll up the curtain and see the whole world do they finally [awaken].

I pick it up. On Huangbo’s staff there is no eye of life; on Dayu’s tongue lies a dragon-spring sword.

“Sit. Gu then withdrew. [The Master] picked up the case:
Linji and Magu were like two armies of a million soldiers arrayed against each other at the front lines;

The pebbles strike one another. Looking at it with the correct eye, what is this but the play of small children?
Verse: The Great Compassionate One’s true eye is revealed in full majesty; A flash of lightning flickers constantly a hundred paces away.
Seized by a wind-crazed physician, he has been blinded; In the darkness, he drags others down from the meditation seat.

To paint a tiger and end up with a wildcat. Verse:
The palace maidens with white hair do not understand sorrow; Yet they still wear flowering branches upon their heads.
Once favored by the King because of Yu'er, she expected her appearance to remain as it was before.

Do you understand? At the immortal altar no guests arrive; at the ghost market the people are full."

How can this compare to sating one's pure dreams in mountain valleys? A waning moon through half the window, pine shadows sway.

He did not go up the mountain to pay his respects. The Master said, "Do not speak of Nanquan appearing in the world; even if the thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, I would still not go to pay my respects.

The Governor said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," whereupon he pulled down the curtain and departed. Upon returning, he related this to Nanquan.
Nanquan said, "I have always suspected this man."
[The Master] picks up [the whisk]. Nanquan and his son met with a fall on level ground; to this day, no one has been able to help them up.

and in the absence of such analytical knowledge, do not discriminate what is real.

Verse: Eating porridge and eating rice, Listening to the wind and listening to the rain while sleeping— The entire splendor of the world has been purchased, Yet not a single coin was spent.

Case: A monk asked, “What is the pure Dharma-body? Yunmen said, “A flower-planting railing.

[The Master] holds up [the whisk]. To advance a person is as if placing them upon one's knees; to retreat a person is as if casting them down a precipice.
Yunmen’s letting go was more foolish; Xuedou’s gathering in was more perilous. Do you all have such a moment?

The Great-Eared Tripitaka Master attained the power of knowing others' minds. One morning he had an audience with Emperor Suzong, who ordered the National Teacher to test his abilities.
Zang bowed to the Master and stood in attendance to his right. The Master said, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds?
Is this so? Zang replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Tell me, where is the old monk right now?
Zang replied, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation; how could he be watching the boat races in Xichuan? The Master asked again. Zang replied, "The Master..."
"Since you are the teacher of an entire nation, how can you be here on Tianjin Bridge watching a monkey being performed?
He asked this a third time: "Where is the old monk now? Zang was ignorant of his whereabouts, and the National Teacher rebuked him, saying: [The text ends here].
This wild fox spirit—where is his power of knowing others' minds? [The Master] picks up the whisk and says:

"Where? he asked. The Master replied, "The National Teacher is the teacher of an entire nation; why then does he ply his trade within a ghost cave?
Had he been able to respond thus, even if the National Teacher had not raised his banner high, he would have been compelled to raise his hands and touch his forehead in reverence.
Verse: A clod of rotten mud wrapped in gold— He does not spare himself as he displays it for all to see;
Having been caught in the breach and exposed to others' scrutiny, In the end, he is once again deceived by that very thing.
King Prasenajit asked: "Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), is there also the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) or not? If one says..."
"There is one who... (and so forth, including the lines about scooping water and splashing the mandarin ducks). The Buddha said: "I now have nothing to say, and you likewise have nothing to hear.

'In various shades of cloud-color they emerge from the mountain peak; in one uniform sound of spring water they fall before the railing.'"

"Mañjuśrī! The old man said, "How can there be two Mañjuśrīs? As Wuzhuo rose to prostrate, the old man did not see him. [The Master] remarked:
"It is laughable that Wuzhuo, with a thief right before his face, could not catch him; he merely shut his door and cried out in distress. What common ground for conversation was there?

The old man has a plan to soar to the heavens; he can even cause one to enter three feet beneath the earth.

through arduous toil, he achieved success. Thus, when the fragrant breeze blew from the south, a coolness arose within the palace halls.

He revealed the place where all Buddhas are born, and the life-force of the "Plucking the Flower" transmission was tied with a single thread capable of supporting a thousand *qun*. Though severed, it was renewed; its great achievement remained without a master.
How could this be anything less than a small contribution? I lament that while I contemplate the ancient canons and classics, I look up to them as if toward the peaks of Mount Dou;

yet now, beholding this Heart Sūtra written by his own hand, with its wondrous calligraphy soaring like dragons and dancing like phoenixes, its brilliant spirit overwhelming the observer, I have bathed it thrice and perfumed it thrice, unable to bear parting with my hands from it.

Were it not for a wondrous realization of ultimate emptiness and a penetrating insight beyond all phenomena, how could one have illuminated the flaws inherent in the void? A "night-light" gem may be found in the market, but such a treasure is difficult to seek.
This is truly difficult. You, O Superior One, must treasure this. The assembly for the *bāzhàn* (vassa) retreat charts the Way of our Patriarchs:
it flourishes when the right person is found, and perishes when the right person is lost. From antiquity, the sages and worthies have served as protectors both within and without.
For example, lutes, harps, and zithers must rely on skilled hands to produce their finest sounds;

phoenixes and qilin appear only at their proper times before they can be considered supreme omens. Now, observing this scroll: those who uphold the Dharma are all dragons among monks, and those who seek the Way are all elites among men.
Even the elderly, the young, and the middle-aged—carrying baskets or leaning on hoes, gathered in circles around thatched cottages—discuss the Unconditioned.
This account of his life treats birth and death as a game; were it not for his authentic practice, how could he have reached such a state?

Alas, when one contemplates his exemplary conduct, one’s forehead breaks into a cold sweat. Nor can this be known as a mere painting. How could it be that a fledgling practitioner would merely run after the heat of the moment like a peddler?

Those who hang up sheep while selling dogs—those who injure and destroy the Dharma-gate—are spoken of in the same breath. Therefore, I have composed a eulogy for each, respectfully inscribed upon them.
It is as if using five colors to embroider the Great Void; yet how could the monastic forests lack those capable of wielding the brush of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* to re-edit this record?
The celestial palace of Vṛtra may serve as its capital; the *Discerning Mirror of Right and Wrong Scriptures* is re-engraved and polished anew to emit pure radiance.
Gold refined a hundred times is supple enough to be bent around a finger, yet the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" lacks the marks of a Great Being.
Instead, you burden others and risk injury to your own hands and feet. Why not simply prepare yourself beneath the bright window? Why?
For if you do not find strange what is strange, that strangeness will vanish of its own accord.
Attendant Qing, you seek the Dharma-talks of Master Bami’an for Attendant Ning, titled "The Thousand Sages’ Crown.
Before parents were born, the "biting the bullet" spiritual mechanism shone with light that illuminated the heavens.

Were it not for the clear penetration of the eye of wisdom, it would be difficult indeed to see through it. Master Mi’an has revealed it directly before us; it is like a thunderclap at the Dragon Gate, where peach blossoms bloom.

The waves are warm; the transformed fish and dragons all rely on the power of their scorched tails. Within this, there is opening and closing, yielding and seizing, sustaining life and destroying the household.
Heretical teachings are difficult to support; one must post talismans at the gates of ghosts. Attendant Qing, do not begrudge sharpening the long sword that reaches the heavens.

He has washed away all demonic influences and vindicated Ning the Attendant from his grievance. He is a true disciple of Liu Xiahui; in these degenerate times, he is like a gourd floating in midstream.
You should take note of him and await his future development.
The verse says:
"Mixing mud with water for many springs; it is only valued that one gains a body by following the current. Deeply dig at the crest of the white waves."
The pit: in old age, one especially understands how to bury people alive.
At the Black Mountain, where Buddhas and patriarchs cannot look up, it is dark and murky, silent and towering. Let go within a flash of lightning.
The Path: pressed upon, the entire body sinks into the Iron Encircling Mountains.

The two streams flow toward the source, their orthodox lineages vying to branch out; which fountainhead would ever allow itself to be lowered? How laughable are those who attempt to cut off the current!
The mats are spread; from the east one passes through, and again from the west.
Yunxi has once and for all cut off the path across the clear waves; dense shadows are layered like a painted bridge. One sets foot upon it without knowing its depth.
In this matter, one must surely break the waist of the blind donkey.
Wuan’s body is like a withered tree leaning against a cold cliff; the profound mystery is utterly consumed, leaving nothing of the sort. One simply persists in such dull stupidity.
*Tat*. Following the teaching, the walls collapsed and the fences fell down.

Old Qian possesses eyes that penetrate all directions; he has cast away his cataracts and blindness. Who would be willing to walk one step ahead of others? He has searched throughout the four continents seeking someone who could surpass him.
Let it be. It appears not to be the work of an old master.

The Dragon Abyss has not yet displayed its claws and talons to stir wind and clouds; the light of the Jade Mirror is cold and clear, unstained by dust. Last night, the cold waves lightly dipped [into it].
The Moon deceives countless seekers of pearls.

Upon the ancient shore, before heaven and earth were yet cleaved, he established a heroic foundation. Snowy waves roll in cold surges, striking the enclosure daily; let those beneath his feet be driven to the brink.
Pressing forward, one goes directly along a single path to return with others.
When the perception of visual objects has been exhausted, the eye-sphere is empty; even if Mount Sumeru were ten thousand layers thick, it would not compare to Lingyun’s preservation of the mirror.
Awakened! The peach blossoms have replaced the master of the house.

Ten thousand streams rush forward before the eyes, severing the cliff; a single aperture amidst the whirlpools is beyond all contrivance. Deep as the abyss, one sees through to the source of spiritual vitality.
At the very bottom, how could even a grain of sand fit?

The great functions of two, three, four, seven, and the evil mechanisms—they vie with one another in their verbal acuity, fighting with feverish deception. There is no need for this mountain monk to strike but once.
Pointing his finger, he cast it all down toward Mount Cakravāḍa;
the old barbarian Wujin transplanted the flowers of the Garden of Enlightenment. Five leaves joined in fragrance, arriving one after another; they vex the spring breeze without ceasing.
Day after day, one branch blooms and another blooms.
The woodcutter Zhiyin has felled a log so heavy he cannot lift it; together with the clouds, he casts it down beside his pillow. His dreams no longer wander into the human world.
The World: Who would dare transmit the broken bowl of Huangmei?
A single face of Stone Wall, steep and towering, beyond all contrivance; the place where one stands is like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Old Lu asked another to write for him—no.
Attained! On spring days, the long mosses flourish; a temporary hut is carved out of empty space, its framework illusory.
From the beginning we have lived together, yet did not know its name; one laughs at those who borrow a position to manifest their merit.
At the very bottom, one mistakenly recognizes the sound of raindrops on the eaves.

When the ladle-stream of Qiandao [Piaoquan] is split open before one's face, the kalpa-jar is shattered; though the source is seen through, the eyes still contain sand. Linji’s grandfather has obtained it.
The ladle. The entanglements are soaked and rotted, yet sprouts emerge once more.

Perching upon crags, he breaks off the branches of the withered vine; leaning against the precipice, he topples the phrase of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Their tracks are vainly sought; there is no place for you to settle.

Ceasing all martial expeditions, he shattered the mirror of Xuanyuan and burned the Yellow Stone Scripture. With his slender cane, his springtime vigor robust, he visits woodcutters and fishermen under the moon.
Snowy Cliffs (II).
Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, one crosses the wind of jade; where there is no place to touch or grasp, there are traces of passage.
Treading out the seal of Vairocana with straw sandals, one sees it clearly even across ten thousand layers.
Empty flowers cloud the eyes, obscuring roots and stems; upon this plain white ground, who knows that such extreme danger has arisen?
Reaching the limit of the single color, one must let go; there is no esoteric path for people to travel.
The style of the western window is the direct transmission from the ancestral patriarch’s house; beneath the low eaves, the setting sun is often seen slanting.
Although one may open wide the eye that penetrates all directions, when the ox passes, its tail still sticks out as before.
The foolish old man’s cleverness is exhausted, leaving him as if blind and deaf; yet when there is no way to adapt, he finds the way to adapt.
Having obtained the bottomless bowl of Huangmei, he opens his aged eyes with a smile and becomes intoxicated by the spring breeze.
The Mirror Hall is neither bright nor dark, nor is it a stand; let the myriad forms appear as reflections at will.
Just as the old barbarian (the Buddha) broke through the wall with his writing—where there was no dust, yet there was dust.
The old recluse has washed away the dust of the thousand sages’ wondrous functions until all is clear; the abyss of the mind is free from dregs and is naturally luminous.
To speak in vain of "effortless function" in one’s white-haired years is like planting flowers in the sky and expecting them to bear fruit.
Yuanzou has grasped that one pivotal mechanism of the primordial state; there is not a single character or trace within his breast.
He sits directly atop the heads of the thousand sages, not permitting his descendants to know it casually.
The level mountain is a single mirror-surface; it is not a place for carving or chipping away. Moreover, it has no heights or depths with which to compete with others.
If you intend to seek the profound path from the very summit, you must guard your footing against treacherous pits.
With eyes fixed on the surface, one spends a lifetime chasing waves and following the current; having not yet seen the source, one refuses to rest. One knows not how deep the caverns may be;
gazing at the precipice, it brings sorrow to all who look.
The Pagoda of Shushan (II):
The monk’s flaws are not even a scattering of stars; he was merely granted a prophecy by a bystander.
As the pine waves of ten thousand ravines shake the bright moon, one mistakenly hears the sound of a reverse vomit across the creek.
Still alive, you were buried by the waters; a single melody from Xinfeng is heard no more.
How pitiable is the young dancer of the Cao family—instead of marrying the spring breeze, she has wed the white clouds.
The master of the "Awake Stone" has already been forcibly given a name; why wait for a trivial single call?
Those who sit so long that they pierce through the stone remain, as ever, in a state of non-awakening.
How many times has the spring breeze played its melodies in the ancient peach immortal garden? After three thousand years, the fruit has finally matured.
Once, with a single drop of blood from a branch, he exchanged the two eyes of Lingyun.
Roasting yams over dung fires, the lingering fragrance fills my midday dream. The rotting *huangdu* tubers serve as a substitute for spring vegetables.
The mountain boy hastens to close the wooden gate, Fearing that stray clouds might lead the imperial summons.
Seeing off Brother Yuan of Xuedou as he returns to Shushan:
The brocade mirror is thickly adorned with flowers in the style of Shu. In a place free of dust, one stirs up dust.
It would be well to go back and tell the daughter of the Cao family: She has already broken through the hall.
Seeing off My Elder Brother Chun for Mount Jiang (a discourse on Jing Mountain, containing the teaching of "selling empty space"):
Old and decrepit as Lingxiao, yet thorough to the bone; I force myself to write a blank deed to sell empty space.
If you wish to use ruler and compass to measure length and shortness, You must go to Mount Zhong to ask Master Baogong.
Sent forth like an elder brother, he saw the withered paulownia tree;
a single word from that withered tree was mistakenly passed down. It has obstructed and blocked countless ordinary people. When everything is shattered into a hundred fragments, you must leap out;
do not let yourself remain sitting by the side of the Dharma.
Sending My Brother Ming to Tiantong (After the Fire at Jingshan) An ancient piece of silk wraps a block of scorched paulownia; its color still bears the crimson glow of the kalpa-ending fires.
I present it to Tiantong to play a single melody, its notes dripping *ding-dong* before the wind and beneath the moon.
I see my elder brother Qing off to visit Tiantong;
he also calls upon the former Baogong and the latter Baogong at Shixi. Their manifested bodies preach the Dharma at Linglong. In seeking them out, there is no need to deliberate on host and guest;
the twelve gates of the face are fundamentally one and the same.
Seeing Brother Jie Return to Ziyun’s Ink Pond (at Mount Jing there is an ink pond of Dongpo):
Holding aloft a slender rattan cane against the wind, I came to explore the ink-washing pool of the Immortal Dongpo. The stains upon my person are difficult to wash away;
Upon returning home, do not let Ziyun know.
Seeing Brother Yue Return to Zhuangjiang to Visit His Mother:
Ten thousand layers of dense shade reflect falling flowers; A single river flows with ripples like seal-script. The mother’s natural countenance is without concealment;
To see it clearly is to have truly arrived home.
Shi Xi fled to Yan-dang to seek refuge; returning to Tiantong, he nested among the clouds.

His eagle-like wings, once keen for soaring to the heavens, now grow weary of such heights. Beneath the crags, amidst deep clouds, he settles securely in his nest. Let him close both eyes to the anxious foxes;
he fears only startling the flock of egrets as they rest upon the cold treetops.
The Geese Peak, carved like jade, locks in layers of shadow; it seems as if the face of the Meiyang miasma has turned to spring. Turning my head, I hear the celestial drum of poison being beaten;
how could the cries of grievance stop at thirteen people? (Hui)
Celebrating the Mountain of Discernment at Heqian, he retired from the Twin Forests to Mount Jinshan;

when the moon rose after three watches and he emerged from his samādhi beneath the twin *tao* trees, he mounted the golden tortoise astride and sported across the eight directions. Tucking the monastery gavel under his sleeve, it struck with a harsh, piercing sound;
even Cloud of Virtue dared not take the lead.
He Tianxin, the Head Seat, has ceased weaving his rush sandals to support his parents. He enters the eye of a gnat to stir up dust and smoke.
Using only the hand that dispatches Yunmen, he further connects with Linglong to take on another person.
Sent to Dongchuan Benzhi Taibai (whose native village has the "Buddha Who Bows His Head").
The perilous road at Wansong Pass winds and turns; The gate is closed by deep clouds, with ample space remaining. It does not hinder the Buddha from bowing his head;
He simply intends for people to see the jewel upon his brow.
The Guest House at Yunwo Hermitage serves those who come;
we look up to its legacy as a true transmission. Receiving people lies entirely within the reach of the mattock; there is no need for idle anxiety when the moment arises.
There is naturally the spring mountain where the wu-erh ferns stand upright like raised fists.

Seeing my elder brother Jun return to Taoyuan to visit his mother, I lament that the dust of the foreign lands obscures our homeland so it cannot be seen. Paddling my boat deep into the family home of Wuling, the wild peach blossoms reflect the face of my mother;
do not let your eyes be like those of Lingyun, who allowed the sands to settle upon them.
Shushan Sends Off Daozhou Returning to Xiangxi (Adept at Portraiture):
The brushwork is elegant and spirited; the gaze is intimate and keen. He has captured the true likeness of Shushan the Dwarf.
Unfurling it gently beside the "Wild Geese" painting, Who would say this is not the man from Daozhou?
Shushan Sees His Brother Return to Xuansha:
Shushan found the daughter of the Cao family; She dances seductively in the western wind, knowing no shame.
Returning to give her blessings to Master Xie, He spared her from being left to rot in a fisherman’s boat.
Lamenting the Age: Master Yuyan’s Imperial Edict flies about the head of his broken bed.
With a high pillow at the foot of a pine root, he sleeps his rest. The mountain birds cry until they are spent, yet he does not wake;
the moss-covered window is empty, locked by the melancholy of evening clouds.
Seeing off My Brother Jing for Tiger Hill:
The tiger at Tiger Rock is too fierce and savage; On level ground it seizes men, bringing them from death back to life.
Turning once against the western wind, It pulls out two or three tufts of whiskers from its chin.
Gathering bracken, parting the clouds to seek it atop the layered peaks; amidst the thornbushes, a path leads through. Lifting up a single fist, he manifests both killing and giving life;
the bottomless leaking basket holds the spring breeze.
Roasting bamboo shoots, the young ones call out to one another as they shed their silken robes; this springtime offering is no less than the ferns of Mount Shou.
Turning over and leaping into the furnace to bathe—only those who can penetrate this "biting the arrowhead" mechanism of the mountain monk may succeed.
Mowing the reeds, a living path opens at the head of the hundred grasses; through the precipice, the mechanism penetrates thousands of layers. Long and short are all excised and eliminated;
gathering and releasing are entirely brought under one's own command.
Splitting firewood, branches and leaves fall in a chaotic tangle like hemp; Without hesitation, he strikes once from the very beginning. Startled, the iron snake hastily flees into the grass;
The sound of the woodcutter’s song reaches the old Lu family home.
I send this purple-sheathed tea, its flavor shared with the "Bamboo Dragon" of Shichiku at Tiger Hill;
it swallows the essence of spring and its fragrance enters the vine-thatched window, making the midday dream pure.
One might laugh to hear the new spring water drawn to trouble Lu Yu, yet it serves to make the eyes of the venerable masters grow ever clearer.
Sent as a congratulatory verse to Master Meiweng of Tiantong (II):
A glutton of eighty years has sprouted new teeth; He chews the void until he spits out its dregs.
Examining the grass beneath Linglong Rock, Every branch and every leaf is a *tánhuā* (dharma-flower).
Receiving people in the chamber of tally-sticks, he refuses to conform; employing living military tactics, he does not meet the blade’s edge.
Holding fast at the secure pass, yet letting others through with ease; one person marks a single pine tree.
To transcribe the verses for seeking the *Avataṃsaka*—
if the Chan monk’s application were to deviate from this, how could he ever be willing to come sniffing at the Dragon Palace? With thick black ink rubbed upon white paper,
layer upon layer of inexhaustible lotus flowers bloom.
In ancient times, before the Seven Buddhas, Guqiao once displayed his wares: it was clearly nothing but a piece of rotten, withered firewood. Old Lu did not know how to carry it;
now there is no place to bury the embers.
The Hui-hsiang monk with no learning and missing teeth performs many antics; he beats a drum in empty space and sings a folk song.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth laugh aloud together, yet they cannot do anything about the deaf man’s ears.
Tiantong sends this to Jianshaozhan at Jiangxin Donggu:
"My life’s livelihood is poverty to the very marrow of my bones. I trouble you to tell it to Elder Brother Liao:
Ever since dwelling among the phoenixes and dragons, No one has entered the jeweled hall to walk beneath the bright moon."
Tiantong sees Brother Shen off as he returns to Huzhou to gather firewood:
He enters deep into the Wansong Pass; Treading through mist and clouds, he traverses several mountains. His shoulder pole breaks, and only then does he realize the bundle of wood is heavy.
Shaking his head, he turns back to sing of the curved moon.
Seeing Brother You off for Yangshan:

Yangshan’s livelihood is truly meager; he has but a small patch of fallow field where he plants his baskets of millet. He goes there and turns the soil with a single hoe to its very depths, then listens as the other joins his palms and asks, "How is it?"
Jingci sends Attendant Gong to Tiantong to consult with Wukong’s Iron Hammer three or five hundred times.
(Dachuan’s words: Forged within the furnace of smelting gold, it is cast forth;
with a single light toss, it strikes open the resonant aperture.
In the Bright Moon Valley, he transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with his own blood. By imperial grace, he was summoned once to the inner court;

he made a vow and broke off a finger from his mother’s hand. His blood stained the spring breeze as various flowers blossomed; their fragrance wafted through the Dragon King’s palace until it filled it entirely.
A barbarian monk caught its scent, and his nose was twisted sideways.
A vast expanse of cold light over Pingxi is profound and still, flowing not. Through all time, who has understood how to seek its source?
Though the lands to the east and west are as level as the palm of a hand, they do not permit Nanquan to idly herd his oxen.

The ancient cypress does not recognize the spring beyond the *Vaiśvānara* eon; it mistakenly uses the intent of the Western Patriarch to deceive people. Most who are in such a flurry merely seek out branches and leaves;
who will penetrate the *dharmakāya* within this withered trunk?

A gushing stream on level ground suddenly turns into waves a thousand feet high; swallowing the void and drenching the sun, its momentum flows on and on. The mechanism for cutting through the current is steep and sharp—no one can recommend it.
In vain do they speak of Taling treading the broken bridge.
Quanshan has personally received the true pulse of the spiritual source; he knows how to turn his body within the mechanism of the precipice.
Do not let the mountain peaks collapse and the deep pools overflow, drowning the vast multitude of people across the great earth.
Originally, there was not a single drop from which Great Waves could arise; once the source is struck, it is as vast as the sea.
Raising the oars, one loses track of the path—how many times has one mistaken peach blossoms for the Valley of Flowers?
Three bamboos bend in the room and two lean askew; the path is straight, and the gate opens like the character "eight.
If you intend to seek the way into the emerald peaks, know that he will deceive how many who come.
Shun’s elder brother, Nanshan, became a monk.

Later, returning to Donglin, he was reborn as a white-fanged tiger whose gaze flickered with light. Unwilling to remain at Nanshan and clinging to his old nest, he turned back toward the west wind and strode away.
People were startled when he could not even pass over the Tiger Brook Bridge.
Because my elder brother sought to stay but could not, he requested that I speak of the "small pit for men" at Qingfeng. At first it was said to be level and smooth, yet suddenly danger arose;
it was not that he would not allow one's feet to lightly step in, but rather he wished for him to seek another path to travel.
I heard that Master Guian has departed for Louzhi, leaving behind a pair of coarse footprints. Clearly, he played with the false and yet made it real. Take up your spades and dig from the very heels;
do not tread upon the spring mud to confuse others.
Sending off Attendant Wù to return to Tiantai to bury his father.
He did not learn from Nàzhā, who tore his own flesh to restore his parents; rather, this young novice possessed a wicked mechanism—delivering a single punch, he killed him and buried him deep.
He turned Tiantai upside down to serve as a "mountain of longevity" (as did Gāo Shāmí of the same monastery).
The current Master Xingkou has sought these words;
the twenty gates of mystery are all swept away. The great void is vast and open, the lunar disc stands solitary. Turning the body, he passes directly beyond the limit of Aeon of Majesty;
once this is attained, there is no more of those mad flowers that cloud the eyes.
Penglai and Weina are called Mount Ao;
seeking words, one severs the fishing reel of Ren Gongzi. Waves surge and peaks stand like pillars for thousands of fathoms; only when Lang Zeng awakens from his dream does he realize the peril.
Letting go at the precipice, the heart that clings to life dies.
My elder brother’s sobriquet is "Immovable.
To seek his words is like trying to turn back ten thousand oxen or break through with a hammer and mallet—a stubborn stone such as this, there is not a second one in the world.

The patched robe, its whole body shattered into a hundred fragments— Who can understand how to mend it? At Mount Kukkuṭapāda, he will carefully store it away; In the future, he shall ask Maitreya about it.
The Great Void.
Vast and empty, utterly devoid of boundaries; a single speck of cloud arises, obscuring the dust before the eyes. When one truly attains non-doubt, the myriad phenomena merge into oneness;
yet one must further know that there is a path to turn the body around.
Seeing off a Monk Returning to Yuelu:

Ink-transmitted Lamp, sleeves dancing in the autumn wind’s tail, slender rattan cane. Returning south to Yuelu to behold the Lamp Transmission, First seeking the ancient hall where he once walked in meditation, To awaken the monk who suffered that fall back in those days.

An ancient patchwork robe, half-draped over the shoulder, embraces a fragment of lingering cloud. Transmitted by the Seven Buddhas down to the present day, it is so tattered and worn that it can barely be held;
yet, as the morning sun shines bright, one may skillfully apply the golden needle.
The Moon-Elder’s midnight light floats within the womb of the jade hare; moving through space without a trace, the mirror-case opens.
The old monk is not to be found within clarity; come, let us meet before birth itself.
Transforming winter fruits, honeyed fruit grows atop the *agallochum* tree. To mark the occasion of the "Clouds Gathering" festival, I pick it up and bring it forth.
Those with eyes on their tongues will be shattered into a hundred pieces; this surpasses Pang’s upward-turning pivot.
The Lazy Old Man’s mouth grows white mold; he fears to speak a word. Time and again he raises himself, only to fall back into sleep. Let the Buddha-dharma rot away through neglect;
the scales of judgment do not rest with this old man.
The old farmer beats the soil on his slash-and-burn field, rejoicing in a bountiful year; this is no mere plaything for children.
When asked about matters prior to the time of Fuxi, he holds his hoe upside down and dances in the spring breeze.
The practitioner Zhiyou sought this verse at the Ancient Mirror Terrace before Mount Taibai in Tiantong:
Dust has settled, yet it stirs up dust once more; Lay down that rotten wooden peg from your shoulder!
Quickly, right here in the hall, smash it to pieces!
The kudzu vines on the slope have spread for years, becoming ever more deep-rooted. With a single stroke they are severed, leaving no cause for rebirth.
One does not realize that where the Great Way has declined, how many people in their frantic haste have been tripped up and brought low.
Master Nü may unleash a torrent of eloquence to deceive the foolish, yet when his principles are exhausted and his words spent, his mouth falters; in his haste, he cannot manage to speak,
only looking at one another as they stroke their white beards.

Seeing off my brother Bian as he returns to Songjiang, I hear the clear cries of gibbons cease amidst the mist and clouds. Though his voice and appearance are pure and true, he has not yet reached home. With a single tune of Wu-song, his return boat is steady;
in Songjiang, snowflakes fall upon white duckweed flowers.
The dark peak reaches the ultimate subtlety, rending asunder ten thousand divergences; the natural bird-path is beyond all contrivance.
If you wish to exhaust the turning-over phrase at the very summit, guard against the precipice within the subtle and profound.
Inscription for Piyun Pavilion: The great earth is vast and dark; the sun and moon have long been shrouded. With a single sweep of my mountain-cane brush, spirit and scene meet.
The eight directions are pure and free of dust; the myriad phenomena are but veils within a mirror. Looking out from beyond the heavens, I laugh as I tear the balustrade to pieces.
Following the head monk back to the hometown of Tianyi, I returned to visit the old fishing cloak of Jingxi.
Beholding the geese’ shadows sinking into the waves across the vast sky, I swept them away with the wind until no trace remained.
How could a pure land ever tolerate a person’s excrement?
An old man stands alone, a veteran of the earth’s axis; his mind has no dual function, rending asunder a thousand distinctions.
Since he first trod the Way beyond the limits of time, how many times has he beheld flowers blooming upon withered stumps?
A man of integrity (Master Chong-lun requests a poem):
A lifetime of steadfast adherence to the principles of Juyan; Having endured every hardship, you have attained mature wisdom. Chrysanthemums spray their late fragrance, pines defy the snow;
With a short staff supporting his frail frame, he seeks his covenant daily.

When Yanqing Hua sat in meditation, his gaze level and his breath suspended, severing all external conditions as he entered samādhi, the matter beneath his heels was as soft as mud. Mudzhou carried him out on a single light wooden board;
his karmic ailments of Zen were cleared away without the need for a physician.

The mountain recluse knows nothing of the profit and fame of the dusty world; he idly listens to the warbling of secluded birds and quietly watches the clouds. In the age of the Sage of the Red Bow (Fuxi), there is inexhaustible joy;
basking his back beneath the thatched eaves, he has achieved some measure of merit.

Perilous peaks and stone boulders make the path of the Dharma difficult to rest upon; its dangers are like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Only upon reaching the summit does one realize how small the world is;
even when the heels of one’s straw sandals are worn through, one must press on further.
Under the hammer and tongs of the iron nail, they turn over; each one seeks to emerge sharp at the vanguard. They nail the void so that there is not a single crack or fissure;
some are complete, some are incomplete.
The lime kiln and bellows come from diligent forging; though the stone be ten times hard, the heart is reduced to ash. The Hall of the Empty King relies on its power;
water and mud are blended together in a single act.
The work of chiseling and hammering the foundation stones is seen to be complete; when moistened, one knows the jade still retains its residual warmth.
Behold them bearing their loads, supporting pillars that reach toward heaven; each and every one has nothing but firm heels.
Yellow boards, fine craftsmen, and thousands of felled trees; like splitting sandalwood, every fragment is fragrant. The Yellow-Faced Gautama receives this canopy and cover;
what harm is there in throwing bricks and striking tiles?
The potter’s toe kicks out a lump of wet clay; the marvel lies in watching where the potter’s wheel turns.
Covering the void without leakage, let the head remain shrouded in dark obscurity.

In the meditation hall, clouds vanish and the wind ceases; all sounds of the world fall silent. The thatched gate is fast-locked in the springtime of green vines. At the stone couch, day is still and the cross-legged posture is secure;
a hundred birds bring flowers, yet they do not see the person.
In the empty heart of Yunxi lay the arrow-tip pivot; who would say his subtle and profound stance was precarious? When the Great Way declined, he maintained his firm integrity;
yet Xiangyan’s single strike had not yet forgotten the knowing mind.
The Moon Rock is as level as a mirror’s surface, yet as precipitous as a cliff. When both light and object are forgotten, ten thousand distinctions shatter. Here there is no place for you to squat;
empty toil only brings one to draw flowers from the sky.
With a heart of leisure, I have intensely cultivated my love for the mountains; it has been scattered as spring across a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies.
Having risked a lifetime of never seeing enough, I seek to turn myself around within the words of the steep precipice.
Seeing an old monk at the heart of the lake, I opened a letter on a hot summer night and composed this impromptu verse:
An Eighty-year-old Mountain Elder Opens a Letter at Night Grasping the brush, my breath falters and beads of sweat flow down. I pity myself for this skeleton of leisure;
For no reason, the fires of domestic life have scorched it to withered ruin.

Master Bak-am’s conduct and hidden depths were truly like those of the ancients; he lacked even the slightest trace of deceptive cleverness. He raised his coarse fist to test the eyes of those yet to come:
had you seen it before even crossing the gate, you would have desisted.
On account of certain matters, I have inscribed this upon my seat:

when we sit close-knit by the cold window for quiet conversation, we may pause to speak of what is right and debate what is wrong. One must know that the winds and waves of the world’s path are treacherous;
with every hundred turns and thousand folds, the mechanisms of calamity are set in place.

The Snow Ox falls into the realm of a single hue of empty solidity; its horns are complete, yet its head is incomplete. On the eastern and western banks of the stream, it is difficult to catch or release;
being pure white, what harm is there in sleeping out in the open?

The Patriarch (the Honored One above the mind) takes the myriad phenomena of the universe as his seal upon the heart; there is not a single thing that can be categorized as near or distant. Daming sat upon this until it became a nest;
even unto old age, how could he ever have known how to turn his body?
Stone Well strikes hard and labors until he reaches the depths; only then does one know there is red dust beneath the water.
He opens up a single thread of the path, yet its surface is so slippery that it deceives and traps how many clear-eyed people!
Shining light upon the guest’s quest for non-obstruction, he caught a single arrow of wild thornweed; with ease, it pierced through the five Sumeru mountains.
Amidst a thousand layers and a hundred enclosures on the path ahead of the mechanism, once the target was broken, there was no longer any resistance or stagnation.
Brother Bao of Jiangxi begs for a path through Dongji and Dangyang;
once the fences are torn down, realization is achieved. Yet the Heart-Mind School of China has nearly perished;
even upon reaching home, one still stands across a vast ocean.
In the mountain retreat, the battle against the barbarians was waged and swept clean; together with the clouds, he monopolized the highest peak.
Holding aloft the matter of the broken hoe, the Buddhas and Patriarchs leave no trace when meeting his challenge.

Qichuan’s words cut off the path of speech and turn the subtle pivot; the mechanisms of the thousand sages all accord with the secret seal. To meet those of the highest caliber, he opens a single road:
when he raises his fist, do not disdain its coarseness.
A single path of solid rock, its surface as slippery as moss before the movement of the mind. Emerging from within the thicket of tangled vines, a spark flies forth upon being struck at ease;
it suddenly causes the eyes of the people of the Great Tang to open wide.
To Master Ze of the Avataṃsaka:
For half my life I have not beheld the Elder De-yun; I imagine him now walking in meditation upon a distant peak.
Once a single atom is shattered, we shall meet face-to-face, overturning the thirteen layers of the Flower Treasury World.
Sending off Mian to see the Huayan patriarch at Qinwang Mountain, he strikes the old lord with a single blow, breaking his nose until it is crooked. The monk’s habitual breath is entirely forgotten;
there is no longer any seeking of fragrance or sniffing of the various flowers.
A single water magpie stands alone on the sand, its head tucked away. Beside it, tobacco plants and withered grasses;
the marsh mist is desolate, the autumn deep. It endures the cold in solitary stillness, too weary to renew its pact with the gulls. The flavors of rivers and lakes grow increasingly harsh.
When you can tuck your head in, tuck your head in.
The youthful clouds emerge from beyond the heavens, immediately sweeping across all directions. Who would believe that such a form can arise from a mindless state?
Refusing to follow the tune set by the dragon’s command, it intends to go west yet travels instead toward the east.
For the Venerable Candrottara, I compose these verses:
The white arum floats in the autumn pool, its fragrance subtle; The cassia blossoms are pure and clear. Thoroughly bottomless, it is traceless, shimmering like crystal.
Only because it was tainted by the mind of Hanshan, To this day, its reflection remains unclear.
The practitioner Daosheng of Zhangting manages the causal conditions.

He sought a verse for the side of the broken hoe, attaining intimacy through its use. Entering the marketplace, he does not brush aside the dust of myriad functions; at the Triple River crossing, he firmly blocks the pass.
He must be seized by those who drift with the waves and follow the current.
The South Bridge has long been used for crossing donkeys and horses; what harm is there in treading through the mud? The people of Jambudvīpa vie with one another in seeking out peril;
they must be made to know the mechanism that cuts off the stream.
The ancient cliff reveals that one pivotal moment of the primordial state. Standing alone and precarious, it is inherently solitary and perilous. Countless people let go at the edge of the precipice;
though the rocks crumble and the pines wither, none take notice.
The璞庵 (Puo-ān) contains within it a jade worthy of a whole city; three times he personally presented it at the court of Chu. Even before crossing the gate, it was already polished and refined;
deep in the spring breeze, it is locked away behind green ivy curtains.
For fourteen years, the heart-mirror and the stone wall have reflected each other’s light within the weeping fence; who would have known that the illumination was lost before the skull?
Now, as spring winds dream around the roads of Fucheng, I can hardly bear to hear the chaotic cries of the cuckoos in the flower groves.

In the Pavilion of the Surging Spring, he unleashes unimpeded eloquence like a cascading river; a foot of water can stir waves ten thousand fathoms high. On level ground, he has established tiers without cause;
those who ascend are few, while those who follow the current are many.
I see off Master Zai as he departs for Tiantong to rely further on the Eye of the Teaching.

Years of practice have made him like one who has lost his sight from constant drumming; now that the golden probe has scraped away the film, his vision is restored. It is said that Tiantong possesses an ointment for cataracts:
a masterly hand applies it lightly, and immediately there is clarity.
After the fire, Great Master De of Tiantong painted five hundred arhats and the "Fifty-three Visits.
He established a hair-cutting storehouse and paved a walkway among the pines. Seeking to record these facts, he presented two verses as a gift:
"The fifty-three spiritual friends of the Southern Inquiry Roll into the five hundred oxen of Tiantai; All are defiled by Dongshan."
It is finished. Donkey jowls and horse jaws—truly shameful!
Having shaved the head until it shines, one lives in joy, singing and walking beneath the shadow of Wansong. From foot to foot is the path that reaches through the heavens;
where it is level, it is solitary and perilous; where it is perilous, it is level.
In the mountain lake beside the burial mounds, reflections swallow the sky; gulls and egrets forget their artifice as ten thousand realms merge. There is no need to bury dark arrows deep;
the one who brings life to others dwells entirely amidst the dead.

The lineage of the Seven Buddhas of Ancient Origin is a profound life-vein; it seeks only to see the tall man upon entering the water. Within the mechanism that cuts off the current lies the path of the blue waves;
as the world flows on and on, who will ask for the ferry?

Dreaming in the hermitage, with arms as pillows, he satiated himself in the "black sweetness" within the misty window. Having roamed through the realm of Huaxu, the cranes dance with grace. In this inconceivable realm, the path of total functioning is complete;
what need is there to raise a fist upon meeting someone?

Though one possesses a mountain of jewels, they are laboriously sought; how much better it is that the jewels on the mountain of form are most intimate. Meeting the source at every turn, one should gather them well;
not even a hair’s breadth is borrowed from another.

In the Unborn Hermitage, the profound mystery is refined away and the myriad realms are empty. A hundred birds carrying blossoms vainly seek its traces. Do not let yourself sit stubbornly in the cave of spirits;
the gate is locked by thousands of layers of chaotic clouds.

The North Mountain divines and decides; in the dark capital, it establishes the solitary and precarious. On all sides, steep cliffs and treacherous mechanisms are densely arrayed. One must turn one’s body within the bucket to dwell securely in its depths;
though many people gaze upward with bated breath, those who reach the summit are rare.
Bamboo windows and dense leaves strain the golden light onto the emerald sand; the moon and plum shadows move coldly across the scene. Xiangyan’s rubble was cast away in vain;
the gate is locked in deep shadow, unable to be opened by a knock.

In the Fanzhao Hall, the numinous root is vast and open, utterly free from even a speck of dust. It is simply valued that one turns the light back to see it intimately. As the sun slants, a plum blossom plays its shadow through half the window;
among those on their journey, there are still those who have not yet returned home.
