Master Yong of Shigan: Through painstaking effort, he has perfected his craft.
The sturdy gate is fastened deep within the mist of green vines. The mechanism of the precipice is so steep that no one can penetrate it;
how many times have we seen the spring mountains where the bracken raises its fists?
I send attendant Shun to visit Master Wanshou Tugeng, who dwells deep within the lakes and mountains tending to his robes and pitcher.
Mistakenly recognizing the sound of "Xiaoyu" being called repeatedly, he hurriedly covers his ears seeking a way out.
The compass needle is already pointing toward the city of Helu.
At the Fàngshān Hall, I saw Master Sòngfāng off. I encountered the Venerable Yǎnxī of Jìngcí;
though the "Tortoise-Nose" of Nánshān has no venom, once touched, it still causes one to lose their life as before. Do not fail to look directly at it while scratching an itch;
even those of "solid steel" are not entirely complete people.
In the Pure and Wondrous Chamber, the bamboo grove serves as the site for the complete and correct teaching that not a single speck of dust stands, where the basis of existence vanishes.
This entire being is numinous clarity, spontaneously radiating light. He boldly opens wide the words of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials;
lacking the power to reach others, he descends from his meditation seat.

Attendant Xianshou Deng, seeking the inexhaustible, radiant lamp of the bodhicitta, makes it shine brightly through the night chambers. One flower blooms, then another blooms; in the Hall of Universal Radiance, they are seen in successive layers.
This authentic transmission has come down from the Seven Buddhas.
Master Song sought the ancient forest’s excellence, extracting the springtime from beyond the kalpa of Wei-yin. How deep is the coiling and entwining of its numinous roots?
It gives rise to the towering tree of Linji and Qingliang, under whose shade all people throughout the great earth come to rest.
A stretch of cool shade in Songzhou has existed since ancient times. Vaguely, Linji personally planted it with his own hands.
Branch after branch and leaf after leaf hang with clear dew, causing the eyes of the people of the entire city to open.
Bieyuan (the Venerable Xianshou) did not continue the orthodox lineage of Caoxi;
rather, he branched off a single stream that flowed toward its source, spreading throughout the vast abode of Qingliang,
where the spring thunder transformed fish and dragons.
At the Moon Ravine, the spiritual source emerges from the place of empty luminosity; one sits at the edge of the profound and the tranquil.
With the resolve to courageously withdraw, the path of the mechanism is set free, overturning light and shadow before they have even arisen.
Attendant Chang seeks this Way;
a single thought of ordinariness tears asunder ten thousand errors. Awakening these people, even in nobility there is no deviance. Ancient and modern, they have all missed the road to Chang’an;
in the spring wind, flowers lie scattered along the path.
The Flower Adornment of Emptiness is named Minghai;
a single expanse of void, solid and clear, it mirrors past and present. Holding a ladle, how can one fathom its depth?
Within the thirteen layers of the Flower Treasury, they manifest in successive tiers, illuminating the hearts of ancient Buddhas within every mote of dust.
The monk Rixingtu of Pengzhou sought a verse, yet was too lazy to receive the elixir of immortality from the divine immortals; he abandoned Mount Penglai to enter a hermit’s cottage.
Do not let him mistakenly utter words about the wind and the banner, for his head has already been shaved smooth by a bystander.
A Letter Presented to Jing:
I do not study the rhymed verses of Hanshan; I turn my body to penetrate the patriarch’s mechanism. From the head of the mortar, I have pounded out the mirror that is neither this nor that;
I mistakenly received the robe of Huangmei at midnight.

The ten matters of the meditation hall and the hundred layers, a thousand folds, of the rush-wicker shrine—though wrapped in these, one still cannot avoid sitting within the Black Mountain. How many throughout ancient and modern times have been born blind! This has led them astray.
The whole body enters the grass;

the paper robe covers the entire person without a single thread hanging loose. This clarifies only the matter of the "one color" boundary. One must understand the "knots and crisscrossing patterns"; ask directly.
The meditation seat and pillow must be divided;
the Zen board requires that one’s practice be made into a single, continuous piece of work. One must rely upon it with one's whole body. Although one may see only one side, this is not yet permitted.
Muzhou carries the burden;
having realized it upon the grass mat at the tip of every blade of grass, what prevents him from striking a clod into a ball? Thus, right here, he cuts off a thousand differences; he is without mind.
It remains as if separated by heavy barriers.

This staff has been selected from beyond the boundaries of the monastic groves. His place of birth was not on Mount Tiantai; yet, though he may have stumbled like a crow or a wolf, his strength sustains us.
No matter how many people come,

as soon as the whisk gains its handle and enters their hands, they immediately wish to scold the Buddhas and revile the Patriarchs; this is what constitutes their true, original character, which is not to be compared with anything else.
In ordinary discourse, the whisk is used;

where the alms bowl is set, there is no leakage at all. When it is employed, its mouth opens toward the heavens, so that all people throughout the great earth are satiated. This is done solely for the sake of...
This one does not know gratitude.
Under the blow of the precept-knife and the cruel tongs, it is not certain that the sharp edge will be revealed; not only can it sever the cat, but it also understands [the Way].
Slaying Buddhas and patriarchs—recognize clearly the ancient seal of the incense-stamp.
Struck once with the hammer, it is complete; burn a stick of sandalwood and cow dung. This is for the patch-robed monk.
The nostrils have been pierced;
once the "itchy child" has been carved by a skilled craftsman, what prevents one from reaching out to support it? When you seize the monk’s itch-spot, I shall reward you.
A single lychee. At Hengjiang (Dedicated to Master Cheshang), the white silk ripples over the flower-waves lapping against the embankment.
Before sound and after sound, the mechanism cuts off the current; on the perilous path of the blue waves, there is no one.
Penetratingly clear. The wind rises through the reeds as white birds fly.
On the Southern Mountain (the Guest Attendant from Jiangnan), the fame of its life-giving peaks has been marked since antiquity.
The ten-thousand-year pines are short yet form a lush green shade. At the eastern fence, one plucks chrysanthemums with easeful grace.
Behold! How precious are the eyes of Yuanming, which possess sinews.
Congratulations on Hongjin’s emergence at Nengren in Yanshan;
the water flows from the mouths of all quarters. How does a single drop compare to the tip of the Dragon’s nose? It rises up, newly rinsing the spring stream.
The brocade strikes the cliff, overturning the waves of the cascading torrent;
in the second month, Cold Spring’s thunder awakens the hibernating insects. The golden-scaled fish, having scorched its tail, transforms into a dragon;
trailing behind it, a drop of water from the tip of its snout washes clean thousands of peaks at Yandang.
The Great Officer Yu of Tuan-huan fashions the phoenix-patterned ball with exquisite artistry; amidst the pitch-black expanse, it becomes truly wondrous.
He makes the foundation firm and solid, so that bystanders may naturally come to paint their own portraits upon it.
King Māndhātṛ beats a drum made of two pieces of hide, deceiving only himself. Each time he strikes it, it is ever new; its sound pierces the heavens like lethal poison.
There are those who, by nature, will stand before the wind and strain their ears to listen.
The Dwarf Wayfarer’s body is like a coconut, his mouth wide open. He has watched all the ghostly performances from every quarter arrive. Letting down one head, people do not recognize him;
Shushan, my junior uncle, is of the same womb.
My neighbor, Master Gan, has been parted from his native land for over forty years; yet in dreams and spirit, he still returns to Sōjō.
At the temple by the winding Nine-Curve Stream, spring breezes stir the blossoms as the willows play with their golden hues.
With a short staff supporting my frail form, I knock upon the misty vines. I inquire after the "Clay Drum Song" of Mount Dongshan. Old and weary, I cannot sing it;
beyond the window, the warbling of secluded birds is even more abundant.
Chanter Liai refines the raw material within the golden furnace; the exquisite carving leaves no trace of axe or chisel. Your substance naturally forms a vessel of jade and precious ritual ware;
I, for my part, am content to be a broken earthen bowl.
Once he propped up the dilapidated hut of Yangqi; Leisurely riding his donkey, he played with its hooves as it walked.
Braving the cold and treading the moonlight upon Cixi, He laughed at the "Elder Brother Plum" for being so excessively thin.

Master Cheng of Japan has swept away all karmic conditions until the myriad dharmas are empty. The clear pool does not permit the blue dragon to lie within. Turning his body, he tramples the path by which he came;
his home is upon the peak beyond the clouds of sea and mountains.

Nanquan Shanshan of Japan slung his staff over his shoulder and traveled through all quarters; the mysterious barrier of the Buddhas and Patriarchs seemed a long road to traverse. Having set aside body and mind, he returned to his former seclusion;
the golden crow continues to rise from the eastern sea as before.

Hurrying along the traveler’s road, one is weary of dust and mud. While the ant’s dream is still in its midst, the butterfly’s dream soars away. Fortunately, there is the weeping cuckoo who understands this sentiment;
with every cry, it urges: "It is better to return home."
At the ancient willow embankment by the transformed fields, the Master of Huacheng unfolds his transformative function. He requires that people, having attained one full meal, forget their hunger.
Who would take the hand that plunders food and drives the plow, and instead sow thorns upon the fertile field?
Carrying the burden of self and others, with bones exposed and skin pierced, one refuses to rest. In the dark mechanism, the Mantis and the Beetle wage war upon the snail.
Having taken both self and others upon a single shoulder, let the entire world be taught as a skull.

The wisdom-seeker Hui-chan weaves the brocade spring of Mount Min and Mount E; it is lamentable that these are now shrouded by the dust of the Hu. The golden cock still carries the remnants of its calamity;
who will follow the divine colt to trample the enemy to death?
The cool shade of Linji’s tree has withered for those who practice Chan; not a single frost-bitten leaf remains to cover his meditative posture.
His descendants do not know how to water and nourish it, instead treating it as a mere scenic illustration for the mountain gate.
A letter from the Scholar of Kiju, Ishibashi, to the Abbot Ning, requesting words (the sender is a fellow villager of Ishibashi in Kiju):
"Your wondrous paintings and heroic talent are peerless in the world; you have mastered both the Zen school and the scriptural teachings, your mind’s eye is agile and alive.
How marvelous! An aged oyster has produced twin pearls. Your legacy remains formidable for a hundred years; those who walk your path shall follow the same way."

They share the same track. The Old Fool has truly attained the "stupidity" of Tiger Head. The Moon Peak’s pure radiance shines like the moon over Mount Emei; the shadows of the parting geese fly each toward the east and west.
How many times have they sighed at their separation amidst the autumn wind? Departing for the Wu heavens, which are as clear as if washed, they join their names in calligraphy with light ink.
Let them teach people to say of themselves: "We are a pair of 'difficult elder' and 'difficult younger' brothers."

This "Flower-Jade Vegetable" from Huārui Garden in Tōngchuān, obtained by the attendant from a manuscript in Zhèyòu, is renowned throughout all of Shǔ; who among them does not cherish it? When night rain gathers upon its clusters, their color dyes them a deep azure;

when the spring breeze blows through its blossoms, they spray a fragrance like musk. One knows not from where these numinous roots were obtained, yet they have been planted everywhere across Mount Niútóu.
Later than before; ancient Buddhas looked down upon it without weariness. The nostrils of the śrāvakas were pierced by it. The Master carried its seeds to Jiangzhe;
its flavor was no different from the ferns of Mount Shouyang. Before Fuhuyan, the pure guest tasted it; the old gourmand chewed through his mother-born tongue.
He shared the remaining fragrance with Old Zhifeng, as if they were both picking small handfuls together in their own gardens. From here on—
Do not dally with trivialities. Treasure your great works as an offering of *sudhā*.
Observe how the guest returns to bury his kin;
seek words from the man of the Way, for only through observation can one know his departure. When entering the gate, one must verify the host within the guest; drink a cup of tea and then turn away.

Body! Who could wag their tongue to debate the ancient and the modern? A crisis of brilliant agility, like a crashing thunderstorm in a drought. The blue hawk’s wings are broken; the hunting dog is roasted.
Old Mingjue raises his hand to his forehead in reverence. Great Uncle Han dares to take the lead.

Deep in autumn, he clears the weeds on the path to Tiantai; he seeks his own ancestral bones to find his true parents. At the edge of the broken hoe, he digs a pit to bury them—the severed monkey wails.
The moonlight and wind whistled through the trees.
The three Vinaya masters, including the Venerable Yulimna, prostrated before the stone Buddha and requested a teaching.

"An old man from Nanshan has violated the true Vinaya. For three lifetimes he has chiseled away at the rocks of a cold cliff; yet, among those who stand upon nothing, he has forcibly established a name."
A name. Where there was no disorder, disorder is created. "Under the knees of one's descendants lies gold. Brushing away the weeds and observing the wind, he sought it afar.
Rising after three prostrations, he let out a sigh: only then did he realize the Old Man had misplaced his attention. The Buddha of innate nature and true self does not concern himself with it;
what kind of bowl could one seek from a stubborn stone? Exhausting the hammer and tongs, many flaws remain; the black staff is held tight.
I took it up and examined it from head to foot.
Attendant Miaoen requested a verse for it:
"A casket of spring brocade vies in its fresh brilliance; compared to ancient rhombus-patterned mirrors, it is exceptionally clear. When reflecting one's image, one should not call it 'small'."
Jade. To this day, travelers from across the lakes and seas harbor lingering feelings for it.
Furthermore, I recall how the Master, having encountered the fierce poisons of various quarters, returned to seek out his old, bone-chilling enemies and dug deep pits to bury them all.
Understood! Who recognizes this iron-faced skin?
The Venerable Monk Gong of Poyang requests words:
"The wind of Fan Yang stirs waves a thousand fathoms deep; he probes to the very bottom regardless of his own life. O Tower Master, call out repeatedly, 'Do not—'"
No. The mechanism for cutting off the stream is steep; I fear it might startle people.
The junior disciple Ling-sou and the attendant Wu-hai requested these words for a stele in the Azure Void.
It is neither cursive, nor regular, nor clerical, nor seal script. Like a mirror, it reflects the Yujiang River to its very depths.

The meaning of the character *Qing* (Clear) is brilliantly manifest, yet few people perceive it. Master Lingzou has treasured it through the deep passage of years. As he comes south to Wu and Yue, people vie to seek it out.

The inscription on the "Buried Crane" stele does not share its same tune; the verses of Hanshan are not for those who truly know the sound. Amidst the clamor of those asking for the characters, who is truly intimate with them?
A hook that is not quite a hook, a *piě* stroke that is not quite a *piě*—how could one hope to rival Lu Ji and match Ban Gu? Only one shouldered this burden.
Carrying firewood, he breaks through the barriers; as he departs, to whom does he secretly entrust it? Do not say that this wondrous place is not transmitted to your son.
With a resolute nature, sweep away the very traces of words: the sky of meaning is clear of clouds, and the moon is solitary and profound.
At the request of the Venerable Xing of Jianzhou:
On the spring mountain the cuckoo cries, Bitterly urging people to return home. Its broken voice mingles with the wind in the bamboo groves; Its blood stains the rain upon the flower tips.
I am old and have no home to which I can return; in my moss-covered window, I sleep soundly as clouds cling to my robes.

A mountain boy nudges me from my pillow, shattering my fragmented dream, announcing that a monk has opened the bamboo gate. "From what direction does this holy one come seeking me? he asks. Unpacking his bundle, he tosses down a copy of the *Qinglong Chao*.
He intends to set fire to it right there in the courtyard, for how could a pure ground be allowed to remain in such disorder? He asks him, "On what day..."
Li Feilai has arrived. For two months he has been rushing about, yet he has not reached home. I urge you to return quickly and find rest;
the spring wind has already caused the flowers of Lin’an to fall.
(Written at the request of Zhou Shuren of Jianzhou.)
I recall in the past, Zhou Dangren, grasping a vajra scepter in his hand, directed his indignant spirit toward the south, vowing to exterminate all the sons of Māra.

An old woman suddenly struck him with a spark, igniting the three minds; he rushed into the dragon pool, his resentment deepening. Having swept away his worldly possessions until not a single cache remained, he wielded his white staff recklessly against the common folk.
As I sit idly in the herding grounds, I contemplate his lofty footsteps; how could I ever hope to join the phoenix when its strings have been severed?
The glue continues to hold. Knocking at the door, he heard that the visitor was from Jianzhou; he rushed out in his slippers to welcome him, nearly breaking his feet.

Beyond the brief exchange of pleasantries, he asked about the purpose of the visit. With palms joined in earnestness, the guest sought a guide; before the paper lantern could even be raised, the matter was explained.
Through the window, the spring birds chirped in melodic harmony.
To Master Guduk Song at the Seon-tu Hermitage on West Mountain:

I have heard that you once expounded upon the Dharma of the void; I write this to resolve my lingering doubts regarding the Way of West Mountain. Amidst misty rain and smoke, the moss-covered rocks are warm; the traces of the Six Treasuries are difficult to seek out.
I cleared the brambles along the narrow path and knocked upon the bamboo gate; when the man of the Way saw me, he smiled.

Raising his brows, he carries his coarse cotton robe across his shoulder, lean as if carved from wood. Holding sacred mantras in his mouth, he never ceases; he sweeps the mats in the cloud-chambered eaves to welcome the summer retreat.
Fragrance of white lotuses wafts through the community of Donglin. The mountain stream and pine winds preach suffering and emptiness;
one need not rely on the intermediate state to attain pure peace. With earnest care, I send this inquiry to the aged solitary pine: within the gate of fullness lies the true lineage. It is manifest!
Hating the Buddha, he refuses to serve him; the phoenix does not dwell upon the wutong tree.
On the fifth day of the fourth month in the Wuchen year, he took leave of Donggao.
From the *Extensive Record* (Guanglu) of Master Xisou, Volume Six.
Recorded Extensively by Master Xishi, Volume Seven:
A Dedication to Shu Xiang on the Subject of a Sitting-Meditation Frog (with a white lotus below).
Once one attains clarity regarding the nature from consciousness, one ceases the clamor of springtime drums and pipes. Leisurely, one locks the gates of the six sense-faculties;
the fragrance of white lotuses disperses as the water and wind grow pure.
Inscription on Zhifu’s Ox Painting:
Three by three, five by five, he frolics across the level marshes. He tramples the spring breeze until the hundred grasses wither. Do not paint the monk from Mount Mui;
Lest people mistake him for a portrait of the Patriarch.
Inscribed on Old Rong’s Painting of a Monkey: (Sitting on a branch, reaching up with its hand to touch a fruit.

Sitting perilously upon a cold Zen branch, it harbors a lethal intent within its grasp of the bitter fruit. Even if it were to actually seize and eat it, one cannot say for certain that its thieving mind has been extinguished.
Inscription on the Painting of Yuanze:
Riding a Cold Calf under the Moon. The matters of three lifetimes have been minutely discussed; they have already been scrutinized by others. Cease playing with the ghostly spirit.
Inscription on the Ox Breaking the Halter:

The trees on the ridges are shrouded in gloom as the sun sinks toward the west; In my bitter craving for fragrant grasses, I have forgotten to return home. The cowherd boy exerts all his strength to pull me back;
Everywhere, the twilight smoke deepens the lush green of the misty heights.
Tanlao requested a colophon for the *Zhennxi Hongzhi Zhuan’an* (True Rest, Vast Wisdom’s Bamboo Hermitage). A Record of Reciprocal Verses from a Joint Excursion to Mount Yan.
Behind the scroll of the original calligraphy:
Three old demons were born together in this world; meeting on a narrow path, there is nothing that can be done. I shall now tear open their entrails and expose them.
Look! Among the many forty-nine turns of the winding path, the inscription on the Mountain Hall reads:
"One blow opens the firm barrier. Stonehead’s spiritual path is as slippery as moss; one must know well how the perils are distributed and the dangers divided.
Few. Pushing open the door, he rolls right in after them.
Du Fu rides his donkey on a spring excursion:
"The traveler's road is as vast as heaven; my singing body is too thin from life's hardships. Having no home to which I may return, I lean upon my lame beast and wander by the spring."
Li Bai Drunk Riding a Donkey:
Thirsty for wine, he longs to drink from the whale’s gullet; having retired early from court at the Golden Phoenix Gate, his drunken body cannot be supported as he bends the old donkey’s waist.
**Inscribed on the Four Orchids in the Autumn Hall:
Wind** Pointing to the jade, it strikes at dawn; its mouth of sandalwood sprays forth spring. Suddenly jealousy arises; the dark gale is unkind.

The morning sun reveals the refined ornaments of the Xiang River blossoms; the robes of Chu announce their stitching. The Yellow Emperor and Fuxi present their fragrance; their variegated colors seem truly authentic.
Rain: The jade pendants hang in disarray; they lie prostrate, buried by moss. The flowers on the eaves inscribe their grief; it is difficult to summon the soul of Chu.
Snow: Secluded rocks are sealed in white; the deep forest conceals its fragrance. Virtue remains hidden and does not shine; why boast of its color and scent?

Inscription on Orchids and Phlox: Their colors are pale yet pure; their integrity is fragrant yet steadfast. They conceal their virtue without ostentation, savoring the blossoms and harboring the essence. They share the same refined purity as the noble man;
their lifelike portrayal does not fall into the traps of mere pigment and ink. It is fitting that they embody the profound spirit of the Xiao and Xiang rivers and the secluded lands of Chu.
A single stem bearing four blossoms, it stands out prominently and excels all others. Its fragrance is like that of the orchid (*lan*), and its appearance is like that of the *zhi* herb.

Its buds cluster like smoke without being excessive; its sturdy nodes remain unbent even in a violent wind. Thus, upon this lofty mountain, it possesses the noble resolve of one who dwells in the forest.

Inscribed on Four Orchids Deeply hidden within crags and valleys, they originally seek no recognition from man. Yet this fragrance is difficult to conceal; when the spring breeze comes with favor, it blows upon them.
Clear skies delight those who play the jade fingers; beneath the forest trees, one beholds a recluse. With the elegant grace of a goddess from the Xiang River, her skin remains unstained by dust.
Rain.

The jade pendants are half scattered and disarrayed; who is it that mourns the excellence of Chu? Her soul remains unreturned amidst the fragrance of wine; in sorrow she listens to the sound of the rattling reeds.
Snow falls once more upon the desolate forest; her entire body is shrouded by the *bìluó* vines. Even if she were buried beneath them, what could be done about her nostrils?

Inscription on Four Orchids in the Autumn Hall The wind of Qu Yuan glorifies the joys of mountain and forest; its fine gauze-like stems are lightly draped, its hidden fragrance released from the heart of the wood, as it dances seductively in the spring breeze.
Intoxicated by fragrance, his strength is difficult to support.

Qíng has long dwelt within the profound seclusion of deep forests; though he conceals his virtue and does not let it shine, when met with the gentle warmth of spring, he smiles and plucks the jade zither.

I point out that tenfold spiritual power is what is required. However, I fear that the customs of Chu prize fragrances; if you were to sew them into a sash as an ornament, it might prevent you from reaching the end of your life—this would be contrary to the Way.
Thus ends the "Yu" (Rain).
When Nüying went to mourn Shun at Mount Jiuyi, her tears fell like rain; her jade pendants were scattered and disarrayed, half of them left behind in the dust and mud.
I fear that even if the "Nine Songs" of the *Li sao* were to exhaust their expressions of grief, they could never fully capture the cold fragrance of her soul, which is ultimately difficult to grasp.

When the snow falls heavily and its severity is proclaimed, the myriad trees are broken and torn asunder; yet alone it can raise its fragrance amidst the freezing rigors. Though subjected to a hundred setbacks, it does not bend;
were it not for what it has long cultivated within, how could it resist the encroachment of external insults?
For Qiu Guiyan, Director of the Bureau of Passports. Inscribed on the Painting of He Jing Viewing Plums After the Snow:
When the lake and mountains break into view at dawn, entering the realm of painting, A small boat rocks through the snow beside the sparse fence. His single mind rests solely upon the plum blossoms;
He does not even realize his own body has been chilled by the cold.
Yuanhui’s Landscape Painting:
Dense clusters of misty forests with wine signs hanging; ancient temples hidden in the mountains, silent and without monks. With my slender staff, I am about to go in search of these secluded spots;
a small boat on the opposite bank calls out, but there is no response.
For Governor Zhang Liangchen:
A Painting of Plums Titled "A Single Skiff of Spring Snow Floating on West Lake. Unaware, one’s body enters the painted scene;
The dark fragrance and sparse shadows remain for a thousand ages— Who says these cold bones cannot be summoned?

In this landscape painting, the monastery lies faintly amidst misty vines. A wine banner flutters slightly in the breeze as the wind brushes against my fishing cloak. I wish to settle in these forested clouds to seek seclusion;
the mountain spirits must surely laugh at how many people they deceive.
An Inscription for My Friend’s Waterfowl (One Water-Crane Standing Alone on the Sand; Head Bowed, with Grass Beside It) Withered grass and mist on the marsh—how desolate this autumn!
Enduring the cold, it stands alone, too weary to renew its pact with the gulls. The character of the rivers and lakes grows increasingly harsh;
When one can tuck in the head, one should simply tuck in the head.
1. The Snowy Old Woman Standing atop a withered lotus in the midst of the whistling west wind’s austere and piercing chill, the dead leaves have shed their remaining broken branches.
Amidst the violent gusts and torrential rains that repeatedly overturn everything, she alone remains standing—her very position is perilous.

From Archxiu Pavilion, ten thousand layers of distant peaks appear lush and green; at dawn’s chill, the empty azure drenches my monk’s robe. A solitary bird calls out as I sit in meditation by the ivy-covered window;
I watch idly as spring clouds, laden with rain, drift home.
For Yuanxue Ya, he inscribed "Waiting for the Moon" (beside which stands a banana tree):
All day long, busily continuing the moonlight, One wishes to see the fabricated *Eight Yang Sutras*.
Even if one reads all the way to the "Circulation" section, It is unlikely that the banana tree will lend an ear to listen.
Acting as the *karmadāna*, I inscribe upon the ancient trees in the shade at Qīlǐtān Head:
The fishing platform of Zǐlíng—eyes empty of the vast seas, an old man casting his line. Without cause, he caught Lǐ Wénshǔ;
Yet he took that sheepskin robe and stained it with the dust of the mundane world.
Inscription on the Painting of Xu You Discarding His Gourd Compared to Yao’s world, his gourd was light;
Tired of hearing the distinct rustling of the wind through the branches, he cast it down. There was no need to look back at it with lingering attachment;
From beginning to end, he preserved for himself the name of the reclusive hermit.

Having already followed the heterodox path by venerating the Great Plum Pagoda as "mind is Buddha," how much more so when you join with Master Pang in scattering sand indiscriminately? From this, thatched cottages will be confused with the traces of the dusty world;
the aged plum tree will be ashamed to put forth its flowers amidst the snow.

**Inscription for the Green Lotus Garment of the Pond (Composed by the Emperor Himself)** The green lotus personally crafted to clothe this destitute body; Its fragrant breeze upon the pool’s surface mists the past and present. A million armies could hide within the fibers of a single lotus root;
Who would have known its density was such that it could pierce the golden needle?
As the head of the assembly, the paper lantern boat is lightly lit, its radiance cool and clear.
Here, it is difficult to halt the oars or dance the paddles; the paths of light and darkness are all illuminated through and through.
Letting go, one never offends against the waves from the very start.
Inscribed on the Buddha’s Footprint Grotto:
Once casting off the body, one penetrates the perilous precipice; The path of the Stonehead Chan master is as slippery as moss. Does the footstep touch the ground or not?
Where has he ever truly set foot upon solid ground?
A Ritual for Chan Master Xiangshan Tang (The eyes of the Patriarch open and close at times.
When sitting in meditation within the silent, empty mountains, The weight of a thousand *jin* rests precariously upon a single strand.
Even if one’s two eyes were to open and close repeatedly, One would still be unable to know, from the outset, where one is situated.
A cotton padded jacket is sent;
its seams and patterns are joined like those of Donggang, revealing its traces. Turn it inside out and let it prick the eyes—let it rest there.
The seams are opened wide, yet the stuffing remains dense; Gautama kicks out his big toe.
Sent as a congratulatory gift: Master Donglin of Jianfu has gone off with his incense burner, leaving no trace behind.
In deep sorrow I watch his shadow sink as geese pass through the void. He has come forth to re-establish a bond with us;
Surely those blue eyes cannot be mere dull copper.
The Wealthy King’s livelihood is entrusted to Donglin; the ancient tomb conceals the deep sting of a hidden arrow. When the trigger is pulled, who hits the mark?
As the sun sets over the empty mountains, how many times does the heart tremble?
The matter of the Dharma-body has been understood for a long time; truly, do not doubt this withered stump.
Strike it lightly with the handleless iron hammer, and the flowers of the mind will blossom brilliantly without sprouting branches.
Lamenting Master Yunquan’s capture of the rhinoceros, he stamps his heels;
on Pingzhou, playing with the moon, patterns form upon the horn. Turning his body to enter the sea, there is no news;
he startles and scatters the flocks of sandpipers and white egrets.
Congratulations on Mount Youshan.

Having newly established the Donggao Guest House and parted from Nanhu over a dozen springs ago, I have recently heard that you have achieved a marvelous feat with this magnificent structure. From the Golden Grain (Śākyamuni), you receive fragrant rice;
as a monk, you welcome the mist and clouds from Donggao. Fresh, tender shoots of ferns from the spring ravines, and pale yellow threads of fresh silk at dawn—[these are the offerings].
Wild celery by the stream—surely you will allow me to share your couch. I shall bask my back in the sunlight at the bright eaves and grow drunk on the evening glow.

Paying respects at the Thousand-Year Pagoda of Yunmen, the Yue mountains are pure and absolute, free from any dust or obscuration; it is not as if some barbarian monk has come and buried it haphazardly. Do not hastily add another "thousand years" to its age.
Longevity—this too must be washed from the very bones. The plum window overflows with sight;
the lake and mountains can never be gazed upon enough. To draw forth pure verse, there is this cloud-chamber, where the moon hangs from the eaves, casting its light across the sparse rafters.
Shadows fall; through the lattice windows, the breeze carries fragrance from the darkness. At night, when the door is closed, one suspects it is the residence of Han Jing;

at dawn, when it opens, all vie to behold the makeup of Shouyang. Let the brother orchid and sister magnolia cease their mutual pity; this small chamber cannot accommodate such a multitude of fragrances.

He knows nothing of hidden brilliance, military conflict, or barbarian campaigns; he delights in the age of the Yellow Emperor and dwells in the seclusion of the "Jia-fei" mountains. His fragrant virtue is quietly concealed within a chamber of orchids and calamus;
his literary brilliance is deeply hidden within a loom of brocade. He sleeps beside wild monks upon the rocks of Mount Song and Shao, drawing from the Mengquan spring to brew *shousui* tea.
Yang Wei: Though one may sate oneself with the flavors of a single bowl and gourd amidst poverty, how can one avoid having the dust of the mortal world stain one’s robes?

Bamboo clouds in spring are like a thousand rolls of brocade; ten thousand stalks of jade stand tall. The mountain mists moisten the emerald hues as the Wei River valley grows cold. With such abundance, they have already followed the dragon.
Trend: I only fear that the immortal pond will find it difficult to transform the hibernating insects.
Wang’an responds to Liu Fujiao’s “Deer Resting on Fragrant Grasses”:
Seals springtime in the courtyard; the moon hangs from the ivy window, half-shut at dawn. An old monk with white hair especially loves this.
Guests, endure the cold together to view the "Scripture Exchanged for Geese.

Wandering the Nine Peaks, we climb stones and grasp at vines to enter the profound gloom. Traversing the void, our spirits involuntarily tremble with awe. From the shadowed cliffs, waterfalls cascade like celestial flowers.
Shattered. Withered leaves turn like frost; the brocade trees flourish. A monk returns from the dragon cave after drawing water;
a man gathering *wei* roots walks upon tiger tracks. The elegant legacy of these two elders remains; their melodies pass through the pines and waves, making ten thousand ravines clear.
(Jiuzhou of the Nine Peaks) The twin gullies rush like battling jade dragons; the stupa is locked by clouds in a thousand layers of green. One shall transmit this memorial alone to Heaven.
Below. The Great Awakened One recognized Jiufeng at the age of a donkey.
When Qingliang paid respects before the portrait of his former master, white clouds obscured the valley and snow covered the steps.
Old and decrepit, Qingliang’s eyes were clouded by sand. If you ask about the distance of the Putong era—
The matter: three thousand li away, one plucks the willow blossoms.

At the gate of Xinghua Monastery, the two ponds are as clear as mirrors; in the east and west corridors, all is silent and still. Within the purple silk curtains, the mechanism is profound and mysterious.
Mystic. Though there are pearls scattered, they have not yet formed;

the "Baking" [text] has been passed down through the old barbarian's edition, deceiving humans and devas. Opening their mouths, they do nothing but spit black smoke. As for "Scorching the Body with the Five Heats," they take pleasure in it themselves.
Receiving [this], I must first rectify my original draft; it will take a donkey’s year to complete.
This was written for Master Wei.

It is not a painted image, yet one enters the shadows of Penglai and Fushan to roam there. Discussing oaths, white birds descend upon the azure isles. Waves are swallowed, and the islands are the body of the giant turtle.

Darkness; pavilions and towers reflect the sun as vapors drift by. The gates open against the tide amidst the clamor of the sea market. Nets are spread along the embankments to dry, and fishing boats cluster together.
Twilight, brightness, sunshine, and rain shift from moment to moment; It is difficult to capture all this with the brushwork of Wang Wei.

Ascending the peak of Mount Jīn'é, I part the azure verdure to reach the perilous summit. The path winds like a sheep’s gut over jagged teeth of stone; only upon reaching the top does one realize how small the world beneath is.

Climbing so high seems as though one were seeking the favor of worldly men—a pursuit they loathe. Azure peaks stretch toward the Penglai Isles amidst a thousand folds of cloud, while the cold light reflects upon the Eastern Sea like a mirror.
A single casket. Returning to the pine-window to be companion to the old Chan master, one never tires of speaking of this mountain’s exquisite charm.
For Shengyu, I praise the orange cliffs:

when autumn deepens at Dongting, the fruit is half green and half yellow; one must wait for the frosty forest to ripen before it naturally becomes fragrant. Do not attempt to pluck them from the precipice yourself.
With hands, one mistakes leather for fire and takes it upon oneself;
hearing the call of the temple in Zhuzhou, one submits to the robe. Thus, this verse was composed:
Silk pipes and flutes resound, drums beaten in chaotic frenzy; The two mountains welcome the arrival of the bestowed robes. I fear the white clouds will be defiled by the mountain elder.
Listen! I shall leave the heavy wooden gate locked and not open it.
In the late autumn of the Patriarchal Hall, sorrow increases with every passing day. Upon seeing the hibiscus, one’s brow unknits; one does not compete with wild flowers over trivialities.
In Zichuan, there happens to be a branch of the "resisting frost" chrysanthemum.
Six lines on dwelling in the mountains:
Wild vegetables grow; flowers fly with butterflies. Ancient vines hang from branches; clear cries echo from gibbons. Leisurely leaning against the thatched gate, I watch until weary.
I rest my head upon my arm, sleeping high among the roots of the clouds.
Accumulated snow seals off the paths; chaotic clouds fill the empty courtyard. Who could possibly sweep it all away?
I shall close my gate and read the remaining sutras.
Fresh green moss seals the flat rocks; tangled blue creepers wind around the broken niche. Awakening me from my lingering dream, the moon filters through—
The shadows of the forest sway gently;
soft fire warms the steamed taro tubers. Pale yellow turnips simmer in a sand-pitcher. After the meal, the black staff takes charge as the young servant busily opens the mountain gate.

Frost gathers on the pine needles by the stony brook; snow dots the bamboo fence and the skin of the plum blossoms. Spring has arrived at the mountain home, yet as the days grow long, I am ashamed that my poverty leaves me with no means to enjoy it.
At dawn, I clear away the brambles from the path; at noon, I prepare the kitchen to entertain the visiting monk. When the lad returns late from sweeping the clouds, I must endure hunger.
Climbing the fragrant wisteria vines, the morning mist hangs low over the curtains.
The hidden birds play their flutes and pipes in springtime. Who would have thought that, though once poor and possessing nothing, I have now become as wealthy as a sovereign?
In the two ear-hearth incense burners, cypress seeds are being burned; in a single stone basin, no iris is cultivated. When guests arrive, do not speak of worldly affairs;
beyond the mere exchange of pleasantries, sit in full lotus posture.

Not even a trace of the mind of gain or loss remains; the mechanism of sagehood and ordinariness is split into a thousand differences. All day long, mountain birds gather, yet there is nothing [to disturb them].
One person goes forth to carry the flower;
another, intoxicated by its fragrance, seeks the plum grove. The sound of a horse’s neighing passes through the hollows of the clouds; quickly, one shuts the wooden gate fast.
Let it be so that the young outsider may practice his *qiāo* and *kāo*.

Lamenting the Chan Master Fangzhou’s inability to bear the deception of a lifetime at the window of the firefly lamp, he turned his body into a tiger of righteousness and walked upon its own head. With the golden needle, he scraped away the film of empty flowers;
joyfully, the eye of the Tiantai teachings was made clear.

Smoke rises from the marsh as spring melts the banks of emerald silk; people gathering orchids vie with one another to chant the *Li Sao*. When the melody ends, it transforms into a tune of non-arising;
upon hearing it, the sorrowful soul seems to vanish like melting snow.
In parting for Lecturer Shanyuan: While residing at Yanqing in Huating, you have successfully completed three cycles of lectures, causing celestial flowers to fall.
Though your Dharma-eye is flawless, it nonetheless possesses a flaw. Do not go to Zhu Jing to seek out the Boatman;
with a single stroke of the oar, he shattered his entire worldly life.
Following the rhyme scheme of Yugoku, my lamentation for the deceased knows no end:
A fine silkworm in the golden cocoon was poisoned; its grievance lies buried deep. Family disgrace is difficult to discuss as time passes by.
Reflecting in silence upon where one suffers loss, One clenches the teeth so tightly that the gums are swallowed.
Snow and pearls fill the courtyard steps; he hastily props up Yangqi’s dilapidated hut. When the arts of death are exhausted, the path of time becomes alive;
riding a donkey backward, he prances about on its hooves.
In his final years, he made a decisive break in Suzhou; with a living hand, he played with a dead snake. Darkly struck by a single bite, his entire body rotted away;
the people of the whole city wept for several days.
The appointed attendant, Ben, rushed to his master’s funeral. The various gentlemen offered a verse, and he requested that one be inscribed upon its back:
"Five rebellious acts stem from long-standing resentment toward my father; I have often thought of devouring this old corpse. Without cause, I was further incited by others;
In a fit of fury, I took up my spade to bury him alive."
Seeing off Brother Yuan of Mount Jingshan as he returns to his hometown after the chaos:
The smoke and dust of the old land are grim, and armor and weapons abound; In this weary life spent all day long, one but hopes for peace and stability.
Taking with you the water from Dragon Abyss in your alms bowl, Why should it hinder your return? Let it wash everything clean.
Written by Cao Taiyu, Provincial Scholar. The Eight Scenic Views of Xiangxiang (*Bǔsuànzǐ*) Autumn air is crisp with night rain over Xiangxiang;
The gloom of twilight darkens the Southern Dipper. On the reed banks, fishing lamps shine through the mist; Men are drunk beneath the pines.
A bowl of fermented wine; suddenly hearing the sound of striking the bamboo screen, I dreamt I entered the realm of nothingness. At dawn, I see the tear-streaks on the *éyīng* bamboo;
my sorrows knot together, twisting through the nine coils of my intestines.
The autumn moon over Lake Dongting.
A single song opens the jade casket. Xi Zi’s makeup is fresh upon her slender wrists. The western wind lifts the curtain as she leans against Mount Yang;

her gaze follows the distant Xiang River. In the still night, she feasts with the moon; a great goblet floats within the golden bowl. The brilliant radiance surpasses the spirit-like jade pendants, scattering like dew across the full jade fields.
The evening bell at the misty temple hangs like fine threads in the clear air. At twilight, many sights unfold: the monk hears the sparse tolling as he returns from his midday meditation;

his robes are damp with cool green moss. The pavilion is hidden deep within the azure clouds; the whale-like roar of the bell makes the vast forest still. Standing throughout the perilous heights, my verse remains unformed—only the moon.
The shadows of green vines are carved into the air;

fishing villages meet with the setting sun as fishing sails return from the distant bays. Gulls, accustomed to humans, vie with one another in flight; the river’s current swallows the void as the evening glow blazes. My heart is fully sated by this contemplation.
Without shoes, sons and grandsons intoxicated by turbid wine together sing the "Canglang" song. Amidst the clustered thatch-roofed eaves, the twilight deepens;
they shift their oars to lodge in the reed cove as wild geese alight upon the level sands.
The green has faded and the water-marks are parched; dredging reveals the fallen shooting stars. A single expanse stretches out, cold as a frozen pass;

gazing forth, there is no end to it. The reeds rise up in clusters; a brief mooring makes it hard to gauge the distance. Ancient characters are written upon the void, with faint ink strokes stretching across;
wings weary, the flight is slow yet firm.
The sail returns to the distant bay; my body is as leisurely as a white gull. Seeking our pact across lakes and seas, the trees at the ferry are shrouded in mist while the water reflects the sky.
It is as if on the road to Mount Yingzhou; ten sails are filled with the western wind. One can faintly discern where the boat travels; my home lies beyond the ancient shore of reeds. The mast—
Moored by the river, the sky turns dusk.

On the mountain market, the clear mists settle over a valley where fields of hemp and mulberry flourish. The wine flag leans askew in the breeze; the recent rain has just ceased as emerald vapors rise. One buys the spring all to oneself.
Priceless. The lanes are obscured by yellowish dust; yellow birds cry out among the *gāngzhà* trees on the ridges. Whose old hermitage is this, large or small?
Ancient walls are stained with the saliva of snails.
The river sky holds lingering snow.

The vapors of the Yangtze River coalesce into layers of gloom; the wings of the sandbirds are frozen and damaged. Heaven’s artistry manifests in a profusion of six-petaled snowflakes, their hue like that of white jade.

Upon touching the water, they melt away instantly; by nightfall, they have piled up once more. How wonderful it is for the lone fisherman on his solitary boat, newly adorning himself with his fishing cloak.
A Memorial for Yan Boyi (Zhuo Shangxue Dou): He delighted in planting paulownias and loving chrysanthemums, yet before he could enjoy them, he passed away while seated in meditation.

Twenty years we pledged our alliance, hand in hand; with a lean staff, we once vowed to scale the perilous peaks. We had not yet succeeded in viewing the waterfalls together at the snowy cliffs, nor did we expect to see lotuses bloom so soon in the jade pond.
Now the paulownia leaves form a shade that grieves at the drawing moon, and the chrysanthemums have no wine to warm their cold.
Enveloped in mist. Looking closely at the newly compiled *Biographies of Donglin*, he is yet another sage among the eighteen worthies.
Sending off Master Jiecao as he dwells in Yan Temple (the hermitage):

In his youth, he was already renowned throughout the ocean of teachings; with a tattered robe and a blue lamp, he investigated a single scripture. He does not borrow from empty space to open his mouth.

He speaks; would he not teach the stubborn rock to nod its head and listen? The Imperial Calligraphy bestowed a mandate to honor the plum groves; the vermilion cassia wafts its fragrance to serve the Hall of Bai.
Before long, one will sit steadily in meditation amidst the white clouds; the mountain spirits have no place left to offer their flowers.
To the South Yang Commandant: A poem inquiring after his well-being.

In response to your verse, I speak of my own humble cultivation among the forests and springs. The fierce battle has startled the Maen and Chuk insects; my heart is ashen and all thoughts are chilled. How could the flames of cruelty ever cease their accumulation?

How lamentable is the Elder Yun! He cherished me as he would a tortoise-shell or a jade ornament; yet I shall no longer be presented at the court of Chu, for in the end, I am destined to be destroyed within my casket.

Entrusting my health and well-being to Chen, the District Magistrate of Meixu, I find myself lacking the leisure for a formal visit upon my arrival. Amidst the fragrant breeze, I report my presence beneath the azure heavens; I have merely brushed away the dust before descending the cloud-capped eaves.
A bed. A vessel newly returned from the sea lands with its gathered treasures; riding on inspiration, I wander lost beneath the willows. Searching through my rhymes, my dream reaches the plum trees.
When shall we clasp hands in the community of Donglin, once more binding the karmic ties that remain unfinished from three lifetimes?

Carrying the "Pine Studio" (Chūryō) for half a lifetime, he has cast off his fish-belt and golden ornaments. Finding deep resonance in springs, rocks, fields, and plains, his secluded inspiration flows forth as silent ink-traces;

where worldly dust is discarded, he calmly contemplates the mind. The crucible of sages and worthies melts away fame and form; through this subtle and profound craftsmanship, the chime of truth resounds.
Past and present, one gazes afar at the Lotus Abode; dreams travel far, yet it should not be easily reached in the Jade Forest.
I entreat County Magistrate Wang (whose style name is Juefei Jushi; his desk-side inscription reads: "Serve the office with integrity and diligence;

maintain your principles through pure poverty"), whose refined elegance follows the tradition of the Eastern Jin, continuing that illustrious fame. He exchanged the *True Copy* for the *Goose Script Classic*. Integrity and diligence naturally bring success within the official sphere.

He pursued the path of poverty and integrity, personally inscribing his "Seat-of-the-Room Inscription. The people, moved by his benevolence, forgot their haste to flee into mountain ravines; his son, enlightened in poetry and ritual, followed him as he entered the courtyard.
Who could have foreseen that a gale would strike down the great beam? The wailing of monkeys and cranes is unbearable to hear.
I heard it said that one should seek out the words of the young to cast the scholar’s cap against the wall-root. Now I have come to serve as an attendant to the monk of Nanyue (Rurufeng);

my poetic chanting is pure and bitter, following the example of the Cold Mountain dweller, and my labor at the mortar and pestle is diligent, emulating the old master Nanquan. I idly gaze upon the flowers reflected in the brocade mirror, their patterns intricate; I playfully strike the jade-like waterfalls cascading down the cliffs.
Layer upon layer. The words "spare even a fraction of a shadow" should serve as a whip and spur. I look forward to you coming to brighten the lamp in my dark room.
Master Ren, you have come from the Western Mountains;

seeking these words, you have read by the window with such diligence that your body has grown emaciated. For a moment, you grasp your cane and visit this rustic fellow. I admire the resilience of your bamboo-like will and hope you will uphold this jade.
A pause. Gazing at the plum blossoms, we idly count the silver whiskers together. The moon is cold on the Western Mountains as I return to invite you into seclusion;
the breeze is clear at the Southern Peak as I wish to set out on foot. Do not let others point the way for you who are so keen-witted; let the boatman simply grow old upon the rivers and lakes.

In this poetic composition on plum blossoms and snow: Spring’s message has reached my thatched cottage at the edge of the white flakes. Who has sent Plum Brother to comfort my solitude? A branch of elegant spirit emerges as tender jade;
five petals of cold brilliance are cut from living silk. The moon shifts its sparse shadows, hanging before the window; the wind carries the fragrant scent through the bamboo.
The wind blows from without; how many souls of poets can it not summon back? I urge my younger brother Lan to read the *Li sao*.
Written by the junior disciple of Master Ling.
Holding the staff and grasping the willow branch, he carries the cloth bag upon his back. Turning his head and looking back, he exerts some effort at Fenghua;
whenever he meets someone, he speaks falsely, seeking copper coins. Beggar, beggar! You have ruined it all.

Bodhidharma departed from the land of Chu and had an audience with the King of Liang; five ghosts descended upon his person as he endured bitter suffering. They gazed at one another, saying they did not recognize him;
on an autumn wind, a single reed-boat hurriedly crossed the Yangtze.
The Girl Lingzhao (holding a bamboo sieve with coins at its edge) engages in a contest of vital mechanisms with Danxia.
Only a lord of malicious intent would understand this. The sieve scoops up a full measure of spring breeze;
not worth a single coin, to whom could it be sold?

The fish-basket woman has her short skirt hitched up; dewdrops cling to her precious form. Her cloud-like hair is neglected in its disarray, enough to bewilder and disturb men. She manages to bring the fish in her basket back to life;
yet, they may not necessarily be able to leap over the Dragon Gate.
When Master Dahui’s fragrant breeze blows from the south, coolness arises within the palace halls. When the Buddhas manifest their bodies, opening one's mouth is already an error—error upon error!
This has won him seventeen years at Hengmei; yet, whether before the donkey or behind the horse, there is no place of refuge.
The countenance and bearing of Master Jilin are as warm as spring;

his character is yet majestic and awe-inspiring. As a tiger of the Vinaya emerges from the forest, he tears asunder the distinctions between what is permitted and prohibited, and what is maintained or transgressed.

As a dragon of the Sūtras churns the ocean, he probes to the depths of the sudden and gradual, the partial and the perfect. His phrasing is fresh and refined; his verse resonates through the mountains.

Zhuang Meizhu: Her breast contains wondrous refinements, encompassing hills, valleys, winds, and mists; she is a friend to scholars and officials, yet not one who seeks the warmth of powerful families;
she upholds the Buddha-dharma, mindful of its heavy burden carried upon her shoulders; amidst the fragrance of roasted yams, she has no thought of wiping away tears.
Reclining amidst the deep clouds, how could one have anticipated ascending to the imperial court? His true countenance remains distant, yet his image is rendered in a bright mirror.

Entrusting him with the family legacy, he is like a divine pearl hidden in the abyss. Such is the son who upholds the lineage of the Forest of Compassion; he is truly the *lāngjiao* (glue of cranes) that mends the severed string.
Bodhidharma (Crossing the River by Breaking a Reed):

He exhausted his fortune of a thousand pieces of gold to learn the art of slaying dragons; he concealed a "blow-off" sword in his sleeve, never revealing its edge. Yet when he encountered the true dragon, he did not recognize it at all;
in a frantic rush, he fled upon a raft of reeds, leaving no trace behind.
The Cloth Bag (a shoulder-measure drag-bag; looking back, a child catches his robe).
A *zhuli* staff slung across the shoulder, dragging a cloth bag behind; turning his head and twisting his brain, the child plays. Do not speak of the affairs within the Tuṣita Palace;
he has already been caught and defeated by that fellow.
The Portrait of Master Bieshan (Composed by Ruijingtou as a Eulogy):
A stern and cold countenance, yet a soft and yielding heart. Facing his fellow practitioners, he sings the *Pusa man*; to those of the same school, he speaks words of no conventional meaning.
He unleashes the hawk’s strike at its prey; he opens the lion’s somersault path. He heals the maladies of monks and descends from heaven.
King Pūṣan’s heart was perfected; he moved to the Tuṣita Palace, exchanging his place for the great conflagration of the long star (Venus).
Though his secret activity and subtle function remain hidden such that even the hawk-eyed cannot trace his path, when examined closely, it is still just the rice-cloth of Guozhou.
The Inner Court of the Cloth Bag (for Wu Shengyuan) refuses to dwell in peace.
Changting willingly accepts his humble lot; the Master’s staff does not understand how to pick it up or bring it forth.
The Cloth Bag relies on him in vain; within its belly it schemes in a hundred ways. It wishes to sleep, yet never succeeds in sleeping. If it could sleep, [it would be] iron.
People of Fenghua must have soft feet.

Regarding the Three Recluses of Tiantai: Hanshan held a scroll and smiled; Shide had a door-knob hanging from his waist, with one hand holding a broom and the other raising a finger in the gesture of lecturing, while Fenggan stood behind them.

Making the gesture of clacking one's teeth, he fails to open the door-bolt with a hook; with his broom, he cannot sweep the floor. He explains and interprets Du’s writings and documents, while someone behind him gnashes his teeth in resentment.
One might think Hanshan listens and believes him, unaware that a hidden blade lurks within the smile.
The crown-mark of Chan Master Fojian is coarse, stubborn, and wild;
it is further augmented by a white tuft of hair. A stone is roasted over both civil and martial fires to extract its fragrance; a head wrapped in hempen cloth will surely cause a person to fall.
Opening five arenas to play with the living pivot—this is a dragon ascending to heaven while a snake slithers into the grass. A thousand do not match ten thousand.
"It is not fitting. Before Fengkou Mountain, I begged for the direction of the path, yet I was subjected to no small amount of humiliation by that old, tattered monk.
To this day, I have forgotten the way back."
Master Daci Huanfeng (a native of Fuzhou):
His inner nature was profoundly adept at using plain glue to catch thieves; he fixed the vision with "eye-obscuring" medicine. He was like a compass for ships upon the vast ocean.

Producing the lotus from the Gate of Wisdom, he changed the nostrils of men. Grasping the broom of Great Compassion, he swept away the dust and smoke of the world. He forgot all taboos and severed all ties of intimacy.
The parent is ill with a malady deep in the vital organs, compounded by the poison of *gū*; it would take even a stone Buddha to break into a sweat all over its body.
Avalokiteśvara (with radiant *āmalaka*-leaf marks, treading upon lotuses)—the hundred-and-eight *maṇi* beads have the radiance of *āmalaka* leaves.
The gateway of universal penetration opens wide day by day; do not rely on the lotus boat to save sentient beings.
Stable. The fierce waves and mad winds trouble themselves. Fenggan adding layers of gauze to his head—what kind of decorum is that?
Eyes fixed on reading the sutras yet unable to recognize a single character; acting out of place and behaving strangely, one is driven by madness.
To act recklessly, pretending to ride a leopard while acting like a tiger, and claiming it is Amitābha—what scriptural authority is there for this?
Governor Lüqiu was like the man from Suzhou.
Master Dàchuān’s face is scraped as white as frost; his spine is cast from forged iron. He playfully manipulates the wretched mechanism; he is truly a native of Fènghuà.
Relying on Nánshān, the white-tiger has lost its majesty; at Lěngquán, the clear waves are locked so there is no way through. This is, indeed, groundless.
It is contrary to human sentiment. He seizes the binding cord and hangs the Buddhas and patriarchs upside down. The Chan practitioners of the four seas loathe this man;
even if the master painter Wei Xuan were to paint him with perfect realism, there would still be no place for him to rest.
Dharma crossed the river on a single reed; for nine years he faced the wall. Pointing directly and transmitting alone, people could not believe it. Facing King Liang, he said, "I do not know.
(Ei! A lump of clay is tossed about in confusion.
A cloth bag sits leaning against a cloth bag; listening to the laughter of the rocky waterfall, he holds a prayer bead rosary in his hand. What is he counting?
Within this inner courtyard, years and months have slipped away in depth. (Silently) He has forgotten the path by which he came.
Facing the moon, I finished reading this remaining scripture;

what a scripture it is! It lacks a translation, and though I have exhausted my efforts, I cannot see through it. Yet, when one can see, the moon hangs from the tips of the pines, and mist enshrouds the moss-covered rocks.
The morning sun pierces through the tattered robe;

it is like a dead iron needle without nostrils. The eyes grow dim and blurred, unable to pass through. Yet, if one can pass through, clouds gather around the monk’s robes and wind arises from the tips of the trees.
Dharma sailed far across the whale-waves into the Great Tang; In vast emptiness, there was no sage to meet King Liang. For nine years he sat coldly in the cave of spirits;
He feared to behold the snow and frost beneath Mount Song.
Master Seong-sik (invited by Mansu Eungam): His countenance is loathsome to others;
yet the autumn moon shines brightly within his skull. In his actions there are no scars; when he employs them, they achieve the most subtle and wondrous efficacy.

Seeing the brilliance, it penetrates through the night-bright curtain; relying on the perfect illumination, one fans the fierce and gentle fires. In several places they shift the field and play with perilous mechanisms;
like lightning rolling and whirlwinds spinning, people fall over in laughter. This is what is called the Wayman of the Stone Chamber.
Previous incarnations and subsequent incarnations are but one dream and two awakenings.

The Grass-Clothed Mañjuśrī (holding a scripture), with hair flowing and shoulders bared, enters the grass with his entire body—this is the true Mañjuśrī. Why must it be so? That which is in his hand cannot be grasped;
it cannot be seen through. Even the Teacher of the Seven Buddhas has no small flaws.
Avalokiteśvara (The Child Sitting Amidst Lotus Leaves; requested by Attendant En):
He manifests tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of bodies according to the kind; To whom does this realm of true perfect penetration belong? The child’s playful antics no one understands:
Ten thousand acres of blue waves, a single leaf of lotus.
The World-Honored One (having returned from his almsround, set down his staff upon the ground and sat with both hands supporting his chin, falling asleep. Master Hongzang requested:
"Having once endured hardships on the Snowy Peaks, he diligently performed the rites of the Seven Buddhas; holding his bowl, he received no food, yet feigned that he did not hear of hunger."
The six rings of my tin staff are heavy; lacking the strength to support it, I let it fall as I rest my chin upon it and sleep for a moment.
To whom can I tell the news from within this dream? Cold Mountain and拾得 (Shide)—one composes a poem, the other grinds the ink.
Guoqing has stealthily obtained some leftover soup and rice; he too acts like a person playing with a bamboo pole before others.
He wishes to write down the "living word" of Duanya—how can his heart, like the autumn moon, remain as it is?
The face is stern and the hair is disheveled; even his grinding of ink is of no use.
He coldly observes the faint characters in others' writings, unaware that he has stained his cloth skirt deep with ink.

Bodhidharma of Central India secretly acquired the skill of slaying dragons; hiding his divine blade in his sleeve, he entered the South Sea. Yet when he beheld the true dragon, he did not recognize it at all;
for nine years he faced the wall—how truly shameful!
A cloth bag, a tattered sack—without a single cache within. Relying upon it, he sleeps soundly, completely unaware that dawn has broken.
If you say this is Maitreya manifesting his divided body, do not come to mock me.
The morning sun pierces through the tattered robe;
where the threads have snapped, there is no path. The needle is bent and its eye missing, yet it is held perfectly whole.
As the golden bird sinks in the west, one faces the moon to finish the remaining sutra.
The tangled vines of the five teachings and three vehicles are exhausted in a single word. When the jade hare rises in the east, the junior disciple writes this true likeness and requests a eulogy:
His eyebrows are as coarse as brooms; his face is like black lacquer. People call him compassionate, but who knows his hidden venom? A fence of mugwort shuts out the fierce beast.

The tiger possesses majesty within its breadth; the brush-stalk nurtures the azure dragon, concealing the curved within the straight. It rejoices that Zang Cang discouraged it, so it did not meet the Duke of Lu;
it endured the hunger of Boyi, refusing to eat the grain of Zhou.
A hemp-sack carrier bearing a hemp-sack, clutching a rattan branch; a belly full of malice, intended to make you all understand. Turning one's head and looking back—who is it?
The Bearded Master understands this meaning; he lets out a cold laugh as the thief’s wind blows.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Qian of Yanqing (At Kongshengfang Hermitage):
His modest virtue shines with brilliance; his compassionate heart embraces all beings. He treats enemies and kin as equals, refusing to engage in calculation or comparison;
he mingles with the mundane world without any sense of separation. His joyful spirit melts the spring into the icy valleys, and his vast capacity swallows the expanse of Yunmeng.
Delighting in the era of Emperor Xīhuáng, he nurtures his grandchildren with honeyed sweets; he spreads out the *tà* of Chén Bān and turns his shoes upside down to welcome guests.
From beneath his eyes, the banners of radiant light shine brilliantly; from beneath his heels, every mote of dust is a pure and flourishing kingdom.

He chooses to be a neighbor in a humble alley, emulating the conduct of the Sage Kǒng when he composed the *Líng* chapter of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*; he scatters bright pearls, like Master Yù crossing a bridge on a donkey.

A Portrait of Dignity. Truly, this is what is meant by "entering the marketplace with hands hanging down. I have cultivated my own mind, continuing the solemn tradition of a hundred generations and beholding the countenance of the ancient Way.
Eulogy for the Zen Assembly Portrait (Eight Sections).
When Danxia saw Layman Pang, Lingzhao stood with her hands folded and set down her vegetable basket.
She tucked her sleeves deeply; she might have deceived Danxia, but it was difficult to deceive herself. Her malicious machinations were known to the Master;
he has smeared red earth on the cow’s udders and given her a reward.

A layman asked Mazu: "If one does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion (to the side is a plantain tree), and since the myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty, with whom would one be a companion? If you can speak of this to perfection, it will be difficult to converse with you.
Even if he were to swallow the Western River in a single gulp, that too is merely the rain on a plantain tree at night."
Gathering in a circle, they speak words of the Unsurpassed;

(while speaking of bamboo and stone), those who were enemies in past lives now huddle head-to-head. Looking at one another face to face, what could they possibly say? Speak in low voices so as not to let others know.
Bamboo and stone are insentient, yet they must laugh themselves down!
The Layman watches the sun; Lingzhao has already passed away.
This little bean-cake of a woman—stump-headed and crooked-legged—plays with ghosts and spirits, seizing the initiative a move ahead.
Watching the sun, Layman Pang is truly a fool in the original edition; he deserves to be buried in one deep pit.
Pang-po replied to her son. The son immediately leaned on his hoe and stood there as he passed away;
the young wife went on ahead. The old man followed behind, having no intention of rushing to the funeral, but hurriedly seeking a path to death.
He brought this widowed mother to the brink of tears; the matters concerning the mattock’s edge were difficult to entrust.

When Li Ao visited Yaoshan, [he saw that] the sky was originally hidden by clouds and the flask was fundamentally filled with water; he did not understand how to read the sutras, so how could he be capable of receiving instruction?
He sent word to Prime Minister Li of the Tang Dynasty: "You need only cast your eyes and listen to the wind in the pines."
When Prime Minister Pei consulted with Huangbo about the "Great and Small Delusions," their dialogue reached such depths that even those listening behind them could not interrupt.
Do not seek the name of an ancient Buddha; you will immediately strike against the taboo name of the noble lord.
Lü Dongbin saw that the Yellow Dragon Cauldron boils heaven and earth;
within it, the world is hidden as fine grain. Even if one attains longevity, it will ultimately end in decay.
It is not that the Yellow Dragon covers him over; how could the Ta’a sword mend his shoes? A needle is surely better.
For the sake of the venerable Master Yue Shang of Changzhou, I praise the Cloth Bag Monk:
(making a gesture of sneezing) His staff cannot be leaned upon; he sits steadily astride his cloth bag. Do not be surprised that he cannot sneeze;
his nostrils have never had any holes.
Acting as the Yuan Xitang, he praised the Boatman: (Holding a fishing rod in hand,) Sanlang of She wears a bamboo hat (and a rain cape;

his lower body is bare flesh). A thousand-jun weight is entrusted to a single thread; three inches away from the hook, it still presses upon the man. Do not say that merely capsizing the boat is the end of the matter;
Jia Shan may not necessarily be the golden-scaled fish.
With rain-hat and smoke-robe, the body is exposed to the wind; he transmits only the fisherman’s trade as the heart of the school.
Had he not crossed Feiyuan Ridge at that time, his entire being would have been nothing but festering pus.
Yanyang and Nanquan—Nanquan’s Great Way.
Before the Boatman had yet penetrated Zhaozhou’s Barrier, the matter of watching the ox grew increasingly complex. One cannot bring a dead snake back to life; it is best simply to tip over the boat.
Zhaozhou asked about the ox tracks; Yuanze struck the horn. Zheng Huangniu and the Old Woman of the Level Field—this beast has always left many evil traces.
Even from the tip of its horn, it knows how to sing wildly. The white heron by the bridge is startled into a fist.
Listen! Quickly kill that stinking old woman who tills the fields!

This is a substitute eulogy for the Arhats (Lord Liu invited the Sixteen Arhats from Wudong to present on the birthday of Vice-Commissioner Meng; seeing Chijue seeking a eulogy, the Abbot ordered this one to be divided among them).

(First Pine Tree. Several Peaks. Arhat holding a scripture with one hand, looking at its title; the other hand grasps the sash of the scripture. Below is a servant boy lighting incense and striking a chime.)
Ancient cypresses hold the mist; green mountains unfold a painting. The title is clear and distinct—what need is there for further deliberation?
Wait until you have finished offering incense and struck the chime once, and it will already be too late.

(A single tree of entanglements. An Arhat holding a fly-whisk sits within a mountain cave; before him are incense and flowers. Below is a youth holding a wheel that grinds objects. One person holds a flask and looks inside.)
Relying on creeping vines and leaning on old pillars; grasping a whisk made of tortoise hair. "Ceasing study and non-action"—this is but a ghost cave in the Black Mountains.
Even if you could pivot the wheel of the mechanism so that you hear fragrance with your eyes and see forms with your ears, I still ask you: what is that thing inside the bottle?
The Chan Saint Pig-Head Monk holds a pig’s head in his hand but does not eat it himself; before him and behind him, ghosts divide the spoils. His failures are manifold, yet no one [can find fault].
Consciousness wins out; it smears over the old Dingguang.
Master Xiange has nothing left but a single scoop-net;

he deceives people with his talk as he wanders the rivers and lakes. With his shrimp-needle, he hooks your very nature. *Note: This is a translation of a verse from the *Wumen Guan* (The Gateless Barrier), Case 13, attributed to Master Xiange. The text utilizes Zen terminology and imagery to describe the nature of mind and the act of realization.*
*Lu*. He has not yet managed to seize the pearl from the dragon’s jaw.
Master Yushan is a wanderer in Chaling with little learning; who can speak of his progress beyond the tip of the pole? He has struck the bright pearl down to the height of a donkey’s waist.
Stop! Do not disbelieve this village elder, the Acarya.

Zheng Huangniu has spent his life in solitary hardship, yet he has stolen a reputation for poetry. Drunk upon the winds and mists, his two eyes are green; his yellow calf has never known the toil of the fields.
Sai. Chanting by the irrigation canal until emaciated and haggard.
Puhua goes to the village feast at Beici Monastery; when he suddenly dies, no one comes to bury him. He acts strangely, soaring into the air and shaking his staff.
Duo! In every direction the spring wind reveals corpses and bones.
Master Duan’s claws and fangs, though wielded, are not yet fully authentic; mottled green and speckled brown cover his entire body, yet he has never let out a roar despite his fine colors.
He attained it. Upon hearing this, people thought he was merely trying to intimidate the villagers.

They said that his mind was so deluded by the *Lotus Sūtra* that he was nearly turned by it; driven mad, he went on a fast and ran to the imperial palace. Thirteen times before the Sage, he cried out, "No!"
Correct. Without cause, he repeatedly and forcefully writes upon the void.
Great Way Master Quan leapt naked into the venomous dragon’s pool; one knows not how many times he fought with blood until death. He has now come forth to beg for his bowl.
Wine. In the sixth month of Chenzhou, the fire-clouds are cold.
The boatman harbors a heart of malignant poison, blazing and fierce; grasping his rough oar upside down, he cares not for heaven. He strikes, and Jia Shan leaps into the water.
Water. Seizing the moment before it entered the sight, he hurriedly turned the boat around.
Fenggan (sitting under a tree, raising a finger as if making a speech; Lüqiu faced him and laughed; a tiger was nearby, sleeping).
Hantsi (holding a broom made of reeds, pointing at the moon and laughing while speaking).
Sitting coldly in the shade of pines, who is there to heed his gestures? He speaks words devoid of meaning, indulging in foolishness. He employs many means to draw forth laughter from Lü Qiū;
though the colors are variegated and beautiful, he does not know how to sleep.
A smile conceals a blade; words feign sincerity. Grasping a raw broom, he stirs up dust and smoke.
He vainly attempts to defile the moon in the autumn pool, yet it is unlikely that the moon would deign to compare itself to him.

The manifestation of leaving the mountains after six years of snow and frost without perishing; seeing the morning star, he spoke of his awakening. Yet once he had run out from the mountains, there was nothing left behind;
people called him the Red-Bearded Barbarian.
At midnight he leaped over the city wall; for six years he dwelt amidst the snow. Starving, his eyes grew dim; freezing, his bones were broken.
When his skill in dying was exhausted, he fled from the mountains. Yet his descendants open their eyes only to be deceived by him.
Carrying a shoulder-bag across the water—this fellow has spent his life playing with danger.
He loves to roll about amidst wind and waves; he carries a cloth bag across the current while remaining unaware of the depth beneath his feet.
Faster than a whistling arrow, he strikes before the trigger; the path passes through a single thread.
Leaning on the cloth bag, gazing at the skull. Not opening the mouth to laugh, nor revealing the lips in a smile.
One has not yet seen through to liberation. Though the cloth bag is leaned upon with firm reliance, the eyes of the withered skull must be revived.
If you wish to live as a person of Fenzhou, strip away your inner organs with no quarter left.

Reclining on your sack and sleeping, you naturally roll along with the dust and toil of the world; within your belly, a thousand schemes and ten thousand transformations arise. Although you lean against your coarse wool blanket, I suspect you.
Sleeping was not yet secure;
he exhausted every manner of "death-technique. Relying his entire body upon the cloth bag, he reflected that it was all merely empty flowers.
It would be better to rouse oneself from this drowsiness.
Relying on a cloth bag, he constantly contemplates his own bare-bones poverty, depending solely on that bag. Reflect upon this carefully:
there is a great matter at hand—to ascend from level ground to the Tuṣita Heaven. Are you, sir, mad or deluded?

The Cloth Bag Man carries a cloth bag; he lets loose his foolishness and stupidity. Turning his head, he laughs once—a thousand strange wonders. Having traveled all over Changting, no one recognized him;
he spoke deceitful words, claiming Maitreya had appeared among men.
The camel-carrier with his sack laughs heartily; his wisdom weighs not a single ounce, yet his flesh weighs a thousand pounds. Turning his head and twisting his neck, he waits for someone;
