the path back to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is far, and his face is covered in dust.
A stinking cloth bag; not a single cave to dwell in. Leaning against it, he sleeps like a fool, completely unaware of whether it is day or night.
If you say this is an emanation of Maitreya, do not come to mock me!
Carrying a staff and a cloth bag, he smiles coldly with an air of solemnity. His belly has no hidden storehouse; his eyes have no sinews.
He has traveled to Changting waiting for someone, but he has failed his purpose. What a clever thief! What a clever thief!
A shoulder-sling bag slung across, pressing down a black staff; a knife hidden within a smile—truly loathsome.
An iron man from Fenghua is made entirely of iron; how could he tolerate such a monk?
When the Cloth Bag Man with his shoulder-load sneers coldly, people know his heart and entrails are full of evil poison. Layer upon layer of failures and flaws are difficult to conceal;
yet he still turns his head back—whom is he looking for?
The morning sun breaks through the hemmed shirt. He shakes it out idly. A needle with a hole in its nose cannot pierce it. When it is pierced, the sun rises from the Fusang tree;

every morning is as it was before. There is no thread to pull it apart; one must exert all effort to maintain this awareness. As the sun grows late, when will it ever be accomplished? In a year of donkeys!
A fragment.
Pressed down, the direct path is opened up. The great thousandfold world is crumpled into the point of a single needle. It cannot be grasped, yet it can be grasped.
With no flaws at all, one finally sees the realization of one's own merit.
Waiting for the moon to pierce through a stack of old paper, yet failing to penetrate; how pitiable that the karmic consciousness remains vast and desolate day after day.
At the very end, there is not a single point of clarity—still waiting for a toad’s mouth to emit light.
The final word: how can it be brought forth? Before you even blink your eyes, the full moon is already facing the door; when has it ever been known where it lands?
The final word is far too clear. Those whose eyes lack the essential faculty cannot see through it. Once seen through, the mind-moon is solitary and perfect, illuminating all differences at once.
Hanshan and Shide grind the ink to inscribe the cliffs;
Guoqing secretly finishes the leftover gruel. They too learn to brandish the bamboo pole before people.
Desiring to write a "living phrase" from the precipice, their minds are like the autumn moon—waiting for what? How pitiable is Shide, gazing askance in vain labor; the ink has its time of exhaustion.
Regret that [this] resentment will not dissipate.
*The Portrait of the Three Sages of Tiantai* (Hanshan holds a scroll in both hands; Shide holds a screen in one hand and points with the other, gazing at each other as they deliberate;
Fenggan leans on a staff, standing beside them).
Dust covers the ground, yet it is not swept away; for no reason, they deliberate and scatter documents. Clearly, the Master was able to carry out his command;
it was not until Fenggan appeared that he let him pass.
The sleeping person has no intent to harm the tiger; the tiger has no intent to injure the person. Since neither side is on guard, what prevents one from waking the sleeper?
— Sixth Patriarch Master Caoxi.
In Xinzhou, he was struck on both shoulders by falling firewood; in Huangmei, he was hit on the waist by a falling stone.
Though he managed to plant the pine tree and preserve his robes and bowl, he thought back in secret how many times his soul had nearly perished in pursuit.
Even within the meaning of the Noble Truths, Bodhidharma did not recognize them as he crossed the river; it must have been difficult to find a path through the clear waves.
For nine years he hid his ineptitude deep within a ghost cave, yet he was nonetheless subjected to the cold gaze of Shen Guang.
Beneath the feet of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, a blue lotus flower is half-blossomed; leaning against a precipitous rock, he sits with his hand turning a prayer-bead rosary.
The true realm of the Universal Gate is difficult to depict, yet it has been forcibly brought into the realm of painted images by human hands.
The Fisherman’s Wife Guanyin does not return to dwell at Little White Flower Rock; she dresses up in an extraordinary manner to deceive the people of the world.
Though she carries a bottomless basket that keeps things alive, it remains uncertain whether she can leap over the Dragon Gate and turn her head around.
A hemp sack, a stinking cloth bag—what is there in it? As soon as you lean upon it, you fall asleep; you do not know on what day you shall descend to be born again.
There is still one finger remaining to count. Wash pot, wash pot! I know you well.
Firmly grasping the mouth of the cloth bag, for a moment it cannot be let go. Though he exhausts all his wicked machinations, he cannot deceive Iron Fenzhou.
How many times has he been defeated and exposed, yet he still turns his head back to look—who is he looking for?
Barefoot, walking through the red dust of the world, he claims to be the true Maitreya. He traffics in this stinking skin-bag, yet no one on earth recognizes him.
No one recognizes him! Hurry and turn back; it is already eight *ke* too late.
The Bagui Bathing in the River:
Willow smoke mists the air, ripples shimmer on the waves. Though he is entirely without reliance, he still clings to dust.
Having rolled his whole body into mud and water, whose child’s play is this that deceives anyone?
Suddenly stirring waves upon level ground, he reveals the raw flesh-ball born of one’s mother.
Though it may deceive the coquettish and foolish girl, the willow tree by the brook cannot be deceived.
For the Venerable Zhou:
On the peak of White Flower Mountain, Guanyin plays with shadows; At the mouth of the Tide-Sound Cave, waves overturn the void. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands open, yet no one enters;
Leisurely grasping his rosary, he stands in the morning breeze.

Seeking praise from a guest for the sake of conditions—no need for hearing, contemplation, or cultivation. The great opening of the path of perfection; yet one still intends to ask: "How so? The prayer beads and the wood *mbala* seeds.
Praising the appearance of leaving the mountains:
for six years he was emaciated by the cold and haggard. Having emerged from the mountains, his eyes were not yet clear. The white wheel of gold broke and could not turn;
in vain did he claim to have seen the morning star at midnight.
Praise for the Portrait of Chijue:

Pure and unadulterated, he had extinguished all artifice and contrivance. He gathered a blade of grass to serve as medicine to clear the eyes, and smelted yellow cinnabar into gold that yields at the touch of a finger.
He provoked the wrathful rebukes of Fenyang, whose words were so piercingly harsh; he was struck by the venomous poison of Caoyuan, a grievance so deep it cuts to the bone. He swept away the foxes...
The hare bares its teeth against the talons of the azure hawk; the pig and dog bite, adding to the tiger’s spirit.
Whether this is the true master or not the true master—Zhang Sengyao could not capture it in brushstrokes; he set down his pen after long hesitation.

Regarding the request for the support of his teaching, Master Yao of Mount Dun was truly one whose countenance was as frost-scrapingly stern and whose azure eyes were like dots of lacquer. Relying on Fengyan, he possessed the capacity to attain realization upon a single hearing;

meeting Huang’an, he wondrously entered the pinnacle of the perfect fusion of the Three Truths. He opened the profound gate and penetrated the abstruse meanings, so that his mind and hand acted in perfect harmony.
Like Wheelwright Bian chiseling a wheel—setting aside rules and categories, sweeping away difficulties and doubts, severing intention and transcending words; resembling the wall-gazing at Shaolin;
expounding the *Jinbi*; rolling a round stone down a cliff of a thousand fathoms; responding to the official decree and rousing the dragon from its hibernation in the ninefold abyss.

In five assemblies he propagated the Great Teaching; from his breast flowed forth waves of wisdom. With single-minded resolve he governed toward the Great Peace, transforming rubble into gold and azure brilliance.
Having entered the Gate of Prajñā, he obtained a tree of a hundred-foot girth, truly intending to serve as a beam for a vast hall.

From the Northern Ocean he stirred winds of ninety thousand *li*, yet who would have thought his wings reaching to the heavens would be broken? His writings and studies were as abundant as a harvest of grain; these are what remain to be bequeathed.

His later descendants have preserved his legacy; the verification of this is evident even today. This is what is meant by saying that the Patriarch of the Cypress Court (Baiting) excelled in upholding his family tradition.
His majestic bearing was so stern that those who beheld him felt their worldly thoughts dissolve, and those who looked up to him lost all sense of their own existence.

Eulogy for Elder Huazhu (Real name Lu; early in life he studied under Tiantai, later attended Master Si, and resided at Jingtu. In his later years, he returned to Guiyin Hermitage where he passed away).
Of noble lineage, he was a descendant of Tiansui; of pure reputation, he was as if a reincarnation of Ying’an. He exhausted the teachings, embodying the essence of Fulong;
he escaped from Chan, following the "stupidity" of Suzhou’s Master Si. Loving plum blossoms, his breast was as clear as ice and snow; he thatched a cottage among springs and rocks.

In pavilions and terraces, he sought inspiration through verse at West Lake’s artful compositions; as a host of fine character, he opened wide his Eastern Gate. Joyful in his reclusion, a hundred birds brought him flowers;
purifying the Pure Land, nine lotuses took the place of the womb. Beholding his remaining image, it is like the blossoms of jade groves and precious trees;
producing his descendant branches, they are the timber for carved beams and painted rafters. To compose this eulogy—is it not to paint too much?
The five colors of emptiness brighten the dust upon the clear mirror.
In praise of the National Master Qingling Sengshou, his countenance is ancient and his spirit is pure;
his temperament is harmonious and his nature is expansive. Using the uncalibrated "hemp-skin head," he blinded the orthodox Dharma-eye of Linji.
Burying the crane of Mount Jiao required no dust from the mundane world; binding the tiger of Fenggan took nothing more than a string of cash.
Eight strange, seven ridiculous, ten horses, nine in disorder—drive them into the ranks of the herd of oxen, where they shall be viewed by people once every year.
A Minor Buddhist Service for Lady Lü, Wife of County Magistrate Lü.
As the rain ceases, the green mists thicken upon the plum branches; the lakes and mountains cluster together as the waters flow vast and deep. The face of one’s own birth remains unobstructed.
Obstruction. Though separated by ten thousand layers, the vision remains distinct and clear.
We reflect together upon the late [Name]: her virtue was as pure as jade within the domestic gates; her character was as refined as the breeze beneath the forest trees.

She was able to follow her father’s instructions, reading the "Book of the Azure Sky" by Chen Zi'ang; she never grew weary of reciting the lines of Lü Mengzheng from amidst the encampment of iron-horsed cavalry.

Though poor, he was single-minded in his devotion; he renounced gold for the sake of his beloved, and through diligent toil, he brought order to his household while remaining utterly free from worldly cravings.

His one daughter married a son-in-law as noble as a dragon, casting aside peacock-patterned cushions to dwell among lotus blossoms. His two sons raised grandsons like soaring phoenixes, perching securely on lofty catalpa trees and standing firm amidst refined jade.
Among his kinsmen, he was universally praised for his benevolence and beauty; his harmonious spirit permeated all who encountered him. Thus he remained steadfast in his solitude.

A widow, cherishing purity and integrity, her resolve as stern as autumn frost. Filled with hope that she would plant the "forget-sorrow" grass in the northern hall, how could she have expected to conceive a lotus of the highest grade from the West?
The sound of the jade flute has ceased; the crane-chariot soars away. The precious mirror is veiled in dust; the phoenix terrace lies desolate.
For seventy-two years, the dream of birth and death has been severed; through hundreds of billions of transformations, he manifests as a son.
The female aspect is forgotten. Although it is said that the path of departure is clear, one must receive direct instruction at the critical moment.
(Holding a torch, he draws a circle. Only when you see through this can you know: "When stillness reaches its ultimate, light penetrates everywhere;
silent illumination contains the void. Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream. Thus, Candrottarā dwells in accordance with Nirvāṇa. Together.
Their tracks differ, yet their paths are one. The Mother from East City was born together with all the Buddhas;
thus their paths are the same, though their tracks differ. At this very moment, tell me: from where does the final radiance of Lady Chen ultimately flare forth?
Do you understand? The twenty-four seasonal winds blow with urgency; standing, one watches the crimson flames cluster like ice flowers.
For the practitioner, dwell beneath the fire of intelligence;
let cleverness be cast away until one is like the blind or the deaf. When the time for transformation arrives, there is transformation.

A yellow plum beneath the ribs, a bottomless bowl—stupid and dazed, one is drunk on the spring breeze all day long. Private possessions are utterly exhausted; one is thoroughly impoverished at the brink of birth and death.
Look up with keen eyes! When the southern mountain burns, the northern mountain turns red.
Master Guānwēng of Yuělín has performed the rite of cremation, wondrously realizing the ultimate void.
Having resided within the inner court, his Way was personally transmitted by Maitreya; his fame reached Chángtīng and became even more manifest.
A single blow divides back and touch; this is the true mountain-dwelling elder. In three places he slays the dull and stubborn; it is the truly authentic "blow-off-hair" sword.

For over eighty years he has unfolded his transformative mechanism; the profound pivot of the thousand sages turns smoothly. Turning the body, one finds the way; the passions of birth and death are emptied.
Like refined gold tempered a hundred times, soft enough to bend around a finger, one must yet enter the fire to achieve complete mastery (Wukong received his training here).

To turn back the subordinate temple’s downward momentum and uphold the ancestral style of Gudong, I have shed several cold sweats. Although ginger may be sold at a high price, it does not lose its essential quality;
once its merit has been fully realized, what harm is there in a single death? True gold is malleable enough to bend between the fingers, yet it becomes even more resilient when entering the fire.
The yellow increases.
Acting as the assistant administrator for Chun, he lit the fire for him—Chun indeed, Chun!

He has passed away, leaving behind neither the distant nor the close. High above hangs the mirror of cause and effect; he was a man who sold ginger in his true colors. His life’s work is now utterly exhausted.
Submitting this confession at the moment of death, he swiftly cast down his sickle for harvesting grain; with the flash of lightning and the spark of a flint, he turned his body in laughter.

Having lived for fifty-eight years under Master Guofa, he understood causes and recognized effects. In the kitchen of Xiangji, he tasted every flavor; on Mount Ruiyan, he was ranked among the foremost.
It has been done. One must not seek the "breaking of the bowl" at Huangmei; look coldly as the wild geese pass through the vast sky.

In a flash, the vital mechanism is turned; the dead merchandise is overturned. In the eighth month, the wind is high and the wild fires are red; the horned iron snake is startled and burrows into the grass.

For the sake of Śuddhodana, the Fire Deity descended from above, joined his bowl, and filled it with fragrant rice; he then distributed portions to Vaiśālī, while clouds of fragrance issued from every pore.
Sweeping away a hundred ailments, it is polished and pure as new. In the coming and going of birth and death, there is no trace; it is like fire meeting fire or gold striking gold.
For the sake of the Chief Administrator Hong, I hold up this torch.

Yangqi’s dilapidated house lacks support; the three-legged donkey also stumbles along its path. Fortunately, the mountain elder extends his aged arm to open wide the gates and provide rest for weary lives.
The great achievement remains unrecorded, yet the confession of death is already complete. Refined gold tempered a hundred times bends to the finger;
it must yet enter the fire for further smelting.
Wei Fen managed the temple funds and held the torch (having previously served as the *zhisui*);

Bo Tu served as the *zhisui*. Si Ji managed the finances; regarding market profits, he did not seek monopolistic advantage. When reclaiming wasteland, his first priority was slash-and-burn cultivation.

He used a scale without stars to weigh even the smallest fraction (*zizhu*), never erring by so much as a hair’s breadth. With a broken hoe, he buried the Buddhas and Patriarchs—how deep? How shallow?
Without deviation, overturn the dead goods and establish a separate livelihood. The path of the mechanism is alive like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning;
nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky.
(The Master) directly addressed the Head of the Kitchen as he performed the cremation rite.
Lifting up the broken hoe, he opens the field to expound the Great Meaning. Should you hesitate, he digs a pit to bury you—who dares to obstruct the harmony of the breath?
His life’s journey is utterly spent; the eye of death is wide open. An iron snake with a head of snow comes darting into the midst of fire.
Master Shu, you who hold the torch, have skillfully turned the profound pivot;
you maintain the secret words with precision. Yet, though you may accord with the sentiments of both sages and ordinary folk, you still remain lost on the path of birth and death.
Even if the golden bell resonates as it soars into the void, this is not yet the Master’s phrase for arriving home. Take up the phrase for arriving home quickly! (With the torch...)
(He struck once and displayed the mudra, saying: "A swift flame passes through the wind; there is no place for you to settle, no place for you to set foot.

Although this practitioner has lived under my guidance and left the household life for over ten years, his body remains idle and at ease in the stable. The jade and stone have not yet been distinguished; the wind and the banner are difficult to discern."
Changing one's form, one finds the Way; the passions of birth and death are emptied. Amidst the flames, the lotus blooms; a fragrant breeze sweeps and scatters.
To kindle fire beneath the barbarian turban (gathering the assembly every month to recite the Buddha’s name)—one need not shamefully sing the *huqia* flute melody that disturbs others.
Skillfully threading the jade thread through the golden needle, one can fashion the clouds of Lu Zhi’s haughty spirit.
[The Master] said: "Excellent! You have well imitated Lin Zong’s ‘bent-horn’ cap; you wear your formal crown with such dignity that it commands the gaze of all who see you.

To have created this new style from the depths of your own mind is truly remarkable. Yet there is yet another extraordinary quality: you diligently recite the Buddha’s name every day, gathering your neighbors together. This is the crowning achievement of your life."
Gathering the causes through the nine grades, he ignited the fire of the Samādhi of the Emptiness of Nature. Upon a purple-golden dais, he spontaneously cremated his own body for Liu Lang.
Having entered Mount Tiantai with him in the same pit years ago, he traveled extensively through the grotto-heavens of the immortals before withdrawing halfway to return to purity.
The Realm welcomes those who carry the Purple-Gold Altar. Brothers yearn with longing; children grieve in sorrow.
Unable to bear the burying of the Jade Tree beneath hills and mountains, the years since the funeral have passed in a flash. Now that an auspicious day has been met, a fine arrangement is made.
With eyes wide open, one watches as the golden furnace melts; the autumn wind blows forth the precious lotus flower.

The kitchen steward Gui has tended the funeral pyre for over eighty years; he roams at will through the Land of Fragrant Accumulation, inspects the bundles of osmanthus blossoms, and bites through the kernels of the yellow plum.
He seasons the soup and boils the wooden slips to test the tongues of the monks; with hoe on shoulder, he enters the vegetable garden to behold the colors of the ancient path.
Sweeping away the techniques of death, one turns the pivot of the life-force. A swift flame passes through the wind, yet people do not perceive it; a fire-serpent’s head bears flying flakes of snow.
Arise, O bone!
The impure is the bamboo sieve; the pure is the wooden ladle. Picked up with the hand of faith, they are used with perfect efficacy. From dry bones, juice is pressed out;
the flavor is complete. From the skull, light is released; the eyes are round and lively—lively indeed! A spring breeze arises amidst the cassia branches;
the straw sandals break through, and the universe is vast.
For the interment of Lady Chen, Consort of the Meritorious Official [Name]:
The snow has cleared and a thousand peaks are draped in shimmering silver; the model of the Palace of Broad Cold has been renewed.

As the sound of the jade flute fades and she mounts her phoenix to depart, one suspects she is a traveler from the Immortal Realm returning with her banner lowered. We respectfully venerate you, [Name]: your heart dwells in kindness and joy, and your nature is endowed with compassion and benevolence.
A rainbow-like brilliance permeates her breast; she nurtures a vast and lofty spirit. A wind arises from beneath her robes; her elegant adornment radiates a refined vitality.

Woven with the patterns of martial valor and the threads of civil wisdom, she emerges as the most distinguished talent among eminent gentlemen of the sea. As pure as ice and as pristine as jade, she attains the integrity of a virtuous matron of the inner chambers.

She admires the Sage Confucius and follows his example in instructing her son at the courtyard gate; she emulates the mother of Tao Kan, cutting off her hair to entertain guests, and brings forth ten thousand...
Boats of *hu* capacity carried away all manner of rare treasures to the nets of Tang; a hall of a thousand bays provided great shelter for the cold scholars among Yao’s people.
From his youth, he applied himself with diligence to the study of books and history; in years of famine, he opened the state treasuries to relieve the orphaned and destitute.

When his daughter returned to her natal home, she was truly a phoenix appearing in person; when his son managed the household affairs, it was nothing other than the age of filial devotion. Within the family, the lutes and zithers were in perfect harmony.
In this chamber, the minor official of the corner [of the world] is humbled before his neighbors; side by side on the Golden Terrace of the Pure Land, he spreads the dawn of the nine lotuses.
Twin jade trees are buried in the auspicious city, melting the spring of ten thousand valleys. Having settled all affairs throughout his life, today he gathers the fruit of his causes.

Furthermore, having received the profound instruction of Ruiyan, he shall find a place to hide his body in the realm beyond yin and yang. (Name of Deceased), if you wish to know the ground beyond yin and yang—[it is here].
(Mo. (Pats the coffin and says: With its tiger-crouch and dragon-coil, the legacy of its shade extends afar; may the descendants enjoy longevity and prosperity like the pine and cypress.
For the burial of the stone residence (the late mother of General Ch’u), Heaven produced a stone woman, capturing the essence of the spirit.
She did not fail the name of the "Yao-tiao" of the *Guanju*; seventy-eight years of a lingering dream.

[Her] hair was cropped to emulate the will of Lady Fan Kan’s mother in entertaining guests; her loom was severed to promote the sentiment of Mencius’s mother in personally instructing her son. She was a model among the female class. *Po*: Wild plum blossoms shed tears that moisten the spring courtyard.

(Name of Person): Her domestic life was graced with refined excellence; her wifely virtue was as pure as ice. She cropped her hair to manifest the resolve of Lady Fan Kan’s mother in hosting guests; she severed her shuttle to emulate the affection of Mencius’s mother in teaching her son. A paragon among women.

Truly steadfast and pure, he served as a model for the ordination of monks; a peerless elder brother and younger sibling, his son-in-law was like one who rides the dragon, bringing joyous radiance to the family gate.

His son managed the household affairs, earning the harmonious acclaim of his clan. Having mastered the principles of domestic governance in his youth, he applied himself with devotion to the recitation of the Buddha's name in his later years.
Now that the five blessings are fully enjoyed and the retribution of this Jambudvīpa is complete, the nine lotuses shall blossom as the merit of his practice in the Pure Land is perfected.
Do not say that when the body is hidden there are no traces; the dragon coils and the tiger crouches to guard the auspicious tomb.
From beginning to end, one’s life is fulfilled. Since this is so, tell me: regarding the phrase "the blessings after interment protect descendants," how would you explain it?
(Striking the coffin, he says: "Shi Chong’s rivaling a state was not true wealth; only the jade pendants and golden cassock are truly glorious."

When he was serving as the kitchen steward (diànzuò), before his bones had even emerged from the mother’s womb, he roamed the Fragrant Accumulation (Xiāngjī) realm, exhausting all the responsive capacities (jī) before him. [It is said:
"This very thing remains as it was before; entering fire, it is not burned; falling into water, it is not destroyed. Like a pearl rolling on a plate, its shadow leaves no obstruction."
The Opening of the Coffin for Brother Jue of Japan (Venerable Jue):

Before his feet had even cleared the ship’s railing, he had already traveled throughout the Great Tang, visiting all the patriarchs. He clearly understood that what is awakened to is empty, yet he did not yet realize the principle of living and dying together.
(An inscription on the coffin reads: "If you see intimately here, there is another path to turn the body; the seas and mountains mark the way."
The azure is without layers.
Acting as a lay street-walker for the original community, he lost his ordination certificate;
barefoot, he ran through the red dust, casting his whole body into the wild weeds. His natal destiny and primal source were utterly lost; he overturned the ocean.
The peaks seek it in vain for its trace. (Holding a torch, he forms a circle with his hands and says: "What is this tiny star?
(The original street-walker assents: "It cannot be called fire."
Sealing the West Hall’s Shrine (for the one surnamed Song’an, the junior disciple of Tudu):
Having personally heard the sound of Tudu, he was not bound by the seal of Vairocana. Entering the weeds to seek out men, his affairs were already at rest;

he lay high upon his single hermitage amidst the shadows of pines and vines. The dream of birth and death is severed; the sentiments of ordinary and sage are empty. (Making a gesture of locking: The golden lock is profound.
There is yet another layer of the barrier:

for when the subtle essence enters the very marrow and the subtlety is exhausted, one relies on non-existence; without preserving reflective awareness, earth and ash merge, and the eyes within the skull come alive. Proceeding directly in this manner—this is it.
He digs a pit and buries it deep; the fragrant flowers of the entire courtyard lie in utter disarray.
For the sake of the senior monk Chang, he casts the iron caltrops of the reliquary chamber onto his face.
He shatters the barrier between life and death, leaving no trace. Though as precious as jade or ceremonial vessels, he treats them as worthless.
It resembles a speck of dust; when this whole mass is split open, it becomes a chaotic mess. Yet it is not chaotic: hook and lock, ring upon ring, it cannot be extracted even with a knife.

This is to reveal the mind of the Superior One’s nirvana and the meaning of birth and death. Manifestation and concealment are no different; the holy and the ordinary are of one essence. If you see this clearly, you can put it to use.
Master Qin burned away thorns and brambles for three thousand li.
For the sake of Master Zong, he locked the shrine (arriving briefly).

Zong’s eye was clear and his thieving mind died. Before even crossing the gate of Mount Ling, he had already realized the phrase of turning back. With a single flick of the pivot, he shifted the entire mechanism.
The faculties respond instantaneously; the barrier of emptiness locks the dream without deviation.
The ancient vessel enters the bones;
it cannot remain within Mount Damei. Before Little Flower Peak, it cannot be pushed away. Now, both going and staying are non-existent.
Relying on this, one clarifies the "live word" within immediate death; piercing through the skull and sweeping away the subtle path, the spiritual trace is not found where the monkeys cry.
Master Jiaoyu raises the bones.
Clouds gather upon the verdant peaks; the moon shines bright upon the azure pool. Entirely free from dust—what is there to bathe? To simply act thus is to be a corpse on level ground.
Not to act thus is to lose one's light before the skull. Before the pivot of the mind, there is a path as straight as a bowstring.
(Jiao the Bath Master, do you still know? Stepping out the door, it is all grass.

For Yunjing the attendant (the son of Zhou of Tiantai), ten thousand miles of white clouds, several pine trees—chanting the poems of Hanshan with a smile, he borrowed lodging at the house of a Zhou woman. A dead artifice.
Exhausted, his skeletal frame is revealed. (Zhiyun, Zhiyun! There is truly a place where you can take hold.
For the sake of West Hall Master Lin, he has established his coffin in the heart of the mountain;
though dead, he keeps the eye that penetrates all quarters open. Having found the path, he travels freely, utterly without fetters—the profound barrier of the thousand sages.
A misstep and all is overturned. The five-colored auspicious qilin strides upon the celestial shore.
For the sake of Elder Da, he raises his bones to return them for burial;
Da quiets his mind and returns to the source, far transcending the shore of birth and death. A spark from a flint loses its total function, yet the skull opens its living eyes.
He simply went on like this; never leaving the road, he concealed his body without a trace. His home is to the east of Haimen.

Having attained the profound essence of the Tiantai school through the repentance rites at Lingjiu Monastery and the locking of the meditation cell, the shadow of his turning the jewel-disk leaves no mark. Birth and death are but a casual play; concentration and wisdom are beyond dual cultivation.
Arriving here, what need is there to speak of Zhuang Zhou dreaming he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming it was Zhuang Zhou? All the sturdy locks are severed;
the clouds disperse, revealing an autumn sky.
For the sake of the Master of Xuehang, I lecture on the Dharma and perform the rite for his re-cremation and burial.

The lecture has ended; the feast of falling flowers is over. With dung-fire, they roast mountain yams, washing away all sentiments of sagehood and worldliness until their rugged, noble bones are revealed.
A single pivot is turned—dust is raised and earth is sifted. The traces of the spirit do not lie where the monkeys cry. Snow-boat, snow-boat! You must advance further still.

Descending from the Red Tree on Vulture Peak with the mountain apes, perching upon the clouds, ancient vines hang as they catch the moon. With a single swift flight, they let out three clear chants. Directly below, clinging and grasping cease;
the path of the mind of birth and death is cut off. No longer shall they wander among the various classes of beings. (Hurling the torch, he says: What harm is there in this mass of fire?
Meeting Shengre, one attains coolness;
entering the bones at Dayue Dongshan, one reaches the Qingliang tree of Linji.
Regarding the "Song of the Earthen Drum" of Dongshan: resting in the shade is small; listening for the resonance is vast.
The roots of death are severed; the eight tones of the rafters vanish. Bones and marrow are exchanged; what prevents one from rolling into the thicket of entanglements?
To sit atop the lamp is to enter the very bone.

The lamp of the awakened mind blazes forth, its brilliance soaring through past and present. Upon touching the dry skull, the thieving mind dies the moment it is pierced; yet within death there is life.
With head resting on Mount Heng and feet treading upon Mount Beiyue.

For the sake of the Head Seat Deng, I enter the stupa to light the lamp of the awakened mind. It blinds the eyes of men and gods; there is clarity within darkness, and there is darkness within clarity.
To overturn the paths of light and dark is still the act of a man playing with shadows and reflections. Ultimately, how is it? It shatters the skull, leaving no trace.
Traces. With one's back to the shady mountains and facing the many sunny peaks, the Venerable Jing has raised this clean and pure shrine, free from roots.
He must further refine it; he must directly pierce through the face given by his mother. (He pats the shrine. Break the mirror!
Come! Let us meet. When both discernment and awareness vanish, the eye of death opens; the foot-roots pull through the red thread.
Master Ying of Zishou performs the cremation (at thirty years of age, seated upon the Iron Ox).
[Name], for thirty years you have labored, refining your practice until it is crystalline. Your power has penetrated the mechanism of the Iron Ox, yet you have not yet stepped across the threshold.
At the mountain peak, he turned his body and found the path; thoroughly awakened, he shattered the hundred-fold barriers of birth and death.
Riding a jade elephant backward while walking through fire—because of this, the Lecturer personally inscribed the *Tiantai Kǒuyì* (Oral Exegesis of Tiantai) for interment in the stupa.
The Buddha’s eye-socket and Tiantai’s very marrow flow forth from his breast, covering heaven and earth.

This is neither a golden probe for scraping away cataracts nor a worn-out rag for wiping sores; it is the subtle and thorough appraisal of the three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment—a deep pit dug and buried, yet still emitting light.
To reach the state of "the old man entering the stupa" (infinite)—Truly reaching it without doubt:
the great void is vast and empty; the nature of both ordinary beings and sages is empty. Birth and death are like dreaming and waking.
Directly beneath, the two eyes within the skull are alive; where there is no place to rest, that is the fit place to rest.
For the old man of Xiangnan, the funeral pyre is lit:

having ceased his southern inquiries amidst the misty waters of a hundred cities, he returns to weave reed sandals to support his aged parents. His livelihood exhausted, he displays his final artifice;
the night rain over Xiao and Xiang truly brings sorrow to the heart. He overturns the path of mystery and penetrates deeply through the golden dust; there is no need to seek further.
Heat. (According to the *Taiju yun*: "Transforming fire to burn one's own body.
For the practitioner who dwells in the lower realm of fire, his age reached seventy-eight.
He realized the true wondrous secret of the kitchen; he concealed a sharp blade in his sleeve, coldly containing it within.
Frost. Finely sliced by the clear breeze, thinly spread by the bright moon. Skillfully cooked is the *mò* soup from the wooden shavings of Mount Dongshan.

Sour and crisp, without skin, it is all pure iron. Only when bitten through does one know the fullness of a hundred flavors. Having thoroughly tested the three-inch tongues of the patch-robed monks, yesterday morning he cast down his broken lead blade.
With a loose-hand throw, he goes forth; the path of the mind is cut off. The path of the mind is cut off. A fire-tortoise wears its head [aloft].
Snow. For Bin-dian, someone sat by the fire.
His character was rustic and his literary style was plain; it had nothing to do with your affairs. He boiled wood shavings for soup, ruining the salt and wasting the vinegar. Yesterday morning—
The art of dying is exhausted. Directly beneath, seek the path home. Seeking the path home, go straight ahead. Before every door is a torch;
this is for Ding the Attendant’s funeral pyre.
Tearing apart the rhinoceros fan, the seeker's wiles are exhausted. The Nāga is always in samādhi; stagnant water does not harbor dragons.

Turning over the path of life, the tracks of a thousand sages are lost. Pure gold refined a hundred times bends at the touch of a finger, yet it must still enter the fire to achieve its full perfection.

Encountering the guest master who descends the funeral pyre, the ancient and modern eyes rightly distinguish dragons from snakes. Meeting him suddenly, one simply drinks tea; when the means of livelihood are exhausted, one displays dead techniques.
Upon the head of the Fire Official, a windmill turns.
To manifest the signs of attaining the Way, he opened the light before Mount Zhengjue;
yet those who saw erroneously have been blind ever since, their vision unclear to this day. Without cause, they have brought blindness upon the eyes of others.
(With his brush, making the gesture of dotting: How could the Jade Milk not serve to provide the pupils?

He expounds the characteristics of dharmas and opens up the light of wisdom by preaching the five wheels entering the grass together; yet who would have known that black smoke rises from his own mouth?
To serve as eyes for others, he acts in such a manner (making a gesture with the brush as if marking a dot): he marks one blind man to lead the multitude of blind men.
Adorning with vajras; opening the light of wisdom, one falls among the ranks of Buddhas.
A ball of rotting mud wrapped in gold; standing tall, one establishes the "Gate-Wind.

Drawing forth iron from behind the head—this fully manifests the brilliance of literary patterns. This is already like placing grit in the eye. Remove the grit! (With the brush, making a dotting gesture: One.
